title: ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Memory capacity is a critical factor determining the performance of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in long-horizon manipulation tasks. Existing memory-augmented architectures primarily rely on linear or flat storage, lacking structural priors for manipulation categories and hierarchical organization. This deficiency hinders efficient experience retrieval and limits generalization to unseen long-horizon task compositions. Inspired by the hierarchical organization of human experience, we propose ECHO (Experience Consolidation and Hierarchical Organization), a novel memory framework operating within a Continuous Hierarchical Space. By employing a hyperbolic autoencoder, ECHO maps VLA hidden states into this space. Leveraging hyperbolic metrics and entailment constraint mechanisms, experience vectors are organized into a semantic memory tree that supports efficient top-down retrieval. In parallel, a background consolidation mechanism continuously refines the memory tree through geometric interpolation and structural splitting, supporting virtual memory synthesis in the continuous space. We integrate ECHO into the $π_0$ foundation model. Evaluations on LIBERO and preliminary real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, notably achieving a 12.8% absolute improvement in execution success rate over the $π_0$ baseline on LIBERO-Long, while improving compositional generalization on cross-suite unseen long-horizon tasks.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a memory framework using hyperbolic space to hierarchically organize VLA model experiences, improving long-horizon manipulation task performance by 12.8% over π₀ baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented VLA architectures use linear/flat storage lacking structural priors for manipulation categories and hierarchical organization, which limits efficient experience retrieval and generalization to unseen long-horizon task compositions.
AI.method: ECHO employs a hyperbolic autoencoder to map VLA hidden states into a Continuous Hierarchical Space, organizes experience vectors into a semantic memory tree using hyperbolic metrics and entailment constraints for top-down retrieval, and uses a background consolidation mechanism with geometric interpolation and structural splitting for virtual memory synthesis.
AI.result: Achieved 12.8% absolute improvement in execution success rate over π₀ baseline on LIBERO-Long and improved compositional generalization on cross-suite unseen long-horizon tasks.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical memory organization in hyperbolic space significantly enhances VLA model performance on long-horizon manipulation tasks and compositional generalization.

title: ForceFlow: Learning to Feel and Act via Contact-Driven Flow Matching
summary: Existing imitation learning methods enable robots to interact autonomously with the physical environment. However, contact-rich manipulation tasks remain a significant challenge due to complex contact dynamics that demand high-precision force feedback and control. Although recent efforts have attempted to integrate force/torque sensing into policies, how to build a simple yet effective framework that achieves robust generalization under multimodal observations remains an open question. In this paper, we propose ForceFlow, a force-aware reactive framework built upon flow matching. For contact-stage policy design, we investigate force signal fusion mechanisms and adopt an asymmetric multimodal fusion architecture that treats force as a global regulatory signal, combined with a joint prediction paradigm that enhances the policy's understanding of instantaneous force and historical information, thereby achieving deep coupling between force and motion. For task-level hierarchical decomposition, we divide manipulation into a vision-dominant approach stage (VLM-based pointing for target localization) and a touch-dominant interaction stage (force-driven contact execution), with a Vision-to-Force (V2F) handover mechanism that explicitly decouples spatial generalization from contact regulation. Experimental results across six real-world contact-rich tasks demonstrate that ForceFlow achieves a 37% success rate improvement over the strong baseline ForceVLA while maintaining significantly lower cost. Moreover, ForceFlow exhibits accurate force signal prediction and demonstrates superior performance in contact force self-regulation and zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.

AI.tldr: ForceFlow is a force-aware reactive framework using flow matching, asymmetric multimodal fusion, and a Vision-to-Force handover mechanism that improves success rate by 37% over ForceVLA on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation tasks remain challenging due to complex contact dynamics requiring high-precision force feedback and control; existing methods lack a simple yet effective framework for robust generalization under multimodal observations.
AI.method: ForceFlow uses (1) asymmetric multimodal fusion treating force as a global regulatory signal with joint prediction for deep force-motion coupling, and (2) task-level hierarchical decomposition with a Vision-to-Force (V2F) handover mechanism separating vision-dominant approach (VLM-based pointing) from touch-dominant interaction stages.
AI.result: 37% success rate improvement over ForceVLA across six real-world contact-rich tasks, with lower cost, accurate force signal prediction, superior contact force self-regulation, and zero-shot OOD generalization.
AI.conclusion: ForceFlow demonstrates that decoupling spatial generalization from contact regulation via asymmetric force fusion and hierarchical task decomposition yields robust and cost-effective force-aware manipulation policies.

title: SEVO: Semantic-Enhanced Virtual Observation for Robust VLA Manipulation via Active Illumination and Data-Centric Collection
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and imitation-learning policies trained via community toolchains on low-cost hardware frequently fail when deployed outside the training environment. Existing evaluations, including the original ACT and SmolVLA benchmarks, demonstrate high success rates under controlled, fixed backgrounds, yet community practitioners report near-zero transfer to new environments. We present SEVO (Semantic-Enhanced Virtual Observation), a data-centric approach that improves cross-environment manipulation robustness without modifying the policy architecture. SEVO transforms the raw RGB camera stream through three mechanisms: (1) body-fixed cameras whose combined fields of view cover the full manipulation workspace, (2) active red-spectrum illumination that physically normalizes object appearance, and (3) real-time YOLO segmentation overlay that provides a background-invariant semantic cue. Critically, we show that a diversified data collection protocol (systematically varying lighting, backgrounds, and distractors during teleoperation) is the single most important factor for generalization. We target transparent water bottles, objects that visually blend with their surroundings, and select a simple pick-and-place task to enable hundreds of controlled real-robot trials across two mobile platforms. The full pipeline achieves 95% grasp success with ACT and 83% with SmolVLA in the training environment, transferring to novel environments at 85% and 75%. Without SEVO, the same policies achieve only 75%/70% in training and collapse to 30-35% in novel environments. Our results demonstrate that principled observation design and environmental diversity during data collection, not model scaling, enable low-cost robots to operate reliably in everyday household environments.

AI.tldr: SEVO (Semantic-Enhanced Virtual Observation) is a data-centric approach combining body-fixed cameras, red-spectrum illumination, YOLO segmentation overlay, and diversified data collection to improve cross-environment manipulation robustness for VLA/imitation-learning policies. It achieves 95%/83% grasp success in training and 85%/75% in novel environments, compared to 75%/70% training and 30-35% transfer without SEVO.
AI.motivation: VLA and imitation-learning policies trained on low-cost hardware fail when deployed outside training environments. Despite high success rates reported in controlled benchmarks (ACT, SmolVLA), community practitioners observe near-zero transfer to new environments.
AI.method: SEVO transforms raw RGB camera stream via (1) body-fixed cameras covering full workspace, (2) active red-spectrum illumination to normalize object appearance, (3) real-time YOLO segmentation overlay providing background-invariant semantic cues. Additionally, a diversified data collection protocol systematically varies lighting, backgrounds, and distractors during teleoperation.
AI.result: SEVO with ACT achieves 95% grasp success in training and 85% in novel environments; with SmolVLA achieves 83% in training and 75% in novel environments. Without SEVO, same policies achieve 75%/70% in training and collapse to 30-35% in novel environments.
AI.conclusion: Principled observation design and environmental diversity during data collection, not model scaling, enable low-cost robots to operate reliably in everyday household environments.

title: ASIP-Planner: Adaptive Planning for UAV Surface Inspection in Partially Known Indoor Environments
summary: Indoor infrastructure inspection, such as tunnels and industrial facilities, requires systematic surface coverage to ensure that all inspection targets are properly observed. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer an alternative to manual inspection by conducting map-guided surface inspection using prior structural models. However, in practice, indoor inspection often relies on floorplan-derived reference maps that may not reflect unforeseen obstacles, such as temporary structures or equipment, leading to occluded viewpoints and degraded inspection quality. Existing coverage planning methods typically assume a fully known inspection environment and perform deterministic global viewpoint optimization based on accurate prior maps, making them vulnerable to environmental discrepancies during execution. This work presents an adaptive UAV inspection framework for partially known structured indoor environments. The proposed method integrates a segment-based global coverage planner with an inspection-oriented local view-angle adaptation module. The global planner organizes planar inspection targets into surface-aligned clusters to generate compact viewpoint sequences with improved orientation consistency. The local planner generates collision-free trajectories and adjusts the viewing direction online to mitigate occlusion-induced coverage loss while preserving the planned trajectory structure. The simulation results across randomized scene configurations demonstrate that the proposed global planner achieves near-complete coverage while reducing trajectory length compared to representative baselines. Real-world flight experiments further validate that the framework produces usable inspection data for downstream analysis. These results indicate that the proposed framework improves inspection efficiency and adaptability in partially known structured indoor environments.

AI.tldr: An adaptive UAV inspection framework for partially known structured indoor environments that integrates a segment-based global coverage planner with an inspection-oriented local view-angle adaptation module to handle unforeseen obstacles and occlusions.
AI.motivation: Indoor infrastructure inspection using UAVs relies on floorplan-derived maps that often fail to reflect temporary structures or equipment, leading to occluded viewpoints and degraded inspection quality. Existing coverage planning methods assume fully known environments and perform deterministic global optimization, making them vulnerable to environmental discrepancies during execution.
AI.method: Proposes an adaptive framework combining (1) a segment-based global coverage planner that organizes planar inspection targets into surface-aligned clusters for compact viewpoint sequences with orientation consistency, and (2) a local view-angle adaptation module that generates collision-free trajectories and adjusts viewing direction online to mitigate occlusion-induced coverage loss while preserving planned trajectory structure.
AI.result: Simulation results across randomized scene configurations show near-complete coverage with reduced trajectory length compared to baselines. Real-world flight experiments validate that the framework produces usable inspection data for downstream analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework improves inspection efficiency and adaptability in partially known structured indoor environments.

title: A Cascaded Generative Approach for e-Commerce Recommendations
summary: Personalized storefronts in large e-commerce marketplaces are often assembled from many independent components: static themes per page section ("placement"), retrieval systems to fetch eligible products per placement, and pointwise rankers to order content. While effective in optimizing for aggregate preferences, this paradigm is rigid and can limit personalization and semantic cohesion across the page. This makes it poorly suited to support dynamic objectives and merchandising requirements over time. To address this, we introduce a cascaded merchandising framework that decomposes storefront construction into two generative tasks: (i) placement-level theme generation and (ii) constrained keyword generation per placement to power product retrieval. Teacher-student fine-tuning is leveraged to improve scalability of this framework under production latency and cost constraints. Fine-tuned model ablations are shown to approach closed-weight LLM performance. We further contribute frameworks for AI-driven content evaluation and quality filtering, enabling safe and automated deployment of dynamic content at scale. Generative output is fused with traditional ranking models to preserve hybrid infrastructure. In online experiments, this framework yields an estimated +2.7% lift in cart adds per page view over a strong baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cascaded merchandising framework that decomposes storefront construction into placement-level theme generation and constrained keyword generation, using teacher-student fine-tuning for scalability, and achieves +2.7% lift in cart adds per page view.
AI.motivation: Traditional personalized storefronts are assembled from independent components (static themes, retrieval systems, pointwise rankers), which limits personalization, semantic cohesion across the page, and adaptability to dynamic objectives and merchandising requirements over time.
AI.method: A cascaded merchandising framework with two generative tasks: (i) placement-level theme generation and (ii) constrained keyword generation per placement for product retrieval. Teacher-student fine-tuning improves scalability under production constraints. AI-driven content evaluation and quality filtering enable safe automated deployment, and generative output is fused with traditional ranking models.
AI.result: Fine-tuned model ablations approach closed-weight LLM performance. Online experiments show an estimated +2.7% lift in cart adds per page view over a strong baseline.
AI.conclusion: The cascaded generative framework improves personalization, semantic cohesion, and adaptability while maintaining hybrid infrastructure with traditional ranking, enabling safe and automated deployment of dynamic content at scale.

title: Forecast-aware Gaussian Splatting for Predictive 3D Representation in Language-Guided Pick-and-Place Manipulation
summary:
We introduce Forecast-aware Gaussian Splatting (Forecast-GS), a predictive 3D representation framework for language-conditioned robotic manipulation. While recent manipulation systems have made progress by grounding language instructions into robot affordances, value maps, or relational keypoint constraints, they usually reason over the current scene and do not explicitly model the task-completed state. This limitation is critical when success depends on satisfying spatial and semantic goals under partial observations, where the robot must evaluate whether a candidate action leads to a feasible task-consistent outcome.
  We validate Forecast-GS on real-world pick-and-place manipulation tasks, including Cutter-to-Box, Apple-to-Bowl, and Sponge-to-Tray. For each task, we conduct 25 real-world trials under varied initial object configurations using the same robot platform and sensing setup. Forecast-GS with automatic candidate selection achieves success rates of 21/25, 23/25, and 16/25 on the three tasks, respectively, outperforming the ReKep baseline, which achieves 15/25, 19/25, and 10/25. A diagnostic human-assisted setting further improves success rates to 23/25, 24/25, and 19/25, suggesting that candidate generation is effective while automatic ranking remains imperfect. These results suggest that explicitly forecasting task-completed 3D states enables more reliable action evaluation, while the gap between automatic and human-assisted selection indicates that robust final-state ranking remains an important challenge for fully autonomous manipulation. Overall, Forecast-GS provides an interpretable bridge between language understanding, 3D perception, and robotic manipulation planning.

AI.tldr: Forecast-GS is a predictive 3D representation framework that forecasts task-completed Gaussian splatting scenes from language instructions to improve robotic pick-and-place manipulation, outperforming baselines on real-world tasks while revealing challenges in automatic candidate ranking.
AI.motivation: Existing manipulation systems reason over the current scene without explicitly modeling the task-completed state, which is critical for evaluating whether candidate actions lead to feasible task-consistent outcomes under partial observations with spatial and semantic goals.
AI.method: Forecast-GS uses Gaussian Splatting to predict task-completed 3D scenes conditioned on language instructions, enabling action evaluation by comparing candidate actions against the forecasted final state. Tested with both automatic candidate selection and a human-assisted diagnostic setting.
AI.result: On three real-world tasks (Cutter-to-Box, Apple-to-Bowl, Sponge-to-Tray), Forecast-GS achieved 21/25, 23/25, 16/25 success rates with automatic selection, outperforming ReKep baseline (15/25, 19/25, 10/25). Human-assisted selection improved to 23/25, 24/25, 19/25.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly forecasting task-completed 3D states enables more reliable action evaluation for manipulation, but automatic final-state ranking remains an important challenge. Forecast-GS offers an interpretable bridge between language understanding, 3D perception, and manipulation planning.

title: EVOCHAMBER: Test-Time Co-evolution of Multi-Agent System at Individual, Team, and Population Scales
summary: We argue that multi-agent test-time evolution is not single-agent evolution replicated N times. A single-agent learner can only evolve its own context and memory. A multi-agent system additionally evolves who collaborates, how they collaborate, and how knowledge flows across the population. These components have no single-agent counterpart and can produce phenomena such as emergent specialization. Yet prior test-time methods either confine experiences to individual agents, forfeiting cross-agent learning, or broadcast symmetrically to all agents, erasing the specialization that makes collaboration valuable. We present EVOCHAMBER, a training-free framework that instantiates test-time evolution at three levels over a coevolving agent pool. At its core is CODREAM (Collaborative Dreaming), a post-task protocol triggered on team failure or disagreement, in which agents collaboratively reflect, distill insights, and route them asymmetrically from strong to weak agents on the failed niche, preserving specialization while filling knowledge gaps. Team-level operators assemble niche-conditioned teams and select collaboration structures online. Population-level lifecycle operators fork, merge, prune, and seed agents under performance pressure. On three heterogeneous task streams with Qwen3-8B, EVOCHAMBER reaches 63.9% on competition math, 75.7% on code, and 87.1% on multi-domain reasoning, outperforming the best baseline by 32% relative on math and confirming asymmetric cross-agent transfer as the primary driver in ablation. Starting from several identically initialized agents, four to five stable niche specialists spontaneously emerge, a structural signature of multi-agent evolution that no single-agent learner can express. See our code at: https://github.com/Mercury7353/EvoChamber

AI.tldr: EVOCHAMBER is a training-free multi-agent test-time evolution framework that enables asymmetric knowledge transfer across agents, outperforming baselines on math, code, and reasoning tasks. It introduces CODREAM for collaborative reflection after failures, team-level operators for niche-conditioned team assembly, and population-level lifecycle operators. Starting from identical agents, 4-5 niche specialists spontaneously emerge, a phenomenon unachievable by single-agent learners.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time methods either isolate experiences per agent (forfeiting cross-agent learning) or broadcast symmetrically to all agents (erasing specialization). The authors argue that multi-agent evolution is not simply single-agent evolution × N — it involves who collaborates, how collaboration happens, and how knowledge flows across the population, components with no single-agent counterpart.
AI.method: EVOCHAMBER operates at three levels: (1) CODREAM protocol — triggered on team failure or disagreement, agents collaboratively reflect, distill insights, and route them asymmetrically from strong to weak agents on the failed niche; (2) Team-level operators — assemble niche-conditioned teams and select collaboration structures online; (3) Population-level lifecycle operators — fork, merge, prune, and seed agents under performance pressure.
AI.result: On three heterogeneous task streams with Qwen3-8B: 63.9% on competition math, 75.7% on code, 87.1% on multi-domain reasoning, outperforming the best baseline by 32% relative on math. Asymmetric cross-agent transfer confirmed as the primary driver via ablation. Four to five stable niche specialists emerge from identical initializations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent test-time evolution enables emergent specialization and asymmetric knowledge transfer that single-agent learners cannot replicate. EVOCHAMBER demonstrates that training-free population-level dynamics can produce structured specialization and superior performance across diverse reasoning domains.

title: Distributed Pose Graph Optimization via Continuous Riemannian Dynamics
summary: We present a framework for distributed Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) by formulating the problem as a second-order continuous-time dynamical system evolving on Lie groups. By modeling pose variables as massive particles subject to damping, the equilibrium points of the resulting Riemannian dynamics coincide with first-order critical points of the original PGO problem. Using the governing damped Euler--Poincaré equations and a semi-implicit geometric integrator, we design an optimization algorithm that generalizes existing algorithms such as Riemannian gradient descent and Gauss--Newton. In multi-robot settings, we present a fully distributed and parallel method based on block-diagonal mass and damping matrices, where each robot solves an ordinary differential equation for its own poses with minimal communication overhead. Moreover, modeling both state and velocity enables principled neighbor prediction that significantly improves convergence under delayed communication. Theoretically, we present an analysis and establish sufficient condition that ensures energy dissipation under the employed geometric discretization scheme. Experiments on benchmark PGO datasets demonstrate that the proposed solver achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art distributed baselines in both synchronous and asynchronous regimes.

title: RankQ: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning via Self-Supervised Action Ranking
summary: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) improves sample efficiency by leveraging pre-collected datasets prior to online interaction. A key challenge, however, is learning an accurate critic in large state--action spaces with limited dataset coverage. To mitigate harmful updates from value overestimation, prior methods impose pessimism by down-weighting out-of-distribution (OOD) actions relative to dataset actions. While effective, this essentially acts as a behavior cloning anchor and can hinder downstream online policy improvement when dataset actions are suboptimal. We propose RankQ, an offline-to-online Q-learning objective that augments temporal-difference learning with a self-supervised multi-term ranking loss to enforce structured action ordering. By learning relative action preferences rather than uniformly penalizing unseen actions, RankQ shapes the Q-function such that action gradients are directed toward higher-quality behaviors. Across sparse reward D4RL benchmarks, RankQ achieves performance competitive with or superior to seven prior methods. In vision-based robot learning, RankQ enables effective offline-to-online fine-tuning of a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model in a low-data regime, achieving on average a 42.7% higher simulation success rate than the next best method. In a high-data setting, RankQ improves simulation performance by 13.7% over the next best method and achieves strong sim-to-real transfer, increasing real-world cube stacking success from 43.1% to 84.7% relative to the VLA's initial performance.

AI.tldr: RankQ introduces a self-supervised multi-term ranking loss that enforces structured action ordering in Q-learning, enabling more effective offline-to-online RL by guiding action gradients toward higher-quality behaviors instead of uniformly penalizing OOD actions.
AI.motivation: Offline-to-online RL faces the challenge of learning accurate critics in large state-action spaces with limited dataset coverage. Prior methods use pessimism by down-weighting OOD actions, but this acts as a behavior cloning anchor that hinders downstream online policy improvement when dataset actions are suboptimal.
AI.method: RankQ augments temporal-difference learning with a self-supervised multi-term ranking loss to enforce structured action ordering. Instead of uniformly penalizing unseen actions, it learns relative action preferences so that Q-function gradients direct policies toward higher-quality behaviors.
AI.result: Competitive or superior to seven prior methods on sparse reward D4RL benchmarks. In vision-based robot learning, RankQ achieves 42.7% higher simulation success rate in low-data regime, 13.7% improvement in high-data regime, and increases real-world cube stacking success from 43.1% to 84.7% compared to the initial VLA performance.
AI.conclusion: RankQ effectively enables offline-to-online fine-tuning by learning structured action preferences via a ranking loss, outperforming prior methods that rely on uniform pessimism, and demonstrates strong sim-to-real transfer capabilities in robot learning.

title: Computational Design of a Low-Visibility UAV Using a Human-Aligned Perceptual Metric
summary: We introduce Phantom Twist, a type of single-propeller UAV designed to achieve low visibility through high-speed spinning and the exploitation of motion blur. We develop a two-stage automated design pipeline that optimizes the placement of functional components including batteries, control PCB, motor-propeller assembly, and counterweights. The pipeline minimizes visibility as measured by a human-aligned perceptual metric (LPIPS) while strictly satisfying inertial and aerodynamic constraints required for stable flight. We validate this approach through fabrication and flight testing of multiple prototypes. These tests confirm that our pipeline produces stable, controllable designs and that the optimized UAV exhibits significantly reduced visual perceptibility compared to conventional quadcopters.

AI.tldr: Introduces Phantom Twist, a single-propeller UAV optimized for low visibility via high-speed spinning and motion blur, using a two-stage design pipeline that balances perceptual invisibility (LPIPS) with flight stability constraints, validated through flight tests showing reduced perceptibility vs. quadcopters.
AI.motivation: To design a UAV with low visual perceptibility (stealth) by exploiting motion blur from high-speed spinning, moving beyond conventional multi-rotor designs that are easily visible.
AI.method: A two-stage automated design pipeline that optimizes placement of functional components (batteries, PCB, motor-propeller, counterweights) to minimize LPIPS (a human-aligned perceptual metric) while satisfying inertial and aerodynamic stability constraints.
AI.result: Fabricated and flight-tested multiple prototypes; the optimized Phantom Twist design is stable, controllable, and exhibits significantly lower visual perceptibility compared to conventional quadcopters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed single-propeller spinning UAV design, guided by perception-aware optimization, is a viable approach for achieving low-visibility flight without sacrificing stability or controllability.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
summary: Large language model agents interleave reasoning, action selection, and observation to solve sequential decision-making tasks. In deployed settings where agents repeatedly handle related multi-step tasks, small action-selection errors can accumulate into wasted tool calls, latency, and reduced reliability. Despite this need for deployment-time improvement, existing inference-time adaptation methods for LLM agents mainly rely on prompting or retrieval, which influence behavior indirectly through context manipulation. For ReAct-style agents, such approaches do not expose an explicit decision layer that can score candidate actions, represent uncertainty, or be updated online from action-level feedback. As a result, they provide limited support for trackable, fine-grained, and uncertainty-aware adaptation during deployment. We propose OLIVIA, an inference-time action adaptation framework for ReAct-style agents. OLIVIA models the LLM's final action-selection layer as a contextual linear bandit over candidate actions, with frozen hidden states as decision contexts. This choice is particularly suitable for deployment because it adapts behavior directly at the action-selection interface, preserves the underlying reasoning process, and provides explicit uncertainty estimates and lightweight online updates from action-level feedback. With upper-confidence-bound exploration, OLIVIA improves the policy sample-efficiently with minimal computational overhead. We instantiate OLIVIA on four benchmarks and show that it consistently improves task performance over static ReAct and prompt-based inference-time baselines. Our results suggest that explicit online decision layers provide an effective alternative to purely prompt- or retrieval-based adaptation for LLM agents during deployment.

AI.tldr: OLIVIA is an inference-time action adaptation framework for ReAct-style LLM agents that models the final action-selection layer as a contextual linear bandit, enabling online updates, uncertainty estimation, and sample-efficient policy improvement with minimal overhead, consistently outperforming static ReAct and prompt-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing inference-time adaptation methods for LLM agents (prompting, retrieval) influence behavior indirectly without an explicit decision layer that can score actions, represent uncertainty, or be updated online from action-level feedback, leading to accumulated errors, wasted tool calls, latency, and reduced reliability in deployed multi-step settings.
AI.method: OLIVIA treats the LLM's final action-selection layer as a contextual linear bandit over candidate actions, using frozen hidden states as decision contexts. It applies upper-confidence-bound (UCB) exploration for sample-efficient improvement and lightweight online updates from action-level feedback, all while preserving the underlying reasoning process.
AI.result: OLIVIA consistently improves task performance over static ReAct and prompt-based inference-time baselines across four benchmarks, with minimal computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Explicit online decision layers, such as the contextual bandit approach used in OLIVIA, provide an effective alternative to purely prompt- or retrieval-based adaptation for LLM agents during deployment, offering trackable, fine-grained, and uncertainty-aware adaptation.

title: Kairos: A Scalable Serving System for Physical AI
summary: Physical AI is experiencing rapid growth with frontier foundation models increasing its capabilities across general environments. Physical AI tasks are characterized by inference properties that are markedly different from digital AI. They consist of multiple rounds of inference and action execution, generating a chunk of actions in each inference round, and asynchronously interleaving inference and execution. This makes existing digital AI serving systems unsuited for physical AI; a shortcoming that is critical for enabling their wide adoption, considering their size and the scale of the robot fleets they have to serve. To fill this gap, we design Kairos, the first multi-robot serving system that makes the generate-execute loop a first-class citizen, with active involvement in the execution phase. Across a wide range of physical AI models and robots, Kairos reduces the average end-to-end task latency by 31.8--66.5% over state-of-the-art digital AI serving practices, with gains scaling with the robot fleet size.

AI.tldr: Kairos is the first multi-robot serving system designed for Physical AI that treats the generate-execute loop as a first-class citizen, reducing end-to-end task latency by 31.8–66.5% compared to traditional digital AI serving systems.
AI.motivation: Physical AI tasks have fundamentally different inference properties (multi-round, chunked actions, asynchronous interleaving) than digital AI, making existing serving systems unsuitable. This gap is critical to address for wide adoption of Physical AI given model sizes and robot fleet scales.
AI.method: Designs Kairos, a multi-robot serving system that makes the generate-execute loop a first-class citizen with active participation in the execution phase, unlike traditional digital AI serving systems.
AI.result: Reduces average end-to-end task latency by 31.8–66.5% over state-of-the-art digital AI serving practices, with gains scaling with robot fleet size.
AI.conclusion: Physical AI serving requires fundamentally different system design from digital AI, and explicitly incorporating the generate-execute loop into the serving architecture yields substantial latency improvements that grow with fleet scale.

title: The Many Faces of On-Policy Distillation: Pitfalls, Mechanisms, and Fixes
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) have emerged as promising post-training methods for large language models, offering dense token-level supervision on trajectories sampled from the model's own policy. However, existing results on their effectiveness remain mixed: while OP(S)D has shown promise in system prompt and knowledge internalization, recent studies also report instability and degradation. In this work, we present a comprehensive empirical study of when OPD and OPSD work, when they fail, and why. We find that OPD on mathematical reasoning is highly sensitive to teacher choice and loss formulation, whereas OPSD fails in our tested settings due to test-time absence of instance-specific privileged information (PI). In contrast, OPSD is effective when PI represents a shared latent rule, such as a system prompt or alignment preference. We identify three failure mechanisms: (1) distribution mismatch between teacher and student caused by conditioning on student-generated prefixes, (2) optimization instability from biased TopK reverse-KL gradients, and (3) an OPSD-specific limitation where the student learns a PI-free policy that aggregates PI-conditioned teachers, which is insufficient when PI is instance-specific. We further show that stop-gradient TopK objectives, RLVR-adapted teachers, and SFT-stabilized students mitigate these failures.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies when on-policy distillation (OPD) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) work or fail for LLMs, identifying three key failure mechanisms: distribution mismatch, optimization instability from TopK reverse-KL, and OPSD's inability to handle instance-specific privileged information. The authors propose mitigation strategies including stop-gradient TopK objectives, RLVR-adapted teachers, and SFT-stabilized students.
AI.motivation: Despite the promise of OPD and OPSD for post-training LLMs via dense token-level supervision, existing results are mixed with reports of instability and degradation. This work aims to resolve the confusion by systematically investigating when these methods succeed, when they fail, and the underlying reasons.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive empirical study analyzing OPD and OPSD on mathematical reasoning tasks. They investigate sensitivity to teacher choice and loss formulation, and identify three specific failure mechanisms: (1) distribution mismatch from conditioning on student-generated prefixes, (2) optimization instability from biased TopK reverse-KL gradients, and (3) OPSD-specific limitation where the student learns a PI-free policy insufficient for instance-specific privileged information. They also propose and evaluate mitigation strategies.
AI.result: OPD on math reasoning is highly sensitive to teacher choice and loss formulation. OPSD fails when privileged information is instance-specific but works when PI represents a shared latent rule (e.g., system prompt). The three identified failure mechanisms are confirmed, and proposed mitigations (stop-gradient TopK, RLVR-adapted teachers, SFT-stabilized students) help alleviate these failures.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of OPD and OPSD depends critically on the nature of privileged information and training setup. OPSD is only suitable when PI is shared across instances, not instance-specific. The identified failure mechanisms and proposed mitigations provide practical guidance for deploying these distillation methods in LLM post-training.

title: Overcoming Dynamics-Blindness: Training-Free Pace-and-Path Correction for VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve remarkable flexibility and generalization beyond classical control paradigms. However, most prevailing VLAs are trained under a single-frame observation paradigm, which leaves them structurally blind to temporal dynamics. Consequently, these models degrade severely in non-stationary scenarios, even when trained or finetuned on dynamic datasets. Existing approaches either require expensive retraining or suffer from latency bottlenecks and poor temporal consistency across action chunks. We propose Pace-and-Path Correction, a training-free, closed-form inference-time operator that wraps any chunked-action VLA. From a single quadratic cost, joint minimization yields a unified solution that decomposes orthogonally into two distinct channels. The pace channel compresses execution along the planned direction, while the path channel applies an orthogonal spatial offset, jointly absorbing the perceived dynamics within the chunk window. We evaluate our approach on a comprehensive diagnostic benchmark MoveBench designed to isolate motion as the sole controlled variable. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free wrappers and dynamic-adaptive methods and improves success rates by up to 28.8% and 25.9% in absolute terms over foundational VLA models in dynamic-only and static-dynamic mixed environments, respectively.

AI.tldr: Pace-and-Path Correction (PPC) is a training-free, closed-form inference-time operator for VLA models that decomposes action correction into pace (along-plan) and path (orthogonal offset) channels, significantly improving performance in dynamic environments.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models are trained under single-frame observation paradigms, making them blind to temporal dynamics and causing severe degradation in non-stationary scenarios. Existing fixes require expensive retraining or suffer from latency bottlenecks and poor temporal consistency.
AI.method: Proposes Pace-and-Path Correction, a training-free closed-form inference-time operator that wraps any chunked-action VLA. From a single quadratic cost minimization, it orthogonally decomposes into pace channel (compresses execution along planned direction) and path channel (applies orthogonal spatial offset) to absorb perceived dynamics within the chunk window.
AI.result: On the MoveBench diagnostic benchmark, PPC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free wrappers and dynamic-adaptive methods, improving success rates by up to 28.8% (dynamic-only) and 25.9% (static-dynamic mixed) over foundational VLA models.
AI.conclusion: A simple, training-free inference-time correction mechanism can effectively compensate for VLA models' blindness to temporal dynamics, offering substantial gains without retraining overhead.

title: Don't Look at the Numbers: Visual Anchoring Bias and Layer-wise Representation in VLMs
summary: Embedded numeric anchors on images systematically bias Vision-Language Model quality judgments across six VLMs from five architectural families (ANOVA eta^2 = 0.18-0.77, all p < 0.001). Anchor effects are 2.5x larger than severe image quality degradation, confirming bias is not reducible to visual changes. Layer-wise probing reveals consistent dissociation: layers where anchor classification saturates (L12-L34) are suboptimal for quality prediction, with optimal layers deeper (R^2 = 0.69-0.91). Fusion analysis identifies architecture-dependent integration -- instant fusion at L1-L2 in two models versus partial or no fusion in three others. These results establish a causal account of visual anchoring bias, linking behavioral susceptibility to representation dynamics.

AI.tldr: Embedded numeric anchors on images bias VLM quality judgments more than severe quality degradation, with anchor effects 2.5x larger. Layer-wise probing shows dissociation between anchor classification and quality prediction layers. Fusion analysis reveals architecture-dependent integration patterns.
AI.motivation: To establish a causal account of visual anchoring bias in Vision-Language Models by systematically linking behavioral susceptibility to internal representation dynamics.
AI.method: Six VLMs from five architectural families were tested. ANOVA measured anchor effects (eta^2=0.18-0.77). Layer-wise probing identified optimal layers for quality prediction (R^2=0.69-0.91). Fusion analysis examined how early (L1-L2) integration occurs across architectures.
AI.result: Anchor effects are 2.5x larger than severe image quality degradation. Anchor classification saturates at L12-L34, while optimal quality prediction layers are deeper. Instant fusion at L1-L2 occurs in two models, partial/no fusion in three others.
AI.conclusion: Visual anchoring bias has a causal explanation grounded in representation dynamics, with architecture-dependent integration patterns and layer-specific dissociation between anchor processing and quality prediction.

title: Offline Policy Evaluation for Manipulation Policies via Discounted Liveness Formulation
summary: Policy evaluation is a fundamental component of the development and deployment pipeline for robotic policies. In modern manipulation systems, this problem is particularly challenging: rewards are often sparse, task progression of evaluation rollouts are often non-monotonic as the policies exhibit recovery behaviors, and evaluation rollouts are necessarily of finite length. This finite length introduces truncation bias, breaking the infinite-horizon assumptions underlying standard methods relying on Bellman equations/principle of optimality. In this work, we propose a framework for offline policy evaluation from sparse rewards based on a liveness-based Bellman operator. Our formulation interprets policy evaluation as a task-completion problem and yields a conservative fixed-point value function that is robust to finite-horizon truncation. We analyze the theoretical properties of the proposed operator, including contraction guarantees, and show how it encodes task progression while mitigating truncation bias. We evaluate our method on two simulated manipulation tasks using both a Vision-Language-Action model and a diffusion policy, and a cloth folding task using human demonstrations. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach more accurately reflects task progress and substantially reduces truncation bias, outperforming classical baselines such as TD(0) and Monte Carlo policy evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a liveness-based Bellman operator for offline policy evaluation in robotic manipulation that handles sparse rewards and finite-horizon truncation bias, outperforming TD(0) and Monte Carlo methods.
AI.motivation: Policy evaluation in robotic manipulation is challenged by sparse rewards, non-monotonic task progression due to recovery behaviors, and finite-length rollouts that introduce truncation bias, breaking infinite-horizon assumptions of standard methods like Bellman equations.
AI.method: Formulates policy evaluation as a task-completion problem using a liveness-based Bellman operator, yielding a conservative fixed-point value function robust to finite-horizon truncation, with theoretical contraction guarantees.
AI.result: Evaluated on simulated manipulation tasks (Vision-Language-Action model, diffusion policy) and a real cloth folding task with human demonstrations; the approach reduces truncation bias and reflects task progress more accurately than TD(0) and Monte Carlo baselines.
AI.conclusion: The liveness-based Bellman operator provides a principled and effective offline policy evaluation framework for robotic manipulation under sparse rewards and finite-horizon settings.

title: Do Vision-Language-Models show human-like logical problem-solving capability in point and click puzzle games?
summary: Vision-Language(-Action) Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied to interactive environments, yet existing benchmarks often overlook the complex physical reasoning required for point-and-click puzzle games. This paper introduces Vision-Language Against The Incredible Machine (VLATIM), a benchmark designed to evaluate human-like logical problem-solving capabilities within the classic physics puzzle game The Incredible Machine 2 (TIM). Unlike existing benchmarks, VLATIM specifically targets the critical gap between high-level logical reasoning and continuous action spaces requiring precise mouse interactions. This benchmark is structured into five progressive parts, assessing capabilities that range from basic visual grounding and domain understanding to multi-step manipulation and full puzzle solving. Our results reveal a significant disparity between reasoning and execution. While large proprietary models demonstrate superior planning abilities, they struggle with precise visual grounding. Consequently, they do not yet show human-like problem-solving capabilities.

AI.tldr: VLATIM is a benchmark for evaluating VLM logical problem-solving in physics puzzle games, revealing a gap between high-level reasoning (strong in proprietary models) and precise visual grounding/execution (lacking in all models).
AI.motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks overlook complex physical reasoning required for point-and-click puzzle games, particularly the gap between high-level logical reasoning and continuous action spaces requiring precise mouse interactions.
AI.method: A benchmark structured into five progressive parts, assessing capabilities from basic visual grounding and domain understanding to multi-step manipulation and full puzzle solving within The Incredible Machine 2.
AI.result: Large proprietary models show superior planning abilities but struggle with precise visual grounding; no model achieves human-like problem-solving.
AI.conclusion: There is a significant disparity between reasoning and execution in current VLMs, highlighting the need for further work on integrating logical reasoning with precise interaction.

title: Coordinated Diffusion: Generating Multi-Agent Behavior Without Multi-Agent Demonstrations
summary: Imitation learning powered by generative models has proven effective for modeling complex single-agent behaviors. However, teaching multi-agent systems, like multiple arms or vehicles, to coordinate through imitation learning is hindered by a fundamental data bottleneck: as the joint state-action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, collecting a sufficient amount of coordinated multi-agent demonstrations becomes extremely costly. In this work, we ask: how can we leverage single-agent demonstration data to learn multi-agent policies? We present Coordinated Diffusion (CoDi), a framework that couples independently trained single-agent diffusion policies through a user-defined multi-agent cost function, without requiring any coordinated demonstrations. We derive a new diffusion-based sampling scheme wherein the diffusion score function decomposes into independent, single-agent pre-trained base policies plus a cost-driven guidance term that coordinates these base policies into cohesive multi-agent behavior. We show that this guidance term can be estimated in a gradient-free manner, making CoDi applicable to black-box, non-differentiable cost functions without additional training. Theoretically and empirically, we analyze the conditions under which this composition can faithfully approximate a target multi-agent behavior. We find a complementary role for demonstration data versus the cost function: single-agent demonstrations must cover the support of the desired multi-agent behavior, while the cost function must promote desired behavior from this product of single-agent policies. Our results in simulation and hardware experiments of a two-arm manipulation task show that CoDi discovers robust coordinated behavior from single-agent data, is more data-efficient than multi-agent baselines, and highlights the importance of joint guidance, base policy support, and cost design.

AI.tldr: Coordinated Diffusion (CoDi) couples independently trained single-agent diffusion policies via a cost-driven guidance term to achieve multi-agent coordination without requiring any multi-agent demonstration data.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent imitation learning suffers from a data bottleneck: the joint state-action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, making coordinated multi-agent demonstrations extremely costly to collect.
AI.method: CoDi decomposes the diffusion score function into independent single-agent pre-trained base policies plus a cost-driven guidance term that coordinates them. The guidance term is estimated in a gradient-free manner, enabling application to black-box, non-differentiable cost functions without additional training.
AI.result: Simulation and hardware experiments on a two-arm manipulation task show CoDi discovers robust coordinated behavior from single-agent data, is more data-efficient than multi-agent baselines, and demonstrates the importance of joint guidance, base policy support, and cost design.
AI.conclusion: Single-agent demonstrations and cost functions play complementary roles: single-agent data must cover the support of the desired multi-agent behavior, while the cost function must promote desired behavior from the product of single-agent policies.

title: PIVOT: Bridging Planning and Execution in LLM Agents via Trajectory Refinement
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents frequently generate seemingly coherent plans that fail upon execution due to infeasible actions, constraint violations, and compounding errors over extended horizons. PIVOT (Plan-Inspect-eVOlve Trajectories) addresses this plan-execution misalignment through a self-supervised framework that treats trajectories as optimizable objects iteratively refined via environment interaction. The framework comprises four stages: PLAN generates candidate trajectories; INSPECT executes them and computes structured losses with textual gradients encoding plan-execution discrepancies; EVOLVE applies these signals to produce improved trajectories; and VERIFY performs a final global check against task constraints. A monotonic acceptance process ensures a non-decreasing solution quality. Empirical evaluations on DeepPlanning and GAIA demonstrate state-of-the-art performance: with human-in-the-loop (HITL) feedback, PIVOT establishes a strong upper bound up to 94% relative improvement in constraint satisfaction, while its fully autonomous variant retains substantial gains, showing that the core trajectory-refinement mechanism remains effective without external supervision. At the same time, PIVOT remains computationally efficient, requiring up to 3x to 5x fewer tokens than competing refinement methods. These findings establish that (self- or human-supervised) feedback-based trajectory optimization is a principled methodology for mitigating plan-execution gaps in autonomous agent systems.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a self-supervised framework that iteratively refines agent trajectories through environment interaction, using structured losses and textual gradients to bridge plan-execution gaps, achieving state-of-the-art results on DeepPlanning and GAIA with up to 94% improvement in constraint satisfaction while using 3x-5x fewer tokens than competing methods.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents generate coherent plans that frequently fail during execution due to infeasible actions, constraint violations, and compounding errors over long horizons, creating a critical plan-execution misalignment problem.
AI.method: PIVOT (Plan-Inspect-eVOlve Trajectories) is a four-stage self-supervised framework: (1) PLAN generates candidate trajectories; (2) INSPECT executes them and computes structured losses with textual gradients encoding discrepancies; (3) EVOLVE applies these signals to produce improved trajectories; (4) VERIFY performs final global constraint checking. A monotonic acceptance process ensures non-decreasing solution quality.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results on DeepPlanning and GAIA benchmarks. With human-in-the-loop feedback, up to 94% relative improvement in constraint satisfaction. Fully autonomous variant retains substantial gains. Requires 3x-5x fewer tokens than competing refinement methods.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-based trajectory optimization (self- or human-supervised) is a principled methodology for mitigating plan-execution gaps in autonomous agent systems.

title: RIO: Flexible Real-Time Robot I/O for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Accepted to Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2026
summary: Despite recent efforts to collect multi-task, multi-embodiment datasets, to design recipes for training Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), and to showcase these models on different robot platforms, generalist cross-embodiment robot capabilities remains a largely elusive ideal. Progress is limited by fragmented infrastructure: most robot code is highly specific to the exact setup the user decided on, which adds major overhead when attempting to reuse, recycle, or share artifacts between users. We present RIO (Robot I/O), an open source Python framework that provides flexible, lightweight components for robot control, teleoperation, data formatting, sensor configuration, and policy deployment across diverse hardware platforms and morphologies. RIO provides abstractions that enable users to make any choice and to switch between them, with minimal reconfiguration effort. We validate RIO on VLA deployment workflows across three morphologies (single-arm, bimanual, humanoid) and four hardware platforms with varying grippers and cameras. Using teleoperated data collected with RIO, we fine-tune state-of-the-art VLAs including $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T on household tasks such as pick-and-place, folding, and bowl scrubbing. By open sourcing all our efforts, we hope the community can accelerate their pace of robot learning on real-world robot hardware. Additional details at: https://robot-i-o.github.io

AI.tldr: RIO is an open-source Python framework providing flexible, lightweight components for robot control, teleoperation, data formatting, sensor configuration, and policy deployment across diverse hardware platforms and morphologies, validated on VLA deployment workflows across three morphologies and four hardware platforms.
AI.motivation: Generalist cross-embodiment robot capabilities remain elusive due to fragmented infrastructure where most robot code is highly specific to exact user setups, adding major overhead when reusing or sharing artifacts between users.
AI.method: RIO provides abstractions that enable users to make any choice and switch between hardware components with minimal reconfiguration effort, validated across three morphologies (single-arm, bimanual, humanoid) and four hardware platforms with varying grippers and cameras. Teleoperated data collected with RIO was used to fine-tune state-of-the-art VLAs including π₀.₅ and GR00T.
AI.result: Successfully validated on VLA deployment workflows across three morphologies and four hardware platforms. Fine-tuned VLAs (π₀.₅ and GR00T) on household tasks including pick-and-place, folding, and bowl scrubbing using teleoperated data collected with RIO.
AI.conclusion: By open sourcing RIO, the authors hope the community can accelerate robot learning on real-world hardware by reducing infrastructure fragmentation and overhead.

title: The Semantic Training Gap: Ontology-Grounded Tool Architectures for Industrial AI Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based AI agents are increasingly deployed in manufacturing environments for analytics, quality management, and decision support. These agents demonstrate statistical fluency with domain terminology but lack grounded understanding of operational semantics -- the relational structure that connects equipment identifiers, process parameters, failure codes, and regulatory constraints within a specific production context. This paper identifies and formalizes the semantic training gap: a structural disconnect between how AI systems acquire domain vocabulary through training and how manufacturing operations define meaning through ontological relationships. We demonstrate that this gap causes operationally incorrect outputs even when model responses are linguistically precise, and that in multi-agent configurations it produces a compounding failure mode we term semantic drift. To close this gap, we present an architecture that embeds manufacturing ontology directly into the AI tool layer as a typed relational configuration, enforcing semantic constraints at runtime rather than relying on model training. The architecture is formalized as a three-operation interface contract -- resolve, contextualize, annotate -- with invariants enforced by an AIOps orchestration layer. In a controlled experiment across six industry configurations (72 tool invocations using Qwen3-32B), unconstrained tool parameters produced a 43% hallucination rate for domain identifiers; ontology-grounded parameters reduced this to 0%. We validate the approach through a digital twin analytics platform demonstrating that a single codebase with domain-specific ontology configurations eliminates tool-call hallucination and achieves cross-domain configurability without application code changes.

AI.tldr: LLM-based AI agents in manufacturing lack grounded understanding of operational semantics, causing semantic drift. An ontology-grounded architecture with resolve-contextualize-annotate interface eliminates tool-call hallucination (43%→0%) and enables cross-domain configurability without code changes.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in manufacturing show statistical fluency with domain terminology but lack grounded understanding of operational semantics (the relational structure connecting equipment IDs, process parameters, failure codes, and regulatory constraints). This semantic training gap causes operationally incorrect outputs despite linguistically precise responses, and produces compounding semantic drift in multi-agent configurations.
AI.method: An architecture embedding manufacturing ontology directly into the AI tool layer as a typed relational configuration, enforcing semantic constraints at runtime rather than relying on model training. Formalized as a three-operation interface contract (resolve, contextualize, annotate) with invariants enforced by an AIOps orchestration layer. Evaluated across six industry configurations (72 tool invocations using Qwen3-32B).
AI.result: Unconstrained tool parameters produced a 43% hallucination rate for domain identifiers; ontology-grounded parameters reduced this to 0%. A single codebase with domain-specific ontology configurations eliminated tool-call hallucination and achieved cross-domain configurability without application code changes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ontology-grounded architecture closes the semantic training gap by enforcing operational semantics at the tool layer, eliminating tool-call hallucination entirely and enabling portable, configurable AI agents across different manufacturing domains without code modification.

title: Sampling-Based Follow-the-Leader Motion Planning for Manipulator-Mounted Continuum Robots
summary: Follow-the-leader (FTL) motion exploits the unique morphology of continuum robots (CRs) to navigate confined spaces by having the body retrace the path of the tip. While extensively studied, existing FTL methods typically assume a fixed base or a single degree-of-freedom insertion mechanism, limiting their applicability to practical systems in which CRs are mounted on robotic manipulators with fully actuated SE(3) base pose. This paper presents a sampling-based motion planner for FTL motion of manipulator-mounted CRs that jointly considers robot configuration and base pose. The key idea is to decouple global shape search from base pose determination by computing the base pose through a closed-form geometric construction, thereby avoiding iterative optimization during online planning. The approach supports general forward models and enables efficient planning by shifting the majority of computation offline. We establish theoretical guarantees including resolution complete shape search and converging tip tracking throughout waypoint traversal and interpolation. Experiments on 120 simulated paths over 3 test classes demonstrate 0% tip error and 1.9% mean shape deviation (w.r.t. robot length) at 100% success rate. We validate the practicality of our approach on a 6-DOF tendon-driven CR mounted on a serial manipulator. Code and visualization available at https://continuumroboticslab.github.io/sb-ftl-cr-planner/.

AI.tldr: A sampling-based motion planner for follow-the-leader motion of continuum robots mounted on manipulators with SE(3) base pose, using offline-computed closed-form geometric construction to decouple shape search from base pose determination.
AI.motivation: Existing FTL methods assume fixed base or single-DOF insertion, limiting applicability to practical systems where CRs are mounted on robotic manipulators with fully actuated SE(3) base pose.
AI.method: Decouples global shape search from base pose determination by computing base pose through closed-form geometric construction, shifting computation offline. Supports general forward models with resolution-complete shape search and converging tip tracking.
AI.result: 120 simulated paths over 3 test classes: 0% tip error, 1.9% mean shape deviation, 100% success rate. Validated on a 6-DOF tendon-driven CR mounted on a serial manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables efficient FTL motion planning for manipulator-mounted CRs with theoretical guarantees and practical validation, avoiding iterative online optimization.

title: Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
summary: Autonomous science promises to augment scientific discovery, particularly in complex fields like biomedicine. However, this requires AI systems that can consistently generate novel and diverse solutions to open-ended problems. We evaluate LLMs on the task of open-ended solution generation and quantify their tendency to mode collapse into low-diversity generations. To mitigate this mode collapse, we introduce analogical reasoning (AR) as a new approach to solution generation. AR generates analogies to cross-domain problems based on shared relational structure, then uses those analogies to search for novel solutions. Compared to baselines, AR discovers significantly more diverse generations (improving solution diversity metrics by 90-173%), generates novel solutions over 50% of the time (compared to as little as 1.6% for baselines), and produces high-quality analogies. To validate the real-world feasibility of AR, we implement AR-generated solutions across four biomedical problems, yielding consistent quantitative gains. AR-generated approaches achieve a nearly 13-fold improvement on distributional metrics for perturbation effect prediction, outperform all baselines on AUPRC when predicting cell-cell communication, infer brain region interactions with a high Spearman correlation ($ρ$=0.729) to published methods, and establish state-of-the-art performance on 2 datasets for oligonucleotide property prediction. The novel and diverse solutions produced by AR can be used to augment the search space of existing solution generation methods.

AI.tldr: LLMs suffer from mode collapse in open-ended solution generation. The proposed analogical reasoning (AR) method uses cross-domain analogies to generate more diverse and novel solutions, achieving 90-173% improvement in diversity metrics and over 50% novel solution rate. AR was validated across four biomedical problems with significant quantitative gains, including a 13-fold improvement in perturbation effect prediction.
AI.motivation: Autonomous science requires AI systems capable of consistently generating novel and diverse solutions to open-ended problems, but current LLMs tend to mode collapse into low-diversity generations, limiting their utility for scientific discovery.
AI.method: Analogical Reasoning (AR) generates analogies to cross-domain problems based on shared relational structure, then uses those analogies to search for novel solutions, mitigating mode collapse in LLM-based solution generation.
AI.result: AR improves solution diversity metrics by 90-173%, generates novel solutions over 50% of the time (vs. as little as 1.6% for baselines), achieves 13-fold improvement in perturbation effect prediction, outperforms all baselines on AUPRC for cell-cell communication, infers brain region interactions with Spearman ρ=0.729, and sets state-of-the-art on 2 oligonucleotide property prediction datasets.
AI.conclusion: Analogical reasoning is an effective approach for generating novel and diverse solutions to open-ended biomedical problems, and can augment the search space of existing solution generation methods for autonomous science.

title: Nautilus: From One Prompt to Plug-and-Play Robot Learning
summary: Robot learning research is fragmented across policy families, benchmark suites, and real robots; each implementation is entangled with the others in a complex combination matrix, making it an engineering nightmare to port any single element. General-purpose coding agents may occasionally bridge specific setups, but cannot close this gap at scale because they lack the procedural priors and validation practices that characterize robotics research workflows. We propose NAUTILUS, an open-source harness that turns a single user prompt -- for example, "Evaluate policy A with benchmark B" -- into ready-to-use reproduction, evaluation, fine-tuning, and deployment workflows. NAUTILUS provides: plug-and-play agent skill sets with distilled priors from robotics research; typed contracts among policies, simulators/benchmarks, and real-world robots; unified interfaces and execution environments; and a trustworthy agentic coding workflow with explicit, automated validation, and testing at each milestone. NAUTILUS can not only automatically generate the required adapters and containers for existing implementations, but also wrap and onboard new or user-provided policies, simulators/benchmarks, and robots, all connected via a uniform interface. This expands cross-validation coverage without hand-written glue code. Like a nautilus shell that grows by adding chambers, NAUTILUS scales by extending its execution in chambered units, making it a research harness for scalability rather than a hand-curated framework, and aiming to reduce the engineering burden of cross-family reproduction and evaluation in the ever-growing robot learning ecosystem.

AI.tldr: NAUTILUS is an open-source harness that converts a single user prompt into reproduction, evaluation, fine-tuning, and deployment workflows for robot learning by providing plug-and-play agent skill sets, typed contracts, unified interfaces, and automated validation, reducing the engineering burden of cross-family porting.
AI.motivation: Robot learning research is fragmented across diverse policy families, benchmarks, and real robots, with implementations intricately entangled, making cross-setup porting an engineering nightmare that general-purpose coding agents cannot resolve at scale due to lack of procedural priors and validation practices specific to robotics.
AI.method: NAUTILUS implements: (1) plug-and-play agent skill sets with distilled robotics priors; (2) typed contracts among policies, simulators/benchmarks, and real robots; (3) unified interfaces and execution environments; (4) a trustworthy agentic coding workflow with automated validation and testing at each milestone; and (5) automatic generation of adapters/containers for existing implementations and onboarding of new components via uniform interface.
AI.result: NAUTILUS can automatically generate required adapters and containers, wrap and onboard new policies/simulators/robots, and expand cross-validation coverage without hand-written glue code, using a chambered unit architecture that scales like a nautilus shell.
AI.conclusion: NAUTILUS serves as a scalable research harness rather than a hand-curated framework, aiming to substantially reduce the engineering overhead of cross-family reproduction and evaluation in the growing robot learning ecosystem.

title: Template-as-Ontology: Configurable Synthetic Data Infrastructure for Cross-Domain Manufacturing AI Validation
summary: LLarge language model (LLM)-based AI agents deployed in manufacturing environments require populated, schema-correct data for validation, yet production MES data is proprietary, privacy-encumbered, and vendor-specific. This paper introduces the Template-as-Ontology principle: a single Python configuration module (700-770 lines, 45 validated exports) serves simultaneously as the specification for a time-stepped manufacturing simulator and as the runtime domain schema for AI analytics tools, producing alignment by construction rather than integration. We formally define the domain template as a typed relational configuration schema and prove that structural alignment between simulation and tool layers is guaranteed by single-source consumption. A five-layer pipeline--simulation, PostgreSQL, CDC/Iceberg lakehouse, star schema, and 12 parameterized AI tools--generates causally coherent, MES-shaped data spanning 66 entity types across four operational domains mapped to ISA-95/IEC 62264. We validate the architecture with six industry templates (aerospace, pharma, automotive, electronics, beverages, warehousing) running on identical framework code. Calibration experiments (60 runs, 10 seeds per template) confirm parametric controllability: observed KPIs fall within configured ranges across all templates. A controlled hallucination experiment (72 tool invocations, Qwen3-32B) demonstrates that ontology-constrained parameters eliminate tool-parameter fabrication (0% constrained vs. 43% unconstrained hallucination rate for the evaluated model, Fisher's exact test p < 10^-12); the 0% constrained rate is an architectural guarantee that holds for any model. The framework provides a reusable data layer for discrete manufacturing AI validation.

AI.tldr: A Python configuration module serving as both simulator specification and runtime schema (Template-as-Ontology) eliminates data alignment issues between simulation and AI analytics; validated across six industry templates, it achieves zero hallucination in tool parameters via architectural guarantee rather than model-dependent checks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based AI agents in manufacturing need schema-correct validation data, but real MES data is proprietary, privacy-protected, and vendor-specific, making it inaccessible or impractical for development and testing.
AI.method: Template-as-Ontology principle: a single Python config module (700-770 lines) serves dual role as simulator spec and AI runtime schema. Five-layer pipeline (simulation → PostgreSQL → CDC/Iceberg lakehouse → star schema → 12 AI tools) generates MES-like data. Proved structural alignment via single-source consumption. Validated with six industry templates (aerospace, pharma, automotive, electronics, beverages, warehousing) on identical codebase.
AI.result: Calibration experiments (60 runs, 10 seeds/template) confirm KPIs within configured ranges. Hallucination experiment (72 invocations, Qwen3-32B): 0% constrained vs 43% unconstrained parameter fabrication (Fisher's p < 10^-12). Zero rate is an architectural guarantee for any model, not model-specific.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reusable, architecturally sound data layer for discrete manufacturing AI validation, eliminating integration overhead and model-dependent hallucination mitigation.

title: A Proprioceptive-Only Benchmark for Quadruped State Estimation: ATE, RPE, and Runtime Trade-offs Between Filters and Smoothers
comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Practice
summary: We compare three state-of-the-art proprioceptive state estimators for quadruped robots: MUSE [1], the Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (IEKF) [2], and the Invariant Smoother (IS) [3], on the CYN-1 sequence of the GrandTour Dataset [4]. Our goal is to give practitioners clear guidance on accuracy and computation time: we report long-term accuracy (Absolute Trajectory Error, ATE), short-term accuracy (translational and rotational Relative Pose Error, RPE), and per-update computation time on a fixed hardware/software stack. On this dataset, RPEs are broadly similar across methods, while IEKF and IS achieve a lower ATE than MUSE. Runtime results highlight the accuracy-latency trade-offs across the three approaches. In the discussion, we outline the evaluation choices used to ensure a fair comparison and analyze factors that influence short-horizon metrics. Overall, this study provides a concise snapshot of accuracy and cost, helping readers choose an estimator that fits their application constraints, with all evaluation code and documentation released open-source at https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/state_estimation_benchmark for full reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Benchmark comparing MUSE, IEKF, and IS state estimators on quadruped robot data, finding similar RPEs but lower ATE for IEKF and IS, with open-source code released.
AI.motivation: To give practitioners clear guidance on accuracy and computation time trade-offs among three state-of-the-art proprioceptive state estimators for quadruped robots.
AI.method: Compare MUSE, IEKF, and IS on the CYN-1 sequence of the GrandTour Dataset using ATE (long-term accuracy), translational/rotational RPE (short-term accuracy), and per-update computation time on a fixed hardware/software stack. Evaluation code and documentation released open-source.
AI.result: RPEs are broadly similar across methods; IEKF and IS achieve lower ATE than MUSE. Runtime results highlight accuracy-latency trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Provides a concise snapshot of accuracy and cost to help readers choose an estimator fitting their application constraints, with full reproducibility via open-source release.

title: LatentRouter: Can We Choose the Right Multimodal Model Before Seeing Its Answer?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have heterogeneous strengths across OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, visual question answering, cost, and latency. Effective MLLM routing therefore requires more than estimating query difficulty: a router must match the multimodal requirements of the current image-question input with the capabilities of each candidate model. We propose LatentRouter, a router that formulates MLLM routing as counterfactual multimodal utility prediction. Given an image-question query, LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, and performs latent communication between these states to estimate how each model would perform if selected. A distributional outcome head predicts model-specific counterfactual quality, while a bounded capsule correction refines close decisions without allowing residual signals to dominate the prediction. The resulting utility-based policy supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing, and handles changing candidate pools through shared per-model scoring with availability masking. Experiments on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench show that LatentRouter outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines. Additional analyses show that the gains are strongest on multimodal task groups where model choice depends on visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented requirements, and that latent communication is the main contributor to the improvement. The code is available at: https://github.com/LabRAI/LatentRouter.

AI.tldr: LatentRouter is a routing method for multimodal large language models that uses counterfactual utility prediction, learned multimodal capsules, and latent communication between query features and model capability tokens to select the best MLLM for each image-question input, outperforming baselines on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench.
AI.motivation: MLLMs have heterogeneous strengths across different tasks (OCR, chart understanding, spatial reasoning, VQA, cost, latency), and effective routing requires more than estimating query difficulty—it must match the multimodal requirements of each input with the capabilities of available models.
