AI.method: LatentRouter extracts learned multimodal routing capsules from the image-question input, represents each candidate MLLM with a model capability token, performs latent communication between these states to estimate counterfactual performance, uses a distributional outcome head for model-specific quality prediction, and applies bounded capsule correction for close decisions. It supports performance-oriented and performance-cost routing with availability masking for changing candidate pools.
AI.result: Outperforms fixed-model, feature-level, and learned-router baselines on MMR-Bench and VL-RouterBench. Gains are strongest on multimodal task groups requiring visual, layout-sensitive, or reasoning-oriented model selection. Latent communication is the main contributor to improvement.
AI.conclusion: Latent communication and counterfactual utility prediction effectively capture heterogeneous model strengths for MLLM routing, enabling flexible routing policies and handling dynamic candidate pools.

title: Rainbow Deep Q-Learning with Kinematics-Aware Design for Cooperative Delta and 3-RRS Parallel Robot Insertion
summary: This paper presents a kinematics-aware deep reinforcement learning framework based on Rainbow Deep Q-Networks (DQN) for cooperative peg-in-hole manipulation by a Delta parallel robot and a 3-RRS (Revolute--Revolute--Spherical) parallel manipulator. A key contribution is the integration of a geometric design-optimization stage that precedes learning: the 3-RRS geometry is tuned to maximize the singularity-free workspace and improve conditioning, which in turn enlarges the safe region in which the reinforcement learning policy can explore. Together the two manipulators expose a 6~degree-of-freedom (DoF) controllable subspace (three Delta translations, two 3-RRS rotations, and one 3-RRS vertical translation); the peg-in-hole task is invariant to rotation about the peg axis, so the task-relevant manifold is five dimensional. The cooperative insertion problem is cast as a Markov Decision Process with a 12-dimensional state vector and a discrete action set containing $6 \times 2 = 12$ incremental commands (one positive and one negative per controlled DoF). A shaped reward combines dense proximity guidance, penalties for kinematic and workspace violations, and sparse bonuses for successful insertions. The Rainbow DQN -- integrating double Q-learning, dueling architecture, prioritized replay, multi-step returns, noisy linear layers for exploration, and a distributional value head -- is trained with a two-stage curriculum. The co-designed framework is validated in a high-fidelity kinematic simulator, where it achieves stable policy convergence, reliable insertions, and reduced constraint violations compared against a vanilla DQN agent and a classical sampling-based planner.

AI.tldr: A kinematics-aware Rainbow DQN framework with geometric design optimization of a 3-RRS manipulator is proposed for cooperative peg-in-hole insertion by a Delta robot and a 3-RRS parallel manipulator, achieving reliable insertions with reduced constraint violations.
AI.motivation: To enable safe and effective cooperative peg-in-hole manipulation using two parallel robots (Delta + 3-RRS) by pre-optimizing the 3-RRS geometry to maximize singularity-free workspace and conditioning, thus expanding the safe exploration region for RL policy learning.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) geometric design optimization of the 3-RRS manipulator to maximize singularity-free workspace and improve conditioning; (2) training a Rainbow DQN (with double Q-learning, dueling architecture, prioritized replay, multi-step returns, noisy linear layers, distributional value head) on a 12-state, 12-action MDP with shaped reward and two-stage curriculum learning.
AI.result: The framework achieves stable policy convergence, reliable insertions, and reduced constraint violations in a high-fidelity kinematic simulator, outperforming a vanilla DQN agent and a classical sampling-based planner.
AI.conclusion: Co-design of robot geometry and deep RL policy improves task success and safety for cooperative parallel-robot peg-in-hole assembly.

title: Constraint-Data-Value-Maximization: Utilizing Data Attribution for Effective Data Pruning in Low-Data Environments
summary: Attributing model behavior to training data is an evolving research field. A common benchmark is data removal, which involves eliminating data instances with either low or high values, then assessing a model's performance trained on the modified dataset. Many existing studies leverage Shapley-based data values for this task. In this paper, we demonstrate that these data values are not optimally suited for pruning low-value data when only a limited amount of data remains. To address this limitation, we introduce the Constraint-Data-Value-Maximization (CDVM) approach, which effectively utilizes data attributions for pruning in low-data scenarios. By casting pruning as a constrained optimization that both maximizes total influence and penalizes excessive per-test contributions, CDVM delivers robust performance when only a small fraction of the data is retained. On the OpenDataVal benchmark, CDVM shows strong performance and competitive runtime.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies limitations of Shapley-based data values for pruning low-value data in low-data scenarios and proposes Constraint-Data-Value-Maximization (CDVM), a constrained optimization approach that maximizes total influence while penalizing excessive per-test contributions, achieving strong performance on OpenDataVal.
AI.motivation: Existing Shapley-based data values are not optimally suited for pruning low-value data when only a limited amount of data remains; there is a need for a method that works effectively in low-data retention scenarios.
AI.method: The CDVM approach casts data pruning as a constrained optimization problem that both maximizes total influence and penalizes excessive per-test contributions, enabling robust performance when only a small fraction of data is retained.
AI.result: CDVM demonstrates strong performance and competitive runtime on the OpenDataVal benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The CDVM approach effectively addresses the limitation of Shapley-based data values for low-data pruning scenarios and offers a robust solution for data attribution-based pruning.

title: Introducing Environmental Constraints to Grasping Strategies for Paper-Like Flexible Materials Using a Soft Gripper
summary: Robotic manipulation of flexible objects is widely required in both industrial and service applications. Among such objects, paper-like materials exhibit distinct mechanical characteristics compared to cloth, being more sensitive to compressive stress, where minor variations in physical properties can significantly affect grasping. This study systematically investigates grasping strategies for paper-like materials using a universal soft gripper by exploiting environmental constraints. Based on manipulation primitives employed in existing grasping strategies, we proposed systematic grasping strategies for flexible materials by exploiting environmental constraints and analyzed their mechanical and kinematic models. To investigate the influence of materials and working conditions on grasping, an evaluation system for measuring grasping force and success rate was defined and experimentally evaluated. Finally, we summarized the specific workspaces and characteristics of different strategies that can satisfy various task requirements and lead to potential applications in household service robots for grasping planar flexible objects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates grasping strategies for paper-like materials using a universal soft gripper with environmental constraints, proposing systematic strategies with mechanical/kinematic models and evaluating their performance via grasping force and success rate measurements.
AI.motivation: Paper-like materials are sensitive to compressive stress and have distinct mechanical characteristics from cloth, making robotic manipulation challenging; minor physical property variations significantly affect grasping success.
AI.method: The authors propose systematic grasping strategies exploiting environmental constraints, analyze mechanical and kinematic models, and define an evaluation system measuring grasping force and success rate.
AI.result: Experimentally evaluated grasping force and success rate for different strategies under varying materials and working conditions; summarized specific workspaces and characteristics of each strategy.
AI.conclusion: Different grasping strategies have distinct workspaces and characteristics that can satisfy various task requirements, with potential applications in household service robots for grasping planar flexible objects.

title: Rethinking Evaluation for LLM Hallucination Detection: A Desiderata, A New RAG-based Benchmark, New Insights
summary: Hallucination, broadly referring to unfaithful, fabricated, or inconsistent content generated by LLMs, has wide-ranging implications. Therefore, a large body of effort has been devoted to detecting LLM hallucinations, as well as designing benchmark datasets for evaluating these detectors. In this work, we first establish a desiderata of properties for hallucination detection benchmarks (HDBs) to exhibit for effective evaluation. A critical look at existing HDBs through the lens of our desiderata reveals that none of them exhibits all the properties. We identify two largest gaps: (1) RAG-based grounded benchmarks with long context are severely lacking (partly because length impedes human annotation); and (2) Existing benchmarks do not make available realistic label noise for stress-testing detectors although real-world use-cases often grapple with label noise due to human or automated/weak annotation. To close these gaps, we build and open-source a new RAG-based HDB called T RIVIA+ that underwent a rigorous human annotation process. Notably, our benchmark exhibits all desirable properties including (1) T RIVIA+ contains samples with the longest context in the literature; and (2) we design and share four sets of noisy labels with different, both sample-dependent and sampleindependent, noise schemes. Finally, we perform experiments on RAG-based HDBs, including our T RIVIA+, using popular SOTA detectors that reveal new insights: (i) ample room remains for current detectors to reach the performance ceiling on RAG-based HDBs, (ii) the basic LLM-as-a-Judge baseline performs competitively, and (iii) label noise hinders detection performance. We expect that our findings, along with our proposed benchmark 1 , will motivate and foster needed research on hallucination detection for RAG-based tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies gaps in existing hallucination detection benchmarks (HDBs)—particularly the lack of long-context RAG-based benchmarks and realistic label noise—and introduces TRIVIA+, a new RAG-based HDB with the longest context in the literature and four sets of noisy labels. Experiments reveal that current detectors still have room for improvement, LLM-as-a-Judge performs competitively, and label noise hurts detection performance.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination detection benchmarks lack key desirable properties, especially long-context RAG-based grounded benchmarks (due to annotation difficulty) and realistic label noise for stress-testing detectors, despite real-world use cases often facing such noise.
AI.method: The authors establish a desiderata for HDBs, identify gaps in existing benchmarks, and construct TRIVIA+—a new RAG-based HDB with rigorous human annotation. It includes the longest context samples to date and four sets of noisy labels with both sample-dependent and sample-independent noise schemes.
AI.result: Experiments on RAG-based HDBs (including TRIVIA+) with SOTA detectors show: (i) current detectors have ample room to reach the performance ceiling, (ii) the basic LLM-as-a-Judge baseline performs competitively, and (iii) label noise hinders detection performance.
AI.conclusion: TRIVIA+ closes critical gaps in hallucination detection benchmarking, and the findings motivate further research on hallucination detection for RAG-based tasks.

title: DreamAvoid: Critical-Phase Test-Time Dreaming to Avoid Failures in VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often brittle in fine-grained manipulation, where minor action errors during the critical phases can rapidly escalate into irrecoverable failures. Since existing VLA models rely predominantly on successful demonstrations for training, they lack an explicit awareness of failure during these critical phases. To address this, we propose DreamAvoid, a critical-phase test-time dreaming framework that enables VLA models to anticipate and avoid failures. We also introduce an autonomous boundary learning paradigm to refine the system's understanding of the subtle boundary between success and failure. Specifically, we (1) utilize a Dream Trigger to determine whether the execution has entered a critical phase, (2) sample multiple candidate action chunks from the VLA via an Action Proposer, and (3) employ a Dream Evaluator, jointly trained on mixed data (success, failure, and boundary cases), to "dream" the short-horizon futures corresponding to the candidate actions, evaluate their values, and select the optimal action. We conduct extensive evaluations on real-world manipulation tasks and simulation benchmarks. The results demonstrate that DreamAvoid can effectively avoid failures, thereby improving the overall task success rate. Our code is available at https://github.com/XianzheFan/DreamAvoid.

AI.tldr: DreamAvoid is a test-time dreaming framework that helps Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models anticipate and avoid failures during critical phases of fine-grained manipulation by using a Dream Trigger, Action Proposer, and Dream Evaluator trained on mixed success/failure/boundary data, improving task success rates in both real-world and simulated tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models are brittle in fine-grained manipulation because minor action errors during critical phases escalate into irrecoverable failures, yet they lack explicit awareness of failure due to training predominantly on successful demonstrations.
AI.method: DreamAvoid consists of three components: (1) a Dream Trigger to detect critical phases, (2) an Action Proposer that samples multiple candidate action chunks from the VLA, and (3) a Dream Evaluator trained on mixed data (success, failure, boundary cases) that simulates short-horizon futures for each candidate, evaluates their values, and selects the optimal action.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on real-world manipulation tasks and simulation benchmarks show DreamAvoid effectively avoids failures and improves overall task success rates.
AI.conclusion: DreamAvoid provides a test-time dreaming mechanism and autonomous boundary learning paradigm that enhances VLA models' ability to anticipate and avoid failures during critical manipulation phases, leading to more robust fine-grained manipulation.

title: CPEMH: An Agentic Framework for Prompt-Driven Behavior Evaluation and Assurance in Foundation-Model Systems for Mental Health Screening
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the AGENT 2026 Workshop (ICSE 2026)
summary: This paper presents CPEMH, an agentic framework designed to evaluate prompt-driven behavior in foundation-model systems operating on transcript-based datasets for mental-health screening. CPEMH serves as an engineering methodology for behavioral assurance in large-scale language systems, introducing an orchestrated architecture that autonomously performs the design, evaluation, and selection of prompt strategies, enabling systematic control of behavioral variability across contexts. Its modular agentic design, combining orchestrator, inference, and evaluation agents, ensures traceability, reproducibility, and robustness throughout the prompting lifecycle. A case study on automated depression screening from interview transcripts demonstrates the framework's capacity to stabilize and audit foundation-model behavior in conversational and clinically sensitive domains. Lessons learned emphasize the role of modular orchestration in behavioral assurance, the prioritization of stability over architectural complexity, and the integration of F1, bias, and robustness as core acceptance criteria.

AI.tldr: CPEMH is an agentic framework for evaluating and controlling prompt-driven behavior in foundation models used for mental-health screening, demonstrated through automated depression screening from interview transcripts.
AI.motivation: To address behavioral variability and lack of systematic control in foundation-model systems applied to clinically sensitive domains like mental-health screening, where prompt-driven behavior must be stable, auditable, and reproducible.
AI.method: CPEMH employs a modular agentic architecture with three agent types: an orchestrator agent for coordinating the prompt lifecycle, inference agents for executing prompts, and evaluation agents for assessing outcomes. The framework autonomously designs, evaluates, and selects prompt strategies to control behavioral variability.
AI.result: Demonstrated through a case study on automated depression screening from interview transcripts, showing the framework's capacity to stabilize and audit foundation-model behavior in conversational and clinically sensitive domains.
AI.conclusion: Key lessons emphasize the importance of modular orchestration for behavioral assurance, prioritizing stability over architectural complexity, and using F1, bias, and robustness as core acceptance criteria for prompt strategies.

title: NavOL: Navigation Policy with Online Imitation Learning
summary: Learning robust navigation policies remains a core challenge in robotics. Offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift and compounding errors at rollout, while reinforcement learning requires reward engineering and learns inefficiently. In this paper, we propose NavOL, an online imitation learning paradigm that interacts with a simulator and updates itself using expert demonstrations gathered online. Built upon a pretrained navigation diffusion policy that maps local observations to future waypoints, NavOL trains in a rollout update loop: during rollout, the policy acts in the simulator and queries a global planner which has privileged access to the global environment for the optimal path segment as ground truth trajectory labels; during update, the policy is trained on the online collected observation trajectory pairs. This online imitation loop removes the need for reward design, improves learning efficiency, and mitigates distribution shift by training on the policy own explored rollouts. Built on IsaacLab with fast, high-fidelity parallel rendering and domain randomization of camera pose and start-goal pairs, our system scales across 50 scenes on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs, collecting over 2,000 new trajectories per hour, each averaging more than 400 steps. We also introduce an indoor visual navigation benchmark with predefined start and goal positions for zero-shot generalization. Extensive evaluations on simulation benchmarks, including the NavDP benchmark and our proposed benchmark, as well as carefully designed real-world experiments, demonstrate the effectiveness of NavOL, showing consistent performance gains in online imitation learning.

AI.tldr: NavOL is an online imitation learning paradigm for robot navigation that iteratively collects expert demonstrations via simulator interaction and updates a diffusion policy, eliminating reward engineering and distribution shift issues from offline methods.
AI.motivation: Offline imitation learning suffers from distribution shift and compounding errors at rollout, while reinforcement learning requires reward engineering and learns inefficiently. Existing methods lack efficient online data collection and scalable training for navigation policies.
AI.method: NavOL uses a pretrained navigation diffusion policy that maps local observations to future waypoints, trained in a rollout-update loop. During rollout, the policy acts in the simulator and queries a global planner with privileged environment access for optimal path segments as ground truth labels. During update, the policy is trained on the online-collected observation-trajectory pairs. Built on IsaacLab with parallel rendering, domain randomization, and scaling across 50 scenes on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs, collecting 2,000+ trajectories/hour (400+ steps each).
AI.result: The system collects over 2,000 new trajectories per hour with more than 400 steps each on average. Extensive evaluations on NavDP benchmark, a proposed indoor visual navigation benchmark, and real-world experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains and effectiveness in online imitation learning for navigation.
AI.conclusion: NavOL effectively removes the need for reward design, improves learning efficiency, and mitigates distribution shift by training on policy's own explored rollouts, showing consistent performance gains in both simulation and real-world settings.

title: CVEvolve: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery for Unstructured Scientific Data Processing
summary: Scientific data processing often requires task-specific algorithms or AI models, creating a barrier for domain scientists who need to analyze their data but may not have extensive computing or image-processing expertise. This barrier is especially pronounced when data are noisy, have a high dynamic range, are sparsely labeled, or are only loosely specified. We introduce CVEvolve, an autonomous agentic harness with a zero-code interface for scientific data-processing algorithm discovery. CVEvolve combines a multi-round search strategy with tools for code execution, evaluation implementation, history management, holdout testing, and optional inspection of scientific data and visual outputs. The search alternates between discovery and improvement actions, and uses lineage-aware stochastic candidate sampling to balance exploration and exploitation. We demonstrate CVEvolve on x-ray fluorescence microscopy image registration, Bragg peak detection, and high-energy diffraction microscopy image segmentation. Across these tasks, CVEvolve discovers algorithms that improve over baseline methods, while holdout test tracking helps identify candidates that generalize better than later over-optimized alternatives. These results show that zero-code, autonomous LLM-powered algorithm development can help domain scientists turn unstructured scientific image data into practical algorithms and downstream scientific discoveries.

AI.tldr: CVEvolve is a zero-code, autonomous agentic system powered by LLMs that discovers scientific data-processing algorithms through multi-round search, demonstrated on microscopy image tasks where it outperforms baseline methods.
AI.motivation: Domain scientists lack computing/image-processing expertise to develop task-specific algorithms for noisy, high-dynamic-range, sparsely labeled scientific data, creating a barrier to analysis and downstream discovery.
AI.method: CVEvolve combines multi-round search (alternating discovery and improvement actions) with code execution, evaluation, history management, holdout testing, and lineage-aware stochastic candidate sampling for exploration/exploitation balance — all accessible through a zero-code interface.
AI.result: On X-ray fluorescence microscopy registration, Bragg peak detection, and high-energy diffraction microscopy segmentation, CVEvolve discovers algorithms that improve over baselines; holdout testing identifies better-generalizing candidates over later over-optimized ones.
AI.conclusion: Zero-code, autonomous LLM-powered algorithm development can empower domain scientists to turn unstructured scientific image data into practical algorithms, lowering the expertise barrier.

title: See What Matters: Differentiable Grid Sample Pruning for Generalizable Vision-Language-Action Model
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable promise in robotics manipulation, yet their high computational cost hinders real-time deployment. Existing token pruning methods suffer from a fundamental trade-off: aggressive compression using pruning inevitably discards critical geometric details like contact points, leading to severe performance degradation. This forces a compromise, limiting the achievable compression rate and thus the potential speedup. We argue that breaking this trade-off requires rethinking compression as a geometry-aware, continuous token resampling in the vision encoder. To this end, we propose the Differentiable Grid Sampler (GridS), a plug-and-play module that performs task-aware, continuous resampling of visual tokens in VLA. By adaptively predicting a minimal set of salient coordinates and extracting features via differentiable interpolation, GridS preserves essential spatial information while achieving drastic compression (with fewer than 10% original visual tokens). Experiments on both LIBERO benchmark and a real robotic platform demonstrate that validating the lowest feasible visual token count reported to date, GridS achieves a 76% reduction in FLOPs with no degradation in the success rate. The code is available at https://github.com/Fediory/Grid-Sampler.

AI.tldr: GridS is a plug-and-play module that replaces token pruning with continuous, geometry-aware token resampling in VLA models, achieving 76% FLOPs reduction with fewer than 10% tokens and no performance loss.
AI.motivation: Existing token pruning methods face a trade-off: aggressive compression discards critical geometric details (e.g., contact points), limiting compression rates and speedup. The authors argue for rethinking compression as geometry-aware, continuous token resampling.
AI.method: GridS (Differentiable Grid Sampler) is a plug-and-play module that adaptively predicts minimal salient coordinate sets and extracts features via differentiable interpolation, performing task-aware continuous resampling in the vision encoder of VLA models.
AI.result: Achieves fewer than 10% visual tokens, 76% FLOPs reduction with no degradation in success rate on LIBERO benchmark and real robotic platform—lowest feasible visual token count reported to date.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware continuous resampling breaks the compression-performance trade-off in VLA, enabling drastic token reduction without losing critical spatial information for robotics manipulation.

title: Causal Bias Detection in Generative Artifical Intelligence
summary: Automated systems built on artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly deployed across high-stakes domains, raising critical concerns about fairness and the perpetuation of demographic disparities that exist in the world. In this context, causal inference provides a principled framework for reasoning about fairness, as it links observed disparities to underlying mechanisms and aligns naturally with human intuition and legal notions of discrimination. Prior work on causal fairness primarily focuses on the standard machine learning setting, where a decision-maker constructs a single predictive mechanism $f_{\widehat Y}$ for an outcome variable $Y$, while inheriting the causal mechanisms of all other covariates from the real world. The generative AI setting, however, is markedly more complex: generative models can sample from arbitrary conditionals over any set of variables, implicitly constructing their own beliefs about all causal mechanisms rather than learning a single predictive function. This fundamental difference requires new developments in causal fairness methodology. We formalize the problem of causal fairness in generative AI and unify it with the standard ML setting under a common theoretical framework. We then derive new causal decomposition results that enable granular quantification of fairness impacts along both (a) different causal pathways and (b) the replacement of real-world mechanisms by the generative model's mechanisms. We establish identification conditions and introduce efficient estimators for causal quantities of interest, and demonstrate the value of our methodology by analyzing race and gender bias in large language models across different datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes causal fairness in generative AI, unifying it with standard ML under a common theoretical framework. It derives new causal decomposition results for quantifying fairness impacts along causal pathways and mechanism replacements, establishes identification conditions with efficient estimators, and demonstrates the methodology by analyzing race and gender bias in large language models.
AI.motivation: Existing causal fairness frameworks are designed for standard ML (single predictive mechanism), but generative AI models construct beliefs about all causal mechanisms, requiring new methodology to address fairness in this more complex setting.
AI.method: The authors formalize causal fairness for generative AI under a unified theoretical framework with standard ML, derive new causal decomposition results for granular fairness quantification along causal pathways and mechanism replacements, establish identification conditions, and introduce efficient estimators.
AI.result: A unified theoretical framework for causal fairness spanning both generative AI and standard ML, along with new decomposition results and efficient estimators demonstrated on race and gender bias analysis in LLMs across different datasets.
AI.conclusion: Causal fairness methodology must be extended to account for generative AI's unique ability to replace multiple real-world causal mechanisms, and the proposed framework enables systematic quantification of such fairness impacts.

title: Mapping Embodied Affective Touch Strategies on a Humanoid Robot
summary: Affective touch in human-robot interaction is shaped not only by emotional intent, but also by robot embodiment, including touch location, physical constraints, and perceived agency or social role. Existing HRI studies typically focus on one or two isolated body parts, limiting understanding of how affective touch generalises across the full humanoid body. We present a study with 32 participants interacting with the iCub robot, which is equipped with full-body distributed tactile sensors. Participants expressed eight emotions under three conditions: free touch, arm-only touch, and torso-only touch. Results show that body region and spatial constraints jointly shaped both touch location and dynamics. In free touch, participants preferred socially accessible upper-body regions, while less frequently touched areas showed stronger emotion-specific selectivity. Emotion-related variation was more evident in motion features for arm-only touch and pressure features for torso-only touch. Touch strategies also did not transfer directly between free and constrained conditions, even within the same coarse body region. Participants reported increased closeness to the robot after interaction, with around 30 percent reporting a change in perceived social relationship. Together, these findings show that affective touch expression is strongly body-region dependent and shaped by embodiment constraints.

AI.tldr: A study with 32 participants interacting with the iCub robot found that affective touch expression is strongly body-region dependent and shaped by embodiment constraints, with free touch favoring socially accessible upper-body regions, emotion-specific selectivity in less-frequently touched areas, and different motion/pressure feature dominance depending on constrained touch conditions, while also increasing perceived closeness in participants.
AI.motivation: Existing HRI studies on affective touch typically focus on isolated body parts, limiting understanding of how affective touch generalises across the full humanoid body. This study aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: 32 participants interacted with the iCub robot (equipped with full-body distributed tactile sensors) to express eight emotions under three conditions: free touch, arm-only touch, and torso-only touch.
AI.result: Body region and spatial constraints jointly shaped touch location and dynamics. Free touch preferred socially accessible upper-body regions; less-frequently touched areas had stronger emotion-specific selectivity. Emotion-related variation was more evident in motion features for arm-only touch and pressure features for torso-only touch. Touch strategies did not transfer directly between conditions. Participants reported increased closeness, with ~30% reporting a change in perceived social relationship.
AI.conclusion: Affective touch expression is strongly body-region dependent and shaped by embodiment constraints, not transferable across conditions, highlighting the need for body-aware designs in HRI.

title: Causal Algorithmic Recourse: Foundations and Methods
summary: The trustworthiness of AI decision-making systems is increasingly important. A key feature of such systems is the ability to provide recommendations for how an individual may reverse a negative decision, a problem known as algorithmic recourse. Existing approaches treat recourse outcomes as counterfactuals of a fixed unit, ignoring that real-world recourse involves repeated decisions on the same individual under possibly different latent conditions. We develop a causal framework that models recourse as a process over pre- and post-intervention outcomes, allowing for partial stability and resampling of latent variables. We introduce post-recourse stability conditions that enable reasoning about recourse from observational data alone, and develop a copula-based algorithm for inferring the effects of recourse under these conditions. For settings where paired observations of the same individual before and after intervention are available (called recourse data), we develop methods for inferring copula parameters and performing goodness-of-fit testing. When the copula model is rejected, we provide a distribution-free algorithm for learning recourse effects directly from recourse data. We demonstrate the value of the proposed methods on real and semi-synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a causal framework for algorithmic recourse that models recourse as a process over repeated decisions on the same individual with latent variable resampling, proposes post-recourse stability conditions for inference from observational data, develops copula-based and distribution-free algorithms for estimating recourse effects, and validates them on real and semi-synthetic datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse methods treat outcomes as counterfactuals of a fixed unit, ignoring that real-world recourse involves repeated decisions on the same individual under possibly different latent conditions. The paper aims to address this gap by modeling recourse as a dynamic process over time.
AI.method: A causal framework modeling recourse as a process over pre- and post-intervention outcomes with partial stability and resampling of latent variables. Introduces post-recourse stability conditions for inference from observational data. Develops a copula-based algorithm for recourse effect inference and, when copula model is rejected, a distribution-free learning algorithm for recourse data (paired observations of the same individual before and after intervention).
AI.result: The proposed methods (copula-based and distribution-free algorithms) are validated on both real and semi-synthetic datasets, demonstrating their practical value for estimating recourse effects.
AI.conclusion: Modeling recourse as a process with latent variable resampling and post-recourse stability conditions enables more realistic reasoning about algorithmic recourse from observational data alone, with flexible inference methods depending on data availability.

title: Learning Action Manifold with Multi-view Latent Priors for Robotic Manipulation
summary: This paper tackles spatial perception and manipulation challenges in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. To address depth ambiguity from monocular input, we leverage a pre-trained multi-view diffusion model to synthesize latent novel views and propose a Geometry-Guided Gated Transformer (G3T) that aligns multi-view features under 3D geometric guidance while adaptively filtering occlusion noise. To improve action learning efficiency, we introduce Action Manifold Learning (AML), which directly predicts actions on the valid action manifold, bypassing inefficient regression of unstructured targets like noise or velocity. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-robot tasks show our method achieves superior success rate and robustness over SOTA baselines. Project page: https://junjxiao.github.io/Multi-view-VLA.github.io/.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Multi-view VLA model that uses a pre-trained multi-view diffusion model to generate latent novel views, a Geometry-Guided Gated Transformer (G3T) for aligning multi-view features under 3D guidance while filtering occlusion noise, and Action Manifold Learning (AML) for efficient action prediction on the valid action manifold.
AI.motivation: VLA models suffer from depth ambiguity due to monocular input and inefficient action learning due to unstructured regression targets like noise or velocity.
AI.method: (1) Pre-trained multi-view diffusion model to synthesize latent novel views; (2) Geometry-Guided Gated Transformer (G3T) to align multi-view features under 3D geometric guidance with adaptive occlusion noise filtering; (3) Action Manifold Learning (AML) to predict actions directly on the valid action manifold.
AI.result: Achieves superior success rate and robustness over SOTA baselines on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-robot tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-view VLA approach effectively resolves depth ambiguity and improves action learning efficiency, leading to better performance in spatial perception and manipulation tasks.

title: LLM-X: A Scalable Negotiation-Oriented Exchange for Communication Among Personal LLM Agents
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, accepted at AGENT 2026 Workshop, co-located with ICSE 2026
summary: We propose a personal-LLM exchange (LLM-X), a scalable negotiation-oriented environment that enables direct, structured communication across populations of personal agents (LLMs), each representing an individual user. Unlike existing tool-centric protocols that focus on agent-API interaction, LLM-X introduces a message bus and routing substrate for LLM-to-LLM coordination with guarantees around schema validity and policy enforcement. We contribute: (1) an architecture for LLM-X comprising federated gateways, topic-based routing, and policy enforcement; (2) a typed message protocol supporting capability negotiation and contract-net-style coordination; and (3) the first empirical evaluation of LLM-based multi-agent negotiation at scale. Experiments span 5, 9, and 12 agents, under distinct negotiation policies (Low, Medium, High), and across both short-run (minutes) and long-run (2h, 12h) load conditions. Results highlight clear policy-performance trade-offs: stricter policies improve robustness and fairness but increase latencies and message volume. Extended runs confirm that LLM-X remains stable under sustained load, with bounded latency drift.

AI.tldr: LLM-X is a scalable negotiation-oriented environment for direct, structured communication between personal LLM agents representing individual users, featuring federated gateways, topic-based routing, policy enforcement, and a typed message protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-centric protocols focus on agent-API interaction; there is a need for direct LLM-to-LLM coordination with schema validity and policy enforcement guarantees across populations of personal agents.
AI.method: Proposes LLM-X architecture with federated gateways, topic-based routing, and policy enforcement; introduces a typed message protocol for capability negotiation and contract-net-style coordination; evaluated empirically with 5, 9, and 12 agents under Low, Medium, and High negotiation policies across short-run and long-run (2h, 12h) loads.
AI.result: Stricter policies improve robustness and fairness but increase latencies and message volume; LLM-X remains stable under sustained load with bounded latency drift.
AI.conclusion: LLM-X enables scalable, policy-enforced LLM-to-LLM negotiation with clear trade-offs between policy strictness and performance, and demonstrates stability in extended runs.

title: EvoNav: Evolutionary Reward Function Design for Robot Navigation with Large Language Models
summary: Robot navigation is a crucial task with applications to social robots in dynamic human environments. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown great promise for this problem, the policy quality is highly sensitive to the specification of reward functions. Hand-crafted rewards require substantial domain expertise and embed inductive biases that are difficult to audit or adapt, limiting their effectiveness and leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose EvoNav, an evolutionary framework that automates the design of robot navigation reward functions via large language models (LLMs). To overcome prohibitively costly policy training, EvoNav evaluates each candidate proposal from the LLM via a progressive three-stage warm-up-boost procedure. EvoNav advances from analytical proxies with low-cost surrogates, such as small datasets and analytic rules, to lightweight rollouts and, finally, to full policy training, enabling computationally efficient exploration under effective feedback. Experiment results show that EvoNav produces more effective navigation policies than manually designed RL rewards and state-of-the-art reward design methods.

AI.tldr: EvoNav is an evolutionary framework using LLMs to automatically design robot navigation reward functions, evaluated via a progressive three-stage warm-up-boost procedure that reduces computational cost, outperforming manually designed rewards and SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Robot navigation policies in RL are highly sensitive to reward function design; hand-crafted rewards require domain expertise, embed hard-to-audit biases, and often lead to suboptimal performance.
AI.method: EvoNav uses LLMs to propose candidate reward functions, which are evaluated through a progressive three-stage warm-up-boost procedure: (1) analytical proxies with low-cost surrogates (small datasets, analytic rules), (2) lightweight rollouts, and (3) full policy training, enabling computationally efficient exploration under effective feedback.
AI.result: EvoNav produces more effective navigation policies than manually designed RL rewards and state-of-the-art reward design methods.
AI.conclusion: Automating reward function design via LLMs with progressive evaluation is a computationally efficient and effective approach for robot navigation tasks.

title: Revisiting Privacy Preservation in Brain-Computer Interfaces: Conceptual Boundaries, Risk Pathways, and a Protection-Strength Grading Framework
summary: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are moving rapidly from laboratory research into clinical, edge, and real-world settings. Under ISO/IEC 8663:2025, a BCI is a direct communication link between central nervous system activity and external software or hardware systems. This link expands privacy risk beyond raw neural-signal leakage: neural data, derived representations, model assets, and decoded outputs can be re-associated with individuals across collection, transmission, storage, training, inference, and feedback, or used to infer information beyond what a task requires. Starting from the general BCI paradigm, this review deffnes privacy-protection boundaries, protection objects, and the relationship between user data privacy and model privacy within a shared risk pathway. It then proposes a three-dimensional framework - protection object, lifecycle stage, and dominant protection-strength level - to classify existing work into four levels of protection strength. Finally, mental privacy and neuroethical risks are treated as open issues, emphasizing that BCI privacy protection should not only obscure data but also disentangle task-irrelevant sensitive information while preserving downstream utility. Keywords: Brain-computer interface, Neural data privacy, User data privacy, Model privacy, Disentanglement of task-irrelevant sensitive information, Protection-strength grading, Neuroethical risks

AI.tldr: This review on BCI privacy defines protection boundaries and objects, proposes a three-dimensional framework (protection object, lifecycle stage, protection-strength level) for classifying existing work into four levels, and identifies mental privacy and neuroethical risks as open issues, advocating for disentangling task-irrelevant sensitive information while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: BCIs are moving into real-world settings, expanding privacy risks beyond raw neural-signal leakage to include derived representations, model assets, and decoded outputs that can be re-associated with individuals or used to infer unintended information.
AI.method: Starting from the general BCI paradigm, the review defines privacy-protection boundaries, objects, and the relationship between user data privacy and model privacy within a shared risk pathway. It then proposes a three-dimensional framework—protection object, lifecycle stage, and dominant protection-strength level—to classify existing work into four levels of protection strength.
AI.result: A three-dimensional classification framework is proposed that categorizes existing BCI privacy protection work into four levels of protection strength based on protection object, lifecycle stage, and dominant protection-strength level.
AI.conclusion: BCI privacy protection should go beyond data obscuring to actively disentangle task-irrelevant sensitive information while preserving downstream utility, with mental privacy and neuroethical risks remaining as open issues.

title: From Reaction to Anticipation: Proactive Failure Recovery through Agentic Task Graph for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Although robotic manipulation has made significant progress, reliable execution remains challenging because task failures are inevitable in dynamic and unstructured environments. To handle such failures, existing frameworks typically follow a stepwise detect-reason-recover pipeline, which often incurs high latency and limited robustness due to delayed reasoning and reactive planning. Inspired by the human capability to anticipate and proactively plan for potential failures, we introduce AgentChord, an agentic system that models a manipulation task as a directed task graph. Before execution, this graph is enriched with anticipatory recovery branches that specify context-aware corrective behaviors, enabling immediate and targeted responses when failures occur. Specifically, AgentChord operates through a choreography of specialized agents: a composer that structures the nominal task graph, an arranger that augments the graph with anticipatory recovery branches, and a conductor that compiles and coordinates executable transitions using low-latency monitors to detect deviations and trigger pre-compiled recoveries without re-planning. Empirical studies on diverse long-horizon bimanual manipulation tasks demonstrate that AgentChord substantially improves success rates and execution efficiency, advancing the reliability and autonomy of real-world robotic systems. The project page is available at: https://shengxu.net/AgentChord/.

AI.tldr: AgentChord is an agentic system that models manipulation tasks as directed task graphs with anticipatory recovery branches, using specialized agents (composer, arranger, conductor) to enable proactive, low-latency error recovery without re-planning, significantly improving success rates and efficiency in long-horizon bimanual manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic manipulation frameworks rely on a stepwise detect-reason-recover pipeline that incurs high latency and limited robustness due to delayed reasoning and reactive planning when task failures occur in dynamic environments.
AI.method: AgentChord models manipulation tasks as directed task graphs enriched with anticipatory recovery branches before execution. It uses three specialized agents: a composer (structures the nominal task graph), an arranger (augments the graph with context-aware corrective behaviors), and a conductor (compiles and coordinates executable transitions using low-latency monitors to detect deviations and trigger pre-compiled recoveries without re-planning).
AI.result: Empirical studies on diverse long-horizon bimanual manipulation tasks demonstrate that AgentChord substantially improves success rates and execution efficiency over existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: AgentChord advances the reliability and autonomy of real-world robotic systems by enabling proactive, anticipatory failure handling with low-latency recovery, inspired by human capability to anticipate and plan for potential failures.

title: Transformer Interpretability from Perspective of Attention and Gradient
summary: Although researchers' attention is more focused on the performance of Transformer models, the interpretation of Transformer can never be ignored. Gradient is widely utilized in Transformer interpretation. From the perspective of attention and gradient, we conduct an in-depth study of Transformer interpretation and propose a method to achieve it by guiding the gradient direction, or more precisely, the attention direction. The method enables more comprehensive interpretation of feature regions, offers detail interpretation, and helps to better understand Transformer mechanism. Leveraging the difference in how Vision Transformer (ViT) and humans perceive images, we alter the class of an image in a way that is almost imperceptible to the human eye. This class rewriting phenomenon may potentially pose security risks in certain scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Transformer interpretation method that guides gradient/attention direction to provide comprehensive, detailed feature analysis, and demonstrates class rewriting (changing image classification imperceptibly to humans) as a security risk in Vision Transformers.
AI.motivation: While Transformer performance receives much attention, interpretation of Transformer models is equally important but underexplored. Existing gradient-based interpretation methods need improvement for more comprehensive feature understanding.
AI.method: The method guides gradient direction (specifically attention direction) to achieve Transformer interpretation, enabling more comprehensive feature region analysis and detailed interpretation of Transformer mechanisms.
AI.result: The proposed method provides more comprehensive interpretation of feature regions and offers detailed interpretation compared to existing approaches. Additionally, the paper reveals a class rewriting phenomenon where ViT's image classification can be altered imperceptibly to humans by exploiting differences between ViT and human visual perception.
AI.conclusion: The proposed gradient/attention guidance method enhances Transformer interpretability, and the discovered class rewriting phenomenon highlights potential security risks in ViT applications that warrant attention.

title: Cooperative Robotics Reinforced by Collective Perception for Traffic Moderation
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Vehicular Technology Conference (VTC2026-Spring)
summary: Collisions at non-line-of-sight (NLOS) intersections remain a major safety concern because drivers have limited visibility of approaching traffic. V2X based warnings can reduce these risks, yet many vehicles are not equipped with V2X and drivers may ignore in vehicle alerts. Collective perception (CP) can compensate for low V2X penetration by extending the awareness of connected vehicles, but it cannot influence unconnected vehicles. To fill this gap, our work introduces a complementary concept that adds a cooperative humanoid robot as an active traffic moderator capable of physically stopping a vehicle that attempts to merge into an unseen traffic stream. The system operates on two parallel perception pathways. A dual camera infrastructure unit detects the position, speed and motion of approaching vehicles and transmits this information to the robot as a collective perception message (CPM). The robot also receives cooperative awareness messages (CAM) from connected vehicles through its onboard V2X unit and can act as a relay for decentralized environmental notification messages (DENM) when safety events originate elsewhere along the road. A fusion module combines these streams to maintain a robust real time view of the main road. A Zone of Danger (ZoD) is defined and used to predict whether an approaching vehicle creates a collision risk for a merging road user. When such a risk is detected, the robot issues a human-like STOP gesture and blocks the merging path until the hazard disappears. The full system was deployed at the Future Mobility Park (FMP) in Rotterdam. Experiments show that the combined vision and V2X perception allows the robot to detect approaching vehicles early, predict hazards reliably and prevent unsafe merges in real world NLOS conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a cooperative humanoid robot as an active traffic moderator for NLOS intersections. The robot uses a dual camera infrastructure unit and V2X communication (CPM, CAM, DENM) to detect approaching vehicles, predict collision risks via a Zone of Danger (ZoD) model, and physically block merging paths with human-like STOP gestures. Real-world deployment at Future Mobility Park in Rotterdam showed reliable hazard prediction and prevention of unsafe merges.
AI.motivation: NLOS intersection collisions remain a major safety concern due to limited driver visibility. Existing V2X warnings suffer from low penetration rates and driver complacency. Collective perception extends awareness for connected vehicles but cannot influence unconnected vehicles. A physical intervention method is needed.
AI.method: The system uses two parallel perception pathways: (1) a dual camera infrastructure unit detects position/speed/motion of approaching vehicles and transmits CPMs to the robot; (2) the robot receives CAMs from connected vehicles via onboard V2X and relays DENMs. A fusion module combines both streams. AI.result: Real-world experiments at Future Mobility Park in Rotterdam demonstrated that combined vision and V2X perception enables early detection of approaching vehicles, reliable hazard prediction, and successful prevention of unsafe merges in real NLOS conditions.
AI.conclusion: Adding a cooperative humanoid robot as a physical traffic moderator can compensate for low V2X penetration and driver inattention at NLOS intersections. The proposed system effectively prevents unsafe merges, suggesting a new direction for mixed-traffic safety interventions.

title: AcuityBench: Evaluating Clinical Acuity Identification and Uncertainty Alignment
comment: 41 pages, 5 figures. Preprint under review for the Track on Evaluations and Datasets at NeurIPS 2026
summary: We introduce AcuityBench, a benchmark for evaluating whether language models identify the appropriate urgency of care from user medical presentations. Existing health benchmarks emphasize medical question answering, broad health interactions, or narrow workflow-specific triage tasks, but they do not offer a unified evaluation of acuity identification across these settings. AcuityBench addresses this gap by harmonizing five public datasets spanning user conversations, online forum posts, clinical vignettes, and patient portal messages under a shared four-level acuity framework ranging from home monitoring to immediate emergency care. The benchmark contains 914 cases, including 697 consensus cases for standard accuracy evaluation and 217 physician-confirmed ambiguous cases for uncertainty-aware evaluation. It supports two complementary task formats: explicit four-way classification in a QA setting, and free-form conversational responses evaluated with a rubric-based judge anchored to the same framework. Across 12 frontier proprietary and open-weight models, we find substantial variation in clear-case acuity accuracy and error direction. Comparing task formats reveals a systematic tradeoff: conversational responses reduce over-triage but increase under-triage relative to QA, especially in higher-acuity cases. In ambiguous cases, no model closely matches the distribution of physician judgments, and model predictions are more concentrated than expert clinical uncertainty. We also compare expert and model adjudication on a subset of maximally ambiguous cases, using those cases to examine the role of clinical uncertainty in label disagreement. Together, these results position acuity identification as a distinct safety-critical capability and show that AcuityBench enables systematic comparison and stress-testing of how well models guide users to the right level of care in real-world health use.

AI.tldr: AcuityBench is a benchmark that evaluates language models' ability to identify appropriate urgency of care from medical presentations across five public datasets, using a four-level acuity framework. It includes 914 cases (697 consensus + 217 ambiguous) and supports QA classification and free-form conversation tasks. Testing 12 models reveals variation in accuracy and error direction, a tradeoff between over-triage and under-triage, and models failing to match physician uncertainty in ambiguous cases.
AI.motivation: Existing health benchmarks focus on medical QA, broad health interactions, or narrow triage tasks but lack a unified evaluation of acuity identification across these settings. AcuityBench addresses this gap.
AI.method: Harmonizes five public datasets (user conversations, forum posts, clinical vignettes, patient portal messages) under a four-level acuity framework (home monitoring to immediate emergency care). Includes 697 consensus cases for accuracy and 217 physician-confirmed ambiguous cases for uncertainty evaluation. Supports two task formats: QA-style four-way classification and free-form conversation evaluated by a rubric-based judge.
AI.result: Substantial variation in clear-case accuracy and error direction across 12 models. Conversational responses reduce over-triage but increase under-triage compared to QA, especially in high-acuity cases. No model matches physician judgment distribution on ambiguous cases; model predictions are more concentrated than expert clinical uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Acuity identification is a distinct safety-critical capability. AcuityBench enables systematic comparison and stress-testing of how well models guide users to the right level of care in real-world health use.

title: Closing the Motion Execution Gap: From Semantic Motion Task Constraints to Kinematic Control
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, to be published in IJCAI 2026
summary: This paper addresses the Motion Execution Gap, the disconnect between high-level symbolic task descriptions using semantic constraints and executable robot motions. Motion Statecharts are introduced as an executable symbolic representation for complex motions. They allow the arbitrary arrangement of motion constraints, monitors or nested statecharts in parallel and sequence. World-centric motion specification and generalization across embodiments are enabled through the use of a unified differentiable kinematic world model of both, robots and environments. Motion execution is realized through a lMPC-based implementation of the task-function approach, in which smooth transitions during task switches are ensured using jerk bounds. Cross-platform transferability was demonstrated by deploying the method on eight robot platforms, operating in diverse environments. The proposed framework is called Giskard and is available open source: https://github.com/cram2/cognitive_robot_abstract_machine.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Giskard, a framework that bridges the Motion Execution Gap between high-level symbolic task descriptions and executable robot motions using Motion Statecharts, a unified differentiable kinematic world model, and lMPC-based task-function execution, demonstrated on eight diverse robot platforms.
AI.motivation: The authors address the Motion Execution Gap, which is the disconnect between high-level symbolic task descriptions using semantic constraints and the actual executable robot motions needed to realize those tasks.
AI.method: Motion Statecharts are introduced as an executable symbolic representation allowing arbitrary arrangement of motion constraints, monitors, or nested statecharts in parallel and sequence. A unified differentiable kinematic world model of both robots and environments enables world-centric motion specification and cross-embodiment generalization. Motion execution uses an lMPC-based implementation of the task-function approach with jerk-bounded smooth transitions during task switches.
AI.result: Cross-platform transferability was demonstrated by deploying the method on eight robot platforms operating in diverse environments. The framework (Giskard) is available as open source.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Giskard framework successfully bridges the Motion Execution Gap by providing an executable symbolic representation for complex motions that generalizes across robot embodiments and environments, enabling seamless transition from high-level task descriptions to low-level motion control.

title: Attributing Emergence in Million-Agent Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can simulate human-like reasoning and decision-making in individual agents. LLM-powered multi-agent systems (MAS) combine such agents to simulate population-scale social phenomena such as polarization, information cascades, and market panics. Such studies require attributing macro emergence to individual agents, but existing axiomatic methods scale combinatorially in $N$ and have been confined to $N \lesssim 10^3$, while the phenomena they explain occur at $N \geq 10^6$. We address this gap by adapting Aumann--Shapley path-integral attribution to LLM-powered MAS at million-agent scale; the resulting method satisfies all four axioms, runs four to five orders of magnitude faster than sampled Shapley on the same hardware. We use this method to test the scale gap empirically: across 14 days of public Bluesky data ($1{,}671{,}587$ active users), we compute the attribution at both full scale and the visibility-biased $N = 10^2$ convenience sample used by small-scale studies, and the two disagree structurally. At full scale the long tail and middle tier jointly carry the majority; the biased small panel attributes almost everything to a few high-follower accounts. We then prove that under any nonlinear macro indicator the disagreement cannot be reduced by post-hoc rescaling: an Attribution Scaling Bias theorem shows that no global rescaling factor can reconcile small-scale and full-scale attribution. Full-scale attribution is therefore not a methodological choice but a theoretical requirement for any nonlinear macro indicator.

Such studies require attributing macro emergence to individual agents, but existing axiomatic methods scale combinatorially in $N$ and have been confined to $N \lesssim 10^3$, while the phenomena they explain occur at $N \geq 10^6$. We address this gap by adapting Aumann--Shapley path-integral attribution to LLM-powered MAS at million-agent scale; the resulting method satisfies all four axioms, runs four to five orders of magnitude faster than sampled Shapley on the same hardware. We use this method to test the scale gap empirically: across 14 days of public Bluesky data ($1{,}671{,}587$ active users), we compute the attribution at both full scale and the visibility-biased $N = 10^2$ convenience sample used by small-scale studies, and the two disagree structurally. At full scale the long tail and middle tier jointly carry the majority; the biased small panel attributes almost everything to a few high-follower accounts. We then prove that under any nonlinear macro indicator the disagreement cannot be reduced by post-hoc rescaling: an Attribution Scaling Bias theorem shows that no global rescaling factor can reconcile small-scale and full-scale attribution. AI.motivation: Existing axiomatic attribution methods for multi-agent systems scale combinatorially and are confined to N ≲ 10³, yet the social phenomena they aim to explain occur at N ≥ 10⁶. This scale gap prevents valid attribution of macro emergence to individual agents in large-scale LLM-powered MAS.
AI.method: Adapts Aumann–Shapley path-integral attribution to LLM-powered MAS, achieving million-agent scale with four to five orders of magnitude speedup over sampled Shapley while satisfying all four axiomatic properties. Empirically tests on 14 days of Bluesky data (1,671,587 active users) comparing full-scale attribution to a visibility-biased N=10² sample. Proves the Attribution Scaling Bias theorem showing no global rescaling can reconcile small-scale and full-scale attribution under any nonlinear macro indicator.

AI.conclusion: Full-scale attribution is not a methodological choice but a theoretical requirement for any nonlinear macro indicator in LLM-powered multi-agent systems.

title: Control of Fully Actuated Aerial Vehicles: A Comparison of Model-based and Sensor-based Dynamic Inversion
summary: Fully actuated multirotor platforms decouple translational force generation from vehicle attitude, enabling independent control of position and orientation and shifting performance limitations from attitude authority to actuator dynamics and control effectiveness. This paper compares a model-based nonlinear dynamic inversion controller (geometric NDI) with a sensor-based incremental dynamic inversion controller (INDI) on a fixed-tilt fully actuated hexarotor. Both controllers share an identical outer-loop structure and are both executed at 500 Hz; therefore, performance differences can be attributed primarily to the inversion strategy. Controller performance is evaluated in five experiments covering attitude step tracking under nominal conditions and under a 50% mismatch in the rotor force coefficient, hover disturbance rejection under an external lateral load, waypoint tracking in the presence of wind gust disturbances, reduced control frequency, and injected sensor degradation. The results show that INDI offers clear advantages under parameter mismatch, gust disturbances, and sensor degradation, and maintains lower position errors across the controller-frequency sweep. However, its advantages are not universal: geometric NDI yields better attitude tracking at reduced control frequencies. To the authors' best knowledge, this work presents the first experimental validation of a full pose tracking INDI controller with decoupled translational and rotational dynamics. These findings highlight the trade-off between measurement-based and model-based inversion for robust control and rapid deployment of fully actuated UAVs.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally compares geometric NDI (model-based) and INDI (sensor-based) controllers on a fixed-tilt fully actuated hexarotor, finding INDI superior under parameter mismatch, gusts, and sensor degradation, while geometric NDI performs better at reduced control frequencies. It provides the first experimental validation of full pose tracking INDI with decoupled translational and rotational dynamics.
AI.motivation: Fully actuated multirotors decouple translation from attitude, shifting performance bottlenecks to actuator dynamics and control effectiveness. A systematic experimental comparison between model-based (geometric NDI) and sensor-based (INDI) inversion strategies on such platforms was lacking.
AI.method: A geometric nonlinear dynamic inversion (NDI) controller and an incremental nonlinear dynamic inversion (INDI) controller were implemented on a fixed-tilt fully actuated hexarotor with identical outer-loop structure and 500 Hz execution. Five experiments assessed attitude step tracking (nominal and with 50% rotor force coefficient mismatch), hover disturbance rejection under lateral load, waypoint tracking under wind gusts, reduced control frequency, and injected sensor degradation.
AI.result: INDI outperforms geometric NDI under parameter mismatch, gust disturbances, and sensor degradation, and achieves lower position errors across varied control frequencies. Geometric NDI yields better attitude tracking at reduced control frequencies.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between measurement-based (INDI) and model-based (NDI) inversion: INDI offers robustness advantages in degraded or uncertain conditions but does not universally outperform NDI, which excels in low-frequency attitude tracking. This is the first experimental validation of full pose tracking INDI with decoupled translational and rotational dynamics on a fully actuated UAV.

title: What Do EEG Foundation Models Capture from Human Brain Signals?
summary: Clinical electroencephalogram (EEG) analysis rests on a hand-crafted feature catalog refined over decades, \emph{e.g.,} band power, connectivity, complexity, and more. Modern EEG foundation models bypass this catalog, learn directly from raw signals via self-supervised pretraining, and match or outperform feature-engineered baselines on most clinical benchmarks. Whether the two representations align is an open question, which we decompose into three sub-questions: \emph{what does the model learn}, \emph{what does the model use}, and \emph{how much can be explained}. We answer them with layer-wise ridge probing, LEACE-style cross-covariance subspace erasure, and a transparent classifier benchmarked against a random-feature baseline. The audit covers three foundation models (CSBrain, CBraMod, LaBraM), five clinical tasks (MDD, Stress, ISRUC-Sleep, TUSL, Siena), and a 6-family 63-feature lexicon. Of the $945$ (model, task, feature) units, $648$ ($68.6\%$) are representation-causal and $199$ ($21.1\%$) are encoded-only. Across tasks, $50$ features qualify as universal candidates with strong support (all three architectures RC) in two or more tasks. Frequency-domain features dominate, but the other five families each contribute substantial causal mass. Confirmed features recover, on average, $79.3\%$ of the foundation model's advantage over the random baseline, with a clean task gradient (MDD $\approx 0.99$ down to Stress $\approx 0.56$): tasks near ceiling are almost fully recovered by the lexicon, while harder tasks leave a non-trivial residual that pinpoints a concrete target for future concept discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether EEG foundation models learn the same features as traditional hand-crafted clinical features. Using layer-wise probing, subspace erasure, and transparent classifiers across 3 models, 5 tasks, and 63 features, they find that 68.6% of feature-model-task units are representation-causal, with 50 universal feature candidates. The lexicon recovers 79.3% of the foundation model's advantage over random baselines, though harder tasks reveal non-trivial residuals for future discovery.
AI.motivation: Clinical EEG analysis traditionally relies on decades-old hand-crafted features (band power, connectivity, complexity, etc.), but modern EEG foundation models bypass this catalog by learning directly from raw signals via self-supervised pretraining, often outperforming feature-engineered methods. The authors pose the open question of whether the representations learned by these foundation models align with the established clinical feature catalog, decomposed into what the model learns, what it uses, and how much can be explained.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic audit using three complementary techniques: (1) layer-wise ridge probing to assess encoding of features, (2) LEACE-style cross-covariance subspace erasure to determine causal reliance on features, and (3) a transparent classifier benchmarked against a random-feature baseline. The study covers three foundation models (CSBrain, CBraMod, LaBraM), five clinical tasks (MDD, Stress, ISRUC-Sleep, TUSL, Siena), and a comprehensive lexicon of 63 features across 6 families.
AI.result: Of the 945 (model, task, feature) units analyzed, 648 (68.6%) are representation-causal (RC) and 199 (21.1%) are encoded-only. Across tasks, 50 features qualify as universal candidates (supported by all three architectures as RC in two or more tasks). Frequency-domain features dominate, but all six feature families contribute substantial causal mass. The confirmed features recover on average 79.3% of the foundation model's advantage over the random baseline, with a clear task gradient from MDD (~0.99) to Stress (~0.56).
AI.conclusion: The hand-crafted feature lexicon substantially aligns with EEG foundation model representations, recovering most of the performance advantage, especially for easier tasks (near ceiling). However, harder tasks leave a non-trivial residual unexplained by the current lexicon, pinpointing concrete targets for future concept discovery. Frequency-domain features are most dominant, but other feature families also contribute meaningfully, suggesting the foundation models learn a richer representation that partially extends beyond traditional clinical knowledge.

title: Learning What Matters: Adaptive Information-Theoretic Objectives for Robot Exploration
summary: Designing learnable information-theoretic objectives for robot exploration remains challenging. Such objectives aim to guide exploration toward data that reduces uncertainty in model parameters, yet it is often unclear what information the collected data can actually reveal. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize a given objective, constructing objectives that reflect parametric learnability is difficult in high-dimensional robotic systems. Many parameter directions are weakly observable or unidentifiable, and even when identifiable directions are selected, omitted directions can still influence exploration and distort information measures. To address this challenge, we propose Quasi-Optimal Experimental Design (Q{\footnotesize OED}), an adaptive information objective grounded in optimal experimental design. Q{\footnotesize OED} (i) performs eigenspace analysis of the Fisher information matrix to identify an observable subspace and select identifiable parameter directions, and (ii) modifies the exploration objective to emphasize these directions while suppressing nuisance effects from non-critical parameters. Under bounded nuisance influence and limited coupling between critical and nuisance directions, Q{\footnotesize OED} provides a constant-factor approximation to the ideal information objective that explores all parameters. We evaluate Q{\footnotesize OED} on simulated and real-world navigation and manipulation tasks, where identifiable-direction selection and nuisance suppression yield performance improvements of \SI{35.23}{\percent} and \SI{21.98}{\percent}, respectively. When integrated as an exploration objective in model-based policy optimization, Q{\footnotesize OED} further improves policy performance over established RL baselines.

AI.tldr: Quasi-Optimal Experimental Design (QOED) is a learnable information-theoretic objective for robot exploration that uses Fisher information eigenspace analysis to identify observable parameter directions and suppress nuisance effects, achieving 35.23% and 21.98% improvements in simulated and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Designing learnable information-theoretic objectives for robot exploration is challenging because it is unclear what information collected data can reveal, parametric learnability is difficult to capture in high-dimensional systems, and many parameter directions are weakly observable or unidentifiable—while even selected observable directions can be distorted by omitted nuisance parameters.
AI.method: QOED (i) performs eigenspace analysis of the Fisher information matrix to identify an observable subspace and select identifiable parameter directions, and (ii) modifies the exploration objective to emphasize these directions while suppressing nuisance effects from non-critical parameters, providing a constant-factor approximation to the ideal objective under bounded nuisance influence.
AI.result: On simulated and real-world navigation/manipulation tasks, identifiable-direction selection improved performance by 35.23% and nuisance suppression by 21.98%. When integrated into model-based policy optimization, QOED improved policy performance over established RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: QOED offers a principled, practical information-theoretic exploration objective that handles unidentifiable parameters and nuisance effects, with empirical gains in both exploration efficiency and downstream policy learning.

title: Under the Hood of SKILL.md: Semantic Supply-chain Attacks on AI Agent Skill Registry
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities through Agent Skills: modular filesystem packages whose SKILL.md files describe when and how agents should use them. While this design enables scalable, on-demand capability expansion, it also introduces a semantic supply-chain risk in which natural-language metadata and instructions can affect which skills are admitted, surfaced, selected, and loaded. We study SKILL.md - only attacks across three registry-facing stages of the Agent Skill lifecycle, using real ClawHub skills and realistic registry mechanisms. In Discovery, short textual triggers can manipulate embedding-based retrieval and improve adversarial skill visibility, achieving up to 86% pairwise win rate and 80% Top-10 placement. In Selection, description-only framing biases agents toward functionally equivalent adversarial variants, which are selected in 77.6% of paired trials on average. In Governance, semantic evasion strategies cause malicious skills to avoid a blocking verdict in 36.5%-100% of cases. Overall, our results show that SKILL.md is not passive documentation but operational text that shapes which third-party capabilities agents find, trust, and use.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that natural-language metadata (SKILL.md files) in autonomous AI agent skills can be adversarially manipulated to influence discovery (up to 86% win rate), selection (77.6% biased choices), and governance (36.5-100% evasion) of third-party agent skills, revealing a semantic supply-chain vulnerability.
AI.motivation: While Agent Skills enable scalable capability expansion for autonomous AI agents, the natural-language metadata (SKILL.md) used to describe when and how agents should use them introduces a semantic supply-chain risk that has not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors conduct three registry-facing attacks across Discovery (embedding-based retrieval manipulation), Selection (description-only framing bias), and Governance (semantic evasion strategies) stages of the Agent Skill lifecycle, using real ClawHub skills and realistic registry mechanisms.
AI.result: Discovery attacks achieved up to 86% pairwise win rate and 80% Top-10 placement; Selection attacks biased agents toward adversarial variants in 77.6% of paired trials; Governance evasion succeeded in 36.5%-100% of cases.
