Brain-like neural networks built on the Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) formalism have re-emerged as a credible alternative to backpropagation-driven deep learning. They deliver state-of-the-art unsupervised representation learning, neuromorphic-friendly sparsity, and existing FPGA implementations that target edge deployment. Despite this momentum, no systematic framework exists for explaining BCPNN decisions -- a gap the present paper fills. We argue that BCPNN is, in the sense of Rudin's interpretable-by-design agenda, an inherently transparent model whose architectural primitives map directly onto established explainable-AI (XAI) families. We make four contributions. First, we propose the first XAI taxonomy for BCPNN. It maps weights, biases, hypercolumn posteriors, structural-plasticity usage scores, attractor dynamics, and input-reconstruction populations onto attribution, prototype, concept, counterfactual, and mechanistic explanation modalities. Second, we introduce sixteen architecture-level explanation primitives (P1--P16), several without analogue in standard ANNs. We provide closed-form algorithms for computing each from quantities the model already maintains. Third, we introduce five design-time Configuration-as-Explanation primitives (Config-P1 to Config-P5) that treat BCPNN hyperparameter choices as an auditable pre-deployment explanation artifact. Fourth, we sketch a roadmap for integration into industrial IoT deployments and discuss EU AI Act alignment, edge feasibility, and Industry 5.0 implications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first systematic explainable-AI (XAI) framework for Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Networks (BCPNN), addressing the gap between BCPNN's suitability for EU AI Act-compliant edge deployment and the lack of interpretability methods for this brain-like architecture. It proposes a taxonomy mapping BCPNN components to five XAI modalities, 16 architecture-level explanation primitives, five design-time configuration-as-explanation primitives, and a deployment roadmap for industrial IoT under EU AI Act alignment.
AI.motivation: The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) mandates transparency for high-risk AI systems from August 2026, creating urgent need for inherently interpretable models deployable on resource-constrained edge devices. BCPNN networks offer unsupervised learning, sparsity, and FPGA feasibility but lack any systematic framework for explaining their decisions, which this paper aims to provide.
AI.method: The paper proposes the first XAI taxonomy for BCPNN, mapping architectural primitives (weights, biases, hypercolumn posteriors, structural-plasticity scores, attractor dynamics, input-reconstruction populations) onto five explanation modalities (attribution, prototype, concept, counterfactual, mechanistic). It introduces 16 closed-form explanation primitives (P1–P16) computed from existing model quantities, plus five Configuration-as-Explanation primitives (Config-P1–Config-P5) treating hyperparameters as auditable pre-deployment artifacts.
AI.result: A comprehensive XAI framework for BCPNN comprising: (1) a taxonomy with 5 explanation modalities, (2) 16 architecture-level explanation primitives with closed-form algorithms, (3) 5 design-time configuration primitives, and (4) a roadmap for EU AI Act-compliant edge deployment in Industry 5.0 and industrial IoT contexts.
AI.conclusion: BCPNN is established as an inherently transparent model under Rudin's interpretable-by-design agenda. The proposed framework fills a critical gap for deploying trustworthy AI on edge devices under the EU AI Act, with implications for neuromorphic computing, industrial IoT, and Industry 5.0.

title: GAR: Carbon-Aware Routing for LLM Inference via Constrained Optimization
summary: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) makes per-request routing essential for balancing response quality and computational cost across heterogeneous model pools. Current routing methods rarely consider sustainable energy use and CO2 emissions as optimization objectives, despite grid carbon intensity varying by time and region, and models differing significantly in energy consumption. To address this gap, we introduce Green-Aware Routing (GAR), a constrained multi-objective optimization framework that minimizes per-request CO2 emissions subject to explicit accuracy floors and p95-latency service-level objectives (SLOs). GAR employs adaptive constraint optimization through per-dataset floor tuning and incorporates lightweight estimators for correctness, tail latency, and carbon emissions, enabling real-time routing decisions without additional inference passes. We present GAR-PD, a practical online primal-dual routing algorithm for rolling carbon budgets, alongside heuristic variants that achieve high feasibility coverage while limiting accuracy degradation. Comprehensive experiments across standard NLP benchmarks with heterogeneous LLM pools (7B-70B) demonstrate that GAR achieves substantial carbon reductions while maintaining competitive accuracy and p95 latency guarantees, providing a practical, theoretically grounded approach to sustainable LLM inference.

AI.tldr: Green-Aware Routing (GAR) is a constrained multi-objective optimization framework that minimizes per-request CO2 emissions for LLM inference routing while satisfying accuracy and latency constraints, achieving substantial carbon reductions across heterogeneous model pools.
AI.motivation: Current LLM routing methods optimize for response quality and computational cost but neglect environmental sustainability (CO2 emissions and energy use), despite time/region-varying grid carbon intensity and heterogeneous model energy consumption.
AI.method: GAR formulates routing as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem minimizing CO2 emissions subject to accuracy floors and p95-latency SLOs. It uses adaptive per-dataset floor tuning, lightweight estimators for correctness/tail latency/carbon, and presents GAR-PD (online primal-dual algorithm) plus heuristic variants for rolling carbon budgets.
AI.result: Experiments on standard NLP benchmarks with LLMs (7B-70B) demonstrate GAR achieves substantial carbon reductions while maintaining competitive accuracy and p95 latency guarantees.
AI.conclusion: GAR provides a practical, theoretically grounded approach to sustainable LLM inference routing by balancing accuracy, latency, and carbon emissions in real-time.

title: CuSearch: Curriculum Rollout Sampling via Search Depth for Agentic RAG
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems from outcome-only supervision. Most existing methods optimize policies from uniformly sampled rollouts, implicitly treating all trajectories as equally informative. However, trajectories differ substantially in search depth and are therefore not equally informative: deeper-search trajectories contain more retrieval decision points and provide denser direct supervision for the retrieval sub-policy. Moreover, this heterogeneity grows over training as the within-batch depth distribution shifts toward higher values, yet uniform rollout sampling remains blind to this shift. To address this, we propose CuSearch, a curriculum rollout sampling framework built on Search-Depth Greedy Allocation (SDGA), a batch-level operator that reallocates a fixed update budget toward deeper-search trajectories. SDGA-Auto always targets the deepest available trajectories in the current batch, yielding an implicit training-aligned curriculum as the depth distribution shifts upward. SDGA-Phase explicitly advances the curriculum threshold as deeper trajectories become sufficiently abundant. Experiments across model types and retrieval frameworks show that CuSearch consistently improves performance, achieving up to 11.8 exact-match points over standard GRPO on ZeroSearch. These results establish per-trajectory search depth as a reliable, annotation-free proxy for retrieval supervision density in RLVR-based agentic RAG training. The code is available at https://github.com/MrToser/CuSearch.

AI.tldr: CuSearch proposes a curriculum rollout sampling framework (SDGA) that prioritizes deeper-search trajectories in RLVR-based agentic RAG training, outperforming uniform rollout sampling by up to 11.8 exact-match points.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR methods sample trajectories uniformly, ignoring that deeper-search trajectories contain more retrieval decision points and therefore provide denser supervision. This heterogeneity grows as training shifts toward deeper searches, yet uniform sampling remains blind to this shift.
AI.method: CuSearch uses Search-Depth Greedy Allocation (SDGA), a batch-level operator that reallocates update budget toward deeper-search trajectories. Two variants: SDGA-Auto (targets deepest trajectories in each batch) and SDGA-Phase (explicitly advances curriculum threshold as deeper trajectories become abundant).
AI.result: CuSearch achieves up to 11.8 exact-match points improvement over standard GRPO on ZeroSearch, with consistent gains across model types and retrieval frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Per-trajectory search depth serves as a reliable, annotation-free proxy for retrieval supervision density in RLVR-based agentic RAG training, and curriculum-aware sampling is more effective than uniform sampling.

title: Nice Fold or Hero Call: Learning Budget-Efficient Thinking for Adaptive Reasoning
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve problem solving through extended reasoning, but often misallocate test-time compute. Existing efficiency methods reduce cost by compressing reasoning traces or conditioning budget on perceived difficulty, yet largely overlook solvability. As a result, they may spend large budgets on queries beyond the model's capability while compressing hard-but-solvable queries that require deeper reasoning. In this work, we formulate adaptive reasoning as a computational investment under uncertainty, where budget should follow the expected return of reasoning rather than perceived difficulty alone. To instantiate this principle, we propose Budget-Efficient Thinking (BET), a two-stage framework that combines behavioral cold-start with GRPO under an investment-cost-aware reward. By aligning solve-or-fold decisions with rollout-derived solvability, BET learns three behaviors: (1) short solve, answering easy queries concisely; (2) nice fold, abstaining early when continued reasoning has near-zero expected return; and (3) hero call, preserving sufficient compute for hard-but-solvable queries. Across seven benchmarks and three base models, BET reduces reasoning tokens by ~55% on average while achieving overall performance improvements, and transfers zero-shot from mathematical reasoning to scientific QA and logical reasoning with comparable efficiency gains.

AI.tldr: BET (Budget-Efficient Thinking) is a two-stage framework that reduces reasoning tokens by ~55% while maintaining or improving performance by aligning compute budgets with expected return of reasoning rather than perceived difficulty alone, enabling adaptive solve-or-fold decisions.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models (LRMs) misallocate test-time compute by spending large budgets on unsolvable queries while compressing hard-but-solvable ones, as existing efficiency methods overlook solvability.
AI.method: BET combines behavioral cold-start with GRPO under an investment-cost-aware reward, using rollout-derived solvability to learn three behaviors: short solve (easy queries), nice fold (abstain when expected return is near-zero), and hero call (preserve compute for hard-but-solvable queries).
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks and three base models, BET reduces reasoning tokens by ~55% on average while achieving overall performance improvements, and transfers zero-shot to scientific QA and logical reasoning with comparable efficiency gains.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive reasoning should follow expected return of reasoning rather than perceived difficulty alone, and BET effectively instantiates this principle.

title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations
comment: DORA stress-tests LLM agents on real-world disaster operations that demand comprehensive orchestration of 108 specialized tools over heterogeneous geospatial data
summary: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports. However, prior work largely isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving the end-to-end workflows of emergency operations underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents.

AI.tldr: DORA is a benchmark with 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disasters, evaluating LLM-based agents on end-to-end disaster response workflows (perception, spatial reasoning, evacuation planning, temporal analysis, report synthesis) using a 108-tool MCP library. Evaluating 13 LLMs reveals persistent challenges in domain grounding, tool selection bottlenecks, and compositional fragility where performance gaps widen from 7% to 56% on longer pipelines.
AI.motivation: Prior work in disaster response isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving end-to-end operational workflows (integrating multi-sensor signals, road networks, evacuation planning, report generation) underexplored. DORA fills this gap by providing a comprehensive agentic benchmark for the full disaster response pipeline.
AI.method: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events (10 types) with 3,500 expert-verified tool-call steps spanning five dimensions: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue/evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents use a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data (optical, SAR, multi-spectral imagery at 0.015-10m GSD, elevation, social vectors). 13 frontier LLMs evaluated.
AI.result: Three persistent challenges identified: (1) disaster-domain grounding failures (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, pipeline composition); (2) double bottleneck from tool selection and argument grounding (gold tool-order hints improve accuracy only 1.08-4.40%, alternative scaffolds yield ≤3.24% gain); (3) compositional fragility scaling with trajectory length (agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines).
AI.conclusion: DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents, revealing that current LLMs struggle significantly with end-to-end disaster response workflows, particularly in domain-specific grounding and compositional reasoning over long pipelines.

title: Seirênes: Adversarial Self-Play with Evolving Distractions for LLM Reasoning
summary: We present Seirênes, a self-play RL framework that transforms contextual interference from a failure mode of LLM reasoning into an internal training signal for co-evolving more resilient reasoners. While RL with verifiable rewards has significantly advanced reasoning capabilities, models can still exhibit fragility when encountering non-idealized contexts: scenarios characterized by superfluous information, tangential instructions, or incidental correlations that differ from the clean distributions typical of standard benchmarks. Seirênes harnesses this vulnerability through a parameter-shared and adversarial self-play loop. Within this framework, a single model is trained to both construct plausible yet distracting contexts that expose its own reasoning blind spots, and solve problems by discerning the essential task from these perturbations to recover the core underlying logic. By pitting these competing objectives against each other, Seirênes compels the model to move beyond superficial pattern matching and anchors its capabilities in robust underlying reasoning. This continuous interaction sustains an informative co-evolutionary curriculum as the model improves. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model scales from 4B to 30B, Seirênes achieves average gains of +10.2, +9.1, and +7.2 points. Besides, distracting contexts produced by the 4B Seirênes model reduce the accuracy of top-tier closed-source models (GPT and Gemini) by roughly 4--5 points, revealing Seirênes' general ability to uncover reasoning models' blind spots.

AI.tldr: Seirênes is a self-play RL framework that improves LLM reasoning robustness by training models to both generate distracting contexts and solve problems within them, achieving significant gains (+7-10 points) on math benchmarks and exposing blind spots in even top-tier models like GPT and Gemini.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit reasoning fragility when faced with non-idealized contexts such as superfluous information, tangential instructions, or incidental correlations that deviate from clean benchmark distributions. The authors aim to transform this vulnerability from a failure mode into a training signal.
AI.method: Seirênes employs a parameter-shared adversarial self-play loop where a single model is trained with two competing objectives: (1) constructing plausible yet distracting contexts that expose its own reasoning blind spots, and (2) solving problems by discerning essential tasks from these perturbations. This co-evolutionary curriculum uses RL with verifiable rewards.
AI.result: Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with models from 4B to 30B parameters, Seirênes achieves average gains of +10.2, +9.1, and +7.2 points. Distracting contexts from the 4B model reduce GPT and Gemini accuracy by approximately 4-5 points.
AI.conclusion: The adversarial self-play framework compels models to move beyond superficial pattern matching toward more robust reasoning. It also serves as a general tool for uncovering blind spots in other LLMs.

title: A CAP-like Trilemma for Large Language Models: Correctness, Non-bias, and Utility under Semantic Underdetermination
summary: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance under network partition. Inspired by this result, this paper formulates a CAP-like conjecture for Large Language Models (LLMs). The proposed trilemma states that, under semantic underdetermination, an LLM cannot always simultaneously guarantee strong correctness, strict non-bias, and high utility. A prompt is semantically underdetermined when the given premises do not determine a unique answer. In such cases, a useful and decisive response requires the model to introduce a selection criterion, preference, prior, or value ordering. If this criterion is not supplied by the user or justified by the available premises, the response becomes biased in a broad selection-theoretic sense. Conversely, if the model avoids unsupported preferences, it may preserve correctness and non-bias but may reduce utility through refusal, hedging, or clarification. The paper formalizes this correctness--non-bias--utility trilemma, develops examples, and argues that certain LLM failures arise not merely from model limitations but from the structure of underdetermined decision requests.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a CAP-theorem-inspired trilemma for LLMs: under semantic underdetermination, an LLM cannot simultaneously guarantee strong correctness, strict non-bias, and high utility. When a prompt lacks sufficient premises for a unique answer, any decisive response introduces implicit preferences (bias), while avoiding such preferences reduces utility through refusal or hedging.
AI.motivation: To explain certain LLM failures not as model limitations but as inherent structural trade-offs when processing underdetermined prompts, analogous to the CAP theorem in distributed systems.
AI.method: Formalizes a correctness–non-bias–utility trilemma for LLMs under semantic underdetermination, develops illustrative examples, and argues that the trade-off is structurally unavoidable.
AI.result: Demonstrates that under semantic underdetermination, an LLM cannot simultaneously achieve strong correctness, strict non-bias, and high utility; at most two of the three can be satisfied.
AI.conclusion: LLM failures in underdetermined scenarios are not merely due to model limitations but reflect a fundamental structural constraint inherent to the decision problem itself.

title: OOM-Free Alpamayo via CPU-GPU Memory Swapping for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Submitted to IEEE RTCSA on March 26, 2026 (KST); Accepted on May 4, 2026 (KST)
summary: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for autonomous driving unify perception, reasoning, and control in a single neural network, achieving strong driving performance but requiring 20-60GB of GPU memory-far exceeding the 12-16GB available on commodity GPUs. We present a framework, which enables memory-efficient VLA inference on VRAM-constrained GPUs through system-level optimization alone, without model modification. Our work proceeds in three stages: (1) Sequential Demand Layering reduces VRAM usage from model-level to layer-level granularity; (2) Pipelined Demand Layering hides parameter transfer time within layer execution time via transfer--compute overlap; and (3) a GPU-Resident Layer Decision Policy, informed by per-module residency benefit analysis, eliminates the residual transfer overhead that pipelining cannot hide. We further propose a performance prediction model that determines the optimal configuration-both the number and placement of resident layers-from a single profiling run with less than 1.3% prediction error across all configurations. Applied to NVIDIA's Alpamayo-R1-10B (21.52GB) on an RTX 5070Ti (16GB), our work achieves up to 3.55x speedup over Accelerate offloading while maintaining full BF16 precision.

AI.tldr: A system-level optimization framework enabling memory-efficient VLA inference on VRAM-constrained GPUs (e.g., 16GB) without model modification, achieving up to 3.55x speedup over baseline offloading.
AI.motivation: End-to-end VLA models for autonomous driving require 20-60GB GPU memory, far exceeding the 12-16GB available on commodity GPUs, creating a practical deployment bottleneck.
AI.method: Three-stage optimization: (1) Sequential Demand Layering (layer-level VRAM granularity), (2) Pipelined Demand Layering (transfer-compute overlap), (3) GPU-Resident Layer Decision Policy (eliminates residual transfer overhead via per-module residency benefit analysis), plus a performance prediction model for optimal configuration.
AI.result: Applied to NVIDIA's Alpamayo-R1-10B (21.52GB) on RTX 5070Ti (16GB), achieving up to 3.55x speedup over Accelerate offloading while maintaining full BF16 precision.
AI.conclusion: System-level optimization alone can bridge the VRAM gap for VLA inference on commodity GPUs without any model modification, with high configuration prediction accuracy (<1.3% error).

title: Explaining and Breaking the Safety-Helpfulness Ceiling via Preference Dimensional Expansion
summary: In the realm of multi-objective alignment for large language models, balancing disparate human preferences often manifests as a zero-sum conflict. Specifically, the intrinsic tension between competing goals dictates that aggressively optimizing for one metric (e.g., helpfulness) frequently incurs a substantial penalty on another (e.g., harmlessness). While prior work mainly focuses on data selection, parameter merging, or algorithmic balancing during training, these approaches merely force compromises between divergent preferences along a fixed Pareto frontier, failing to fundamentally resolve the inherent trade-off. In this work, we approach this problem from a novel perspective of multi-dimensional rewards. By scaling up the model's rollouts and analyzing the outputs across different reward dimensions, we arrive at a critical conclusion: the conflict among multiple objectives stems from the fact that the prompt itself inherently restricts the achievable multi-dimensional rewards. Based on this core observation, we propose MORA: Multi-Objective Reward Assimilation. Specifically, MORA isolates single-reward prompts through pre-sampling and expands their reward diversity by rewriting the original questions to incorporate multi-dimensional intents. Extensive experiments demonstrate that: (1) in sequential alignment, MORA achieves single-preference improvements ranging from 5% to 12.4%, with exceptional gains in harmlessness, after multiple-preference alignment across helpful, harmless, and truthful dimensions. (2) In simultaneous alignment, MORA achieves an average overall reward improvement of 4.6%. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MORA-MPA.

AI.tldr: MORA is a novel method for multi-objective alignment of LLMs that addresses inherent trade-offs between competing preferences (e.g., helpfulness vs. harmlessness) by identifying that prompt content fundamentally restricts achievable multi-dimensional rewards. It isolates single-reward prompts via pre-sampling and rewrites questions to incorporate multi-dimensional intents, achieving 5-12.4% improvement in single preferences and 4.6% average overall reward improvement.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-objective alignment methods (data selection, parameter merging, algorithmic balancing) only force compromises along a fixed Pareto frontier without fundamentally resolving the inherent zero-sum conflict between competing preferences like helpfulness and harmlessness.
AI.method: MORA (Multi-Objective Reward Assimilation) isolates single-reward prompts through pre-sampling, then expands reward diversity by rewriting original questions to incorporate multi-dimensional intents, enabling models to achieve higher rewards across multiple objectives simultaneously.
AI.result: (1) In sequential alignment, MORA achieves 5-12.4% single-preference improvements with notable harmlessness gains after multi-preference alignment across helpful, harmless, and truthful dimensions. (2) In simultaneous alignment, MORA achieves 4.6% average overall reward improvement.
AI.conclusion: The conflict among multiple objectives stems from prompts inherently restricting achievable multi-dimensional rewards, and MORA effectively resolves this by rewriting prompts to incorporate diverse intents, enabling better multi-objective alignment without forced compromises.

title: Persistent and Conversational Multi-Method Explainability for Trustworthy Financial AI
summary: Financial institutions increasingly require AI explanations that are persistent, cross-validated across methods, and conversationally accessible to human decision-makers. We present an architecture for human-centered explainable AI in financial sentiment analysis that combines three contributions. First, we treat XAI artifacts -- LIME feature attributions, occlusion-based word importance scores, and saliency heatmaps -- as persistent, searchable objects in distributed S3-compatible storage with structured metadata and natural-language summaries, enabling semantic retrieval over explanation history and automatic index reconstruction after system failures. Second, we enable multi-method explanation triangulation, where a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant compares and synthesizes results from multiple XAI methods applied to the same prediction, allowing users to assess explanation robustness through natural-language dialogue. Third, we evaluate the faithfulness of generated explanations using automated checks over grounding completeness, hallucinated claims, and method-attribution behavior. We demonstrate the architecture on an EXTRA-BRAIN financial sentiment analysis pipeline using FinBERT predictions and present evaluation results showing that constrained prompting reduces hallucination rate by 36\% and increases method-attribution citations by 73\% compared to naive prompting. We discuss implications for trustworthy, human-centered AI services in regulated financial environments.

AI.tldr: An architecture for human-centered explainable AI in financial sentiment analysis that treats XAI artifacts as persistent searchable objects, enables multi-method explanation triangulation via RAG, and evaluates faithfulness; demonstrating a 36% hallucination reduction and 73% increase in method-attribution citations using constrained prompting.
AI.motivation: Financial institutions need AI explanations that are persistent, cross-validated across methods, and conversationally accessible to human decision-makers for trustworthy and regulated environments.
AI.method: (1) Persistent XAI artifacts as searchable S3-compatible objects with metadata and summaries; (2) Multi-method explanation triangulation via RAG assistant comparing LIME, occlusion scores, and saliency heatmaps; (3) Faithfulness evaluation through automated checks on grounding completeness, hallucinated claims, and method-attribution behavior.
AI.result: Constrained prompting reduces hallucination rate by 36% and increases method-attribution citations by 73% compared to naive prompting on FINBERT-based EXTRA-BRAIN financial sentiment analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture supports trustworthy, human-centered AI services in regulated financial environments by enabling persistent, triangulated, and verifiable explanations.

title: Toward Stable Value Alignment: Introducing Independent Modules for Consistent Value Guidance
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values typically relies on post-training or inference-time steering that directly manipulates the backbone's parameters or representation space. However, a critical gap exists: the model's residual stream is highly dynamic, in which values exist as fragile, low-dimensional properties, inherently incompatible with the stability required for consistent value expression. In this paper, we propose the Stable Value Guidance Transformer (SVGT), which addresses this gap through an independent value module incorporating two key designs: (1) independent value modeling, maintaining normative representations in a dedicated value space isolated from the backbone, and (2) explicit behavioral guidance, transducing these stable signals into learnable latent Bridge Tokens. These tokens serve as dynamic value anchors to explicitly steer the generative trajectory, ensuring robust adherence across diverse contexts without disrupting the backbone's internal representations. Experiments across multiple backbones and safety benchmarks show that SVGT generally reduces harmful scores by over 70% while maintaining generation fluency, demonstrating the efficacy of architecturally grounded value modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/Clervils/SVGT.git.

AI.tldr: SVGT introduces an independent value module with dedicated value space and learnable Bridge Tokens to stably guide LLM generation, reducing harmful outputs by over 70% without compromising fluency.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment methods fail because values in the residual stream are fragile and low-dimensional, lacking stability for consistent value expression across contexts.
AI.method: SVGT uses (1) independent value modeling that isolates normative representations in a dedicated value space from the backbone, and (2) explicit behavioral guidance via learnable latent Bridge Tokens that act as dynamic anchors to steer generation without disrupting internal representations.
AI.result: Across multiple backbones and safety benchmarks, SVGT reduces harmful scores by over 70% while maintaining generation fluency.
AI.conclusion: Architecturally grounded value modeling is an effective alternative to post-training or inference-time steering for stable value alignment in LLMs.

title: SafeSteer: A Decoding-level Defense Mechanism for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are gaining increasing attention. Due to the heterogeneity of their input features, they face significant challenges in terms of jailbreak defenses. Current defense methods rely on costly fine-tuning or inefficient post-hoc interventions, limiting their ability to address novel attacks and involving performance trade-offs. To address the above issues, we explore the inherent safety capabilities within MLLMs and quantify their intrinsic ability to discern harmfulness at decoding stage. We observe that 1) MLLMs can distinguish the harmful and harmless inputs during decoding process, 2) Image-based attacks are more stealthy. Based on these insights, we introduce SafeSteer, a decoding-level defense mechanism for MLLMs. Specifically, it includes a Decoding-Probe, a lightweight probe for detecting and correcting harmful output during decoding, which iteratively steers the decoding process toward safety. Furthermore, a modal semantic alignment vector is integrated to transfer the strong textual safety alignment to the vision modality. Experiments on multiple MLLMs demonstrate that SafeSterr can improve MLLMs' safety by up to 33.40\% without fine-tuning. Notably, it can maintain the effectiveness of MLLMs, ensuring a balance between their helpfulness and harmlessness.

AI.tldr: SafeSteer is a decoding-level defense mechanism for MLLMs that uses a lightweight Decoding-Probe to detect and correct harmful outputs during decoding, plus a modal semantic alignment vector to transfer textual safety alignment to vision modality, improving safety by up to 33.40% without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: MLLMs face significant jailbreak defense challenges due to input feature heterogeneity. Current defenses rely on costly fine-tuning or inefficient post-hoc interventions, limiting their ability to address novel attacks and involving performance trade-offs.
AI.method: SafeSteer introduces Decoding-Probe, a lightweight probe for detecting and correcting harmful output during decoding, iteratively steering the decoding process toward safety. It also integrates a modal semantic alignment vector to transfer textual safety alignment to the vision modality.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple MLLMs demonstrate up to 33.40% improvement in safety without fine-tuning, while maintaining a balance between helpfulness and harmlessness.
AI.conclusion: SafeSteer effectively improves MLLM safety by leveraging inherent safety capabilities at the decoding stage, avoiding costly fine-tuning while preserving model effectiveness.

title: OptArgus: A Multi-Agent System to Detect Hallucinations in LLM-based Optimization Modeling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language optimization problems into mathematical formulations and solver code, but matching the reference objective value is not a reliable test of correctness: an artifact may agree numerically while still changing the underlying optimization semantics. We formulate this issue as \emph{optimization-modeling hallucination detection}, namely structural consistency auditing over the problem description, symbolic model, and solver implementation. We develop, to our knowledge, the first fine-grained hallucination taxonomy specifically for optimization modeling, spanning objective, variable, constraint, and implementation failures. We use this taxonomy to design OptArgus, a multi-agent detector with conductor routing, specialist auditors, and evidence consolidation. To evaluate this setting, we introduce a three-part benchmark suite with $484$ clean artifacts, $1266$ controlled injected artifacts, and $6292$ natural LLM-generated artifacts. Against a matched single-agent baseline, OptArgus produces fewer false alarms on clean artifacts, more accurate top-ranked localization on controlled single-error cases, and stronger detection on natural model outputs. Together, these contributions turn optimization-modeling hallucination detection into a concrete empirical problem and suggest that modular, taxonomy-grounded auditing is a practical route to more reliable optimization modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces optimization-modeling hallucination detection, proposes a taxonomy of errors, develops OptArgus (a multi-agent detector), and creates a benchmark suite, showing that structured auditing outperforms single-agent baselines.
AI.motivation: Matching reference objective values is insufficient for verifying LLM-generated optimization models because artifacts can numerically agree while altering the underlying optimization semantics, creating a need for structural consistency auditing.
AI.method: The authors design a fine-grained hallucination taxonomy for optimization modeling (covering objective, variable, constraint, and implementation failures) and build OptArgus, a multi-agent detector with conductor routing, specialist auditors, and evidence consolidation. They also construct a three-part benchmark suite with 484 clean artifacts, 1,266 controlled injected artifacts, and 6,292 natural LLM-generated artifacts.
AI.result: OptArgus produces fewer false alarms on clean artifacts, more accurate top-ranked localization on controlled single-error cases, and stronger detection on natural model outputs compared to a matched single-agent baseline.
AI.conclusion: The work formalizes optimization-modeling hallucination detection as a concrete empirical problem and demonstrates that modular, taxonomy-grounded auditing is a practical approach to improving reliability in LLM-based optimization modeling.

title: When Reasoning Traces Become Performative: Step-Level Evidence that Chain-of-Thought Is an Imperfect Oversight Channel
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces are increasingly used both to improve language model capability and to audit model behavior, implicitly assuming that the visible trace remains synchronized with the computation that determines the answer. We test this assumption with a step-level Detect-Classify-Compare framework built around an answer-commitment proxy that is cross-validated with Patchscopes, tuned-lens probes, and causal direction ablation. Across nine models and seven reasoning benchmarks, latent commitment and explicit answer arrival align on only 61.9% of steps on average. The dominant mismatch pattern is confabulated continuation: 58.0% of detected mismatch events occur after the answer-commitment proxy has already stabilized while the trace continues producing deliberative-looking text, and a vacuousness analysis shows that the committed answer does not change during these steps. In architecture-matched Qwen2.5/DeepSeek-R1-Distill comparisons, the reasoning pipeline changes failure composition more than aggregate alignment, most clearly at 32B where confabulated steps decrease as contradictory states increase. Lower step-level alignment is also associated with larger CoT utility, suggesting that the settings that benefit most from CoT are often the least temporally faithful. Paired truncation and a complementary donor-corruption test further indicate that much post-commitment text is not load-bearing for the final answer. These findings suggest that CoT can remain useful while still being an unreliable report of when the answer was formed.

AI.tldr: CoT traces misalign with actual answer-commitment time in ~38% of steps, primarily due to confabulated continuation, and lower alignment correlates with greater CoT utility.
AI.motivation: To test the common assumption that visible chain-of-thought traces faithfully reflect the timing and process of answer formation in language models.
AI.method: A step-level Detect-Classify-Compare framework using an answer-commitment proxy cross-validated with Patchscopes, tuned-lens probes, and causal direction ablation; evaluated across 9 models and 7 reasoning benchmarks.
AI.result: Average alignment between latent commitment and explicit answer arrival is 61.9%; dominant mismatch is confabulated continuation (58.0% of mismatches); lower alignment correlates with higher CoT utility; post-commitment text is often not load-bearing.
AI.conclusion: CoT remains useful for performance but is an unreliable temporal report of when answers are formed; its utility and faithfulness are inversely related.

title: Towards Visually Grounded Multimodal Summarization via Cross-Modal Transformer and Gated Attention
summary: Multimodal summarization requires models to jointly understand textual and visual inputs to generate concise, semantically coherent summaries. Existing methods often inject shallow visual features into deep language models, leading to representational mismatches and weak cross-modal grounding. We propose a unified framework that jointly performs text summarization and representative image selection. Our system, SPeCTrA-Sum (Sampler Perceiver with Cross-modal Transformer and gated Attention for Summarization), introduces two key innovations. First, a Deep Visual Processor (DVP) aligns the visual encoder with the language model at corresponding depths, enabling hierarchical, layer-wise fusion that preserves semantic consistency. Second, a lightweight Visual Relevance Predictor (VRP) selects salient and diverse images by distilling soft labels from a Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) teacher. SPeCTrA-Sum is trained using a multi-objective loss that combines autoregressive summarization, cross-modal alignment, and DPP-based distillation. Experiments show that our system produces more accurate, visually grounded summaries and selects more representative images, demonstrating the benefits of depth-aware fusion and principled image selection for multimodal summarization.

AI.tldr: SPeCTrA-Sum is a unified multimodal summarization framework that jointly generates text summaries and selects representative images. It uses a Deep Visual Processor (DVP) for depth-aware visual-language alignment and a Visual Relevance Predictor (VRP) with DPP-based distillation for salient image selection, outperforming prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal summarization methods inject shallow visual features into deep language models, causing representational mismatches and weak cross-modal grounding.
AI.method: Proposes SPeCTrA-Sum with two key innovations: (1) Deep Visual Processor (DVP) for hierarchical, layer-wise fusion aligning visual encoder with language model at corresponding depths; (2) Visual Relevance Predictor (VRP) for salient and diverse image selection via distilling soft labels from a Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) teacher. Trained with multi-objective loss combining autoregressive summarization, cross-modal alignment, and DPP-based distillation.
AI.result: Produces more accurate, visually grounded summaries and selects more representative images, demonstrating the benefits of depth-aware fusion and principled image selection.
AI.conclusion: Depth-aware fusion and DPP-guided image selection significantly improve multimodal summarization quality and cross-modal grounding.

title: Beyond Inefficiency: Systemic Costs of Incivility in Multi-Agent Monte Carlo Simulations
summary: Unconstructive debate and uncivil communication carry well-documented costs for productivity and cohesion, yet isolating their effect on operational efficiency has proven difficult. Human subject research in this domain is constrained by ethical oversight, limited reproducibility, and the inherent unpredictability of naturalistic settings. We address this gap by leveraging Large Language Model (LLM) based Multi-Agent Systems as a controlled sociological sandbox, enabling systematic manipulation of communicative behavior at scale. Using a Monte Carlo simulation framework, we generate thousands of structured 1-on-1 adversarial debates across varying toxicity conditions, measuring convergence time, defined as the number of rounds required to reach a conclusion, as a proxy for interactional efficiency. Building on a prior study, we replicate and extend its findings across two additional LLM agents of varying parameter size, allowing us to assess whether the effects of toxic behavior on debate dynamics generalize across model scale. The convergence latency of 25% reported in the previous study was confirmed. It was found that this latency is significantly bigger for models with fewer parameters. We further identify a significant first-mover advantage, whereby the agent initiating the discussion wins significantly above chance regardless of toxicity condition.

AI.tldr: This study uses LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems as a controlled sociological sandbox with Monte Carlo simulations to systematically manipulate toxicity in adversarial debates. Replicating prior work, they confirm a 25% convergence latency due to toxic behavior, find this effect is larger in smaller models, and identify a significant first-mover advantage where the initiating agent wins above chance regardless of toxicity.
AI.motivation: Unconstructive debate and uncivil communication harm productivity and cohesion, but isolating their effect on operational efficiency is difficult due to ethical constraints, limited reproducibility, and unpredictability in human subject research. The authors aim to address this gap using LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems as a controlled sandbox for systematic manipulation.
AI.method: LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems; Monte Carlo simulation framework; structured 1-on-1 adversarial debates across varying toxicity conditions; replication and extension across two additional LLM agents of varying parameter size.
AI.result: Confirmed the 25% convergence latency from the prior study; found significantly larger latency for models with fewer parameters; identified a significant first-mover advantage where the initiating agent wins above chance regardless of toxicity condition.
AI.conclusion: Toxic behavior causes measurable convergence delays in adversarial debates, with the effect amplified in smaller models. The first-mover advantage is robust across toxicity conditions, indicating that debate structure itself biases outcomes beyond the content of communication.

title: Why Users Go There: World Knowledge-Augmented Generative Next POI Recommendation
summary: Generative point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results by formulating next POI prediction as a sequence generation task. However, the knowledge encoded in these models remains fixed after training, making them unable to perceive evolving real-world conditions that shape user mobility decisions, such as local events and cultural trends. To bridge this gap, we propose AWARE (Agent-based World knowledge Augmented REcommendation), which employs an LLM agent to generate location- and time-aware contextual narratives that capture regional cultural characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events relevant to each user. Rather than introducing generic or noisy information, AWARE further anchors these narratives in each user's behavioral context, grounding external world knowledge in personalized spatial-temporal patterns. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AWARE consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 12.4% relative improvement.

AI.tldr: AWARE is an LLM agent-based framework that generates personalized, location- and time-aware contextual narratives to augment POI recommendation, outperforming baselines by up to 12.4%.
AI.motivation: Existing generative POI recommendation models based on LLMs have fixed knowledge after training, making them unable to perceive evolving real-world conditions such as local events, seasonal trends, and cultural trends that influence user mobility.
AI.method: AWARE employs an LLM agent to generate location- and time-aware contextual narratives capturing regional culture, seasonal trends, and events, then anchors these narratives in each user's behavioral context to ground external world knowledge in personalized spatial-temporal patterns.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets show AWARE consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 12.4% relative improvement.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating evolving world knowledge via LLM agent-generated, user-grounded narratives significantly improves generative POI recommendation performance.

title: Beyond World-Frame Action Heads: Motion-Centric Action Frames for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly with stronger backbones, broader pre-training, and larger demonstration datasets, yet their action heads remain largely homogeneous: most directly predict action commands in a fixed world coordinate frame. We propose \textbf{MCF-Proto}, a lightweight action head that equips VLA policies with a Motion-Centric Action Frame (MCF) and a prototype-based action parameterization. At each step, the policy predicts a rotation $R_t \in SO(3)$, composes actions in the transformed local frame from a set of prototypes, and maps them back to the world frame for end-to-end training, using only standard demonstrations without auxiliary supervision. This simple design induces stable emergent structure. Without explicit directional labels, the learned local frames develop a stable geometric structure whose axes are strongly compatible with demonstrated end-effector motion. Meanwhile, actions in the learned representation become substantially more compact, with variation captured by fewer dominant directions and more regularly organized by shared prototypes. These structural properties translate into improved robustness, especially under geometric perturbations. Our results suggest that adding lightweight geometric and compositional structure to the action head can materially improve how VLA policies organize and generalize robotic manipulation behavior. An anonymized code repository is provided in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: MCF-Proto is a lightweight action head for VLA policies that uses a motion-centric action frame and prototype-based action parameterization to induce stable geometric structure in learned representations, improving robustness under geometric perturbations.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models use homogeneous action heads that directly predict actions in a fixed world coordinate frame, lacking geometric and compositional structure to organize manipulation behavior effectively.
AI.method: MCF-Proto predicts a rotation R_t ∈ SO(3) at each step to transform the action frame to a motion-centric local frame, parameterizes actions via a set of prototypes in this local frame, then maps back to world frame for end-to-end training using only standard demonstrations without auxiliary supervision.
AI.result: Learned local frames develop stable geometric structure compatible with demonstrated end-effector motion without explicit directional labels; actions become more compact with variation captured by fewer dominant directions and more regularly organized by shared prototypes; improved robustness under geometric perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Adding lightweight geometric and compositional structure to the action head can materially improve how VLA policies organize and generalize robotic manipulation behavior.

title: Automated Reformulation of Robust Optimization via Memory-Augmented Large Language Models
summary: Robust optimization (RO) provides a principled framework for decision-making under uncertainty, but its practical use is often limited by the need to manually reformulate uncertain optimization models into tractable deterministic counterparts. Recent large language models (LLMs) have been shown promising for automating optimization formulation, yet RO reformulation remains challenging because it requires precise multi-step reasoning and mathematically consistent transformations. To facilitate systematic evaluation of LLM-based reformulation, for which no dedicated benchmark currently exists, we develop AutoRO-Bench, a benchmark featuring an automated data generation pipeline for the core RO reformulation task and a curated dataset for the RO application task. To address the reformulation challenge, we propose Automated Reformulation with Experience Memory (AutoREM), a tuning-free memory-augmented framework that autonomously builds a structured textual experience memory by reflecting on past failed trajectories through a tailored offline adaptation procedure. AutoREM requires neither domain-specific expert knowledge nor parameter updates, and the resulting memory readily transfers across different base LLMs. Experimental results show that AutoREM consistently improves the accuracy and efficiency of RO reformulation across in-distribution datasets, out-of-distribution datasets, and diverse base LLMs.

AI.tldr: AutoRO-Bench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM-based robust optimization reformulation, and AutoREM is a tuning-free, memory-augmented framework that improves reformulation accuracy and efficiency by autonomously learning from past failures without expert knowledge or parameter updates.
AI.motivation: Robust optimization reformulation is difficult for LLMs because it requires precise multi-step reasoning and mathematically consistent transformations, and no dedicated benchmark exists for systematically evaluating LLM-based RO reformulation.
AI.method: AutoREM is a tuning-free memory-augmented framework that autonomously builds structured textual experience memory by reflecting on past failed trajectories through a tailored offline adaptation procedure, requiring no domain-specific expert knowledge or parameter updates.
AI.result: AutoREM consistently improves the accuracy and efficiency of RO reformulation across in-distribution datasets, out-of-distribution datasets, and diverse base LLMs.
AI.conclusion: AutoREM effectively addresses the RO reformulation challenge for LLMs, and its memory is transferable across different base LLMs without requiring parameter updates or expert knowledge.

title: MedMemoryBench: Benchmarking Agent Memory in Personalized Healthcare
summary: The large-scale deployment of personalized healthcare agents demands memory mechanisms that are exceptionally precise, safe, and capable of long-term clinical tracking. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on daily open-domain conversations, failing to capture the high-stakes complexity of real-world medical applications. Motivated by the stringent production requirements of an industry-leading health management agent serving tens of millions of active users, we introduce MedMemoryBench. We develop a human-agent collaborative pipeline to synthesize highly realistic, long-horizon medical trajectories based on clinically grounded, synthetic patient archetypes. This process yields a massive, expertly validated dataset comprising approximately 2,000 sessions and 16,000 interaction turns. Crucially, MedMemoryBench departs from traditional static evaluations by pioneering an "evaluate-while-constructing" streaming assessment protocol, which precisely mirrors dynamic memory accumulation in production environments. Furthermore, we formalize and systematically investigate the critical phenomenon of memory saturation, where sustained information influx actively degrades retrieval and reasoning robustness. Comprehensive benchmarking reveals severe bottlenecks in mainstream architectures, particularly concerning complex medical reasoning and noise resilience. By exposing these fundamental flaws, MedMemoryBench establishes a vital foundation for developing robust, production-ready medical agents.

AI.tldr: MedMemoryBench introduces a benchmark for evaluating memory mechanisms in personalized healthcare agents, featuring a synthetic long-horizon medical trajectory dataset (~2,000 sessions, ~16,000 turns), a streaming "evaluate-while-constructing" protocol, and systematic analysis of memory saturation, revealing severe limitations in mainstream architectures for medical reasoning and noise resilience.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on daily open-domain conversations and fail to capture the high-stakes complexity and stringent production requirements of real-world medical applications for personalized healthcare agents with memory mechanisms.
AI.method: A human-agent collaborative pipeline synthesizes realistic, long-horizon medical trajectories from clinically grounded synthetic patient archetypes, producing ~2,000 sessions and ~16,000 turns. A streaming "evaluate-while-constructing" assessment protocol is introduced to mirror dynamic memory accumulation in production environments. Memory saturation phenomena are formalized and systematically investigated.
AI.result: Comprehensive benchmarking reveals severe bottlenecks in mainstream architectures, especially in complex medical reasoning and noise resilience. The phenomenon of memory saturation (sustained information influx degrading retrieval and reasoning robustness) is identified and characterized.
AI.conclusion: MedMemoryBench exposes fundamental flaws in existing memory mechanisms and establishes a vital foundation for developing robust, production-ready medical agents.

title: On-Policy Self-Evolution via Failure Trajectories for Agentic Safety Alignment
summary: Tool-using LLM agents fail through trajectories rather than only final responses, as they may execute unsafe tool calls, follow injected instructions, comply with harmful requests, or over-refuse benign tasks despite producing a seemingly safe answer. Existing safety-alignment signals are largely response-level or off-policy, and often incur a safety-utility trade-off: improving agent safety comes at the cost of degraded task performance. Such sparse and single-objective rewards severely limit real-world usability. To bridge this gap, we propose FATE, an on-policy self-evolving framework that transforms verifier-scored failures into repair supervision without expert demonstrations. For each failure, the same policy proposes repair candidates, which are then re-scored by verifiers and filtered across security, utility, over-refusal control, and trajectory validity. This dense trajectory-level information is then used as a supervision signal for agent self-evolution. During this process, we further introduce Pareto-Front Policy Optimization (PFPO), combining supervised warmup with Pareto-aware policy optimization to preserve safety-utility trade-offs. Experiments on AgentDojo, AgentHarm, and ATBench show that FATE improves safety across different models and scales while preserving useful behavior. Compared with strong baselines, FATE reduces attack success rate by 33.5%, harmful compliance by 82.6%, and improves external trajectory-safety diagnosis by 6.5%. These results suggest that failed trajectories can provide structured repair supervision for safer self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: FATE is an on-policy self-evolving framework that converts agent trajectory failures into repair supervision using verifier scoring and Pareto-Front Policy Optimization, improving LLM agent safety (reducing attack success by 33.5% and harmful compliance by 82.6%) without sacrificing task utility.
AI.motivation: Existing safety-alignment signals for LLM agents are response-level or off-policy, leading to a safety-utility trade-off where improving safety degrades task performance. Sparse, single-objective rewards limit real-world usability of agent systems.
AI.method: FATE employs an on-policy self-evolving loop: verifier-scored failures (in security, utility, over-refusal, trajectory validity) are used to generate repair candidates from the same policy, which are re-scored and filtered. The dense trajectory-level supervision is then used with Pareto-Front Policy Optimization (PFPO), combining supervised warmup and Pareto-aware optimization to balance safety and utility.
AI.result: On AgentDojo, AgentHarm, and ATBench, FATE reduces attack success rate by 33.5%, harmful compliance by 82.6%, and improves external trajectory-safety diagnosis by 6.5% across different models and scales, while preserving useful behavior.
AI.conclusion: Failed trajectories can provide structured repair supervision for safer self-evolving agents without requiring expert demonstrations, effectively mitigating the safety-utility trade-off in LLM agent alignment.

title: From Clever Hans to Scientific Discovery: Interpreting EEG Foundational Transformers with LRP
summary: Emerging foundation models (FMs) in electroencephalography (EEG) promise a path to scale deep learning in diagnostics and brain-computer interfaces despite data scarcity, yet their opaque nature remains a barrier to wider adoption. We investigate attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) as a post-hoc attribution method for EEG-FMs, extending LRP's use on convolutional neural network (CNN)-based EEG models to the Transformer architectures that current FMs are based on. We find that LRP can both verify EEG-FM decisions and surface novel, biologically plausible hypotheses from them. In motor imagery, it unmasks 'Clever Hans' behavior where models prioritize task correlated ocular signals over the intended motor correlates. In a naturalistic paradigm for affect prediction, it reveals a recurring reliance on a central electrode cluster, suggesting a candidate sensorimotor signature of arousal. Though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in this complex domain, the results position LRP as a tool for both verification and exploration of EEG-FMs, a role that will grow in both importance and discovery potential as the underlying models mature.

AI.tldr: This paper applies attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to EEG foundation models (Transformers) for post-hoc attribution, showing it can verify model decisions (e.g., detecting 'Clever Hans' behavior in motor imagery) and uncover biologically plausible hypotheses (e.g., a central electrode cluster linked to arousal in affect prediction).
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models are promising but opaque, limiting adoption. The authors aim to extend LRP from CNN-based EEG models to Transformer-based EEG-FMs to enable post-hoc interpretability, both for verification and hypothesis generation.
AI.method: Attention-aware Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) is adapted for Transformer architectures used in EEG foundation models. The method is evaluated on motor imagery and naturalistic affect prediction tasks.
AI.result: LRP revealed 'Clever Hans' behavior in motor imagery (models relying on ocular signals instead of motor correlates) and identified a central electrode cluster in affect prediction, suggesting a sensorimotor signature of arousal.
AI.conclusion: LRP serves as both a verification and exploration tool for EEG-FMs, with growing importance as models mature, though heatmap interpretation remains ambiguous in complex domains.

title: Toward Modeling Player-Specific Chess Behaviors
summary: While artificial intelligence has achieved superhuman performance in chess, developing models that accurately emulate the individualized decision-making styles of human players remains a significant challenge. Existing human-like chess models capture general population behaviors based on skill levels but fail to reproduce the behavioral characteristics of specific historical champions. Furthermore, the standard evaluation metric, move accuracy, inherently penalizes natural human variance and ignores long-term behavioral consistency, leading to an incomplete assessment of stylistic fidelity. To address these limitations, an architecture is proposed that adapts the unified Maia-2 model to champion-specific embeddings, further enhanced by the integration of a limited Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process to enrich tactical exploration during move selection. To robustly evaluate this approach, a novel behavioral metric based on the Jensen-Shannon divergence is introduced. By compressing high-dimensional board representations into a latent space using an AutoEncoder and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), move distributions are discretized on a common grid to compare behavioral similarities. Results across 16 historical world champions indicate that while integrating MCTS decreases standard move accuracy, it improves stylistic alignment according to the proposed metric, substantially reducing the average Jensen-Shannon divergence. Ultimately, the proposed metric successfully discriminates between individual players and provides promising evidence toward more comprehensive evaluations of behavioral alignment between players and AI models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adapted Maia-2 model with champion-specific embeddings and limited MCTS to emulate individual chess champions' styles, and introduces a Jensen-Shannon divergence-based behavioral metric using AutoEncoder and UMAP for evaluating stylistic fidelity beyond move accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing human-like chess models capture general population behaviors based on skill levels but fail to reproduce the behavioral characteristics of specific historical champions, and the standard move accuracy metric penalizes natural human variance while ignoring long-term behavioral consistency.
AI.method: An architecture adapts Maia-2 to champion-specific embeddings with limited MCTS for tactical exploration; a behavioral metric uses Jensen-Shannon divergence by compressing board representations via AutoEncoder and UMAP, then discretizing move distributions on a common grid.
AI.result: Across 16 historical world champions, integrating MCTS decreased standard move accuracy but improved stylistic alignment, substantially reducing average Jensen-Shannon divergence.
AI.conclusion: The proposed metric successfully discriminates between individual players and provides promising evidence toward more comprehensive evaluations of behavioral alignment between players and AI models.

title: Rethinking Supervision Granularity: Segment-Level Learning for LLM-Based Theorem Proving
summary: Automated theorem proving with large language models in Lean 4 is commonly approached through either step-level tactic prediction with tree search or whole-proof generation. These two paradigms represent opposite granularities for constructing supervised training data: the former provides dense local signals but may fragment coherent proof processes, while the latter preserves global structure but requires complex end-to-end generation. In this paper, we revisit supervision granularity as a training set construction problem over proof trajectories and propose segment-level supervision, a training data construction strategy that extracts locally coherent proof segments for training policy models. We further reuse the same strategy at inference time to trigger short rollouts for existing step-level models. When trained with segment-level supervision on STP, LeanWorkbook, and NuminaMath-LEAN, the resulting policy models achieve proof success rates of 64.84%, 60.90%, and 66.31% on miniF2F, respectively, consistently outperforming both step-level and whole-proof baselines. Goal-aware rollout further improves existing step-level provers while reducing inference costs. It increases the proof success rate of BFS-Prover-V2-7B from 68.77% to 70.74% and that of InternLM2.5-StepProver from 59.59% to 60.33%, showing that appropriate supervision granularity better aligns model learning with proof structure and search. Code and models are available at https://github.com/NJUDeepEngine/SEG-ATP.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes segment-level supervision for automated theorem proving in Lean 4, extracting locally coherent proof segments as training data. This approach outperforms both step-level and whole-proof methods across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to 70.74% success rate on miniF2F while reducing inference costs.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for automated theorem proving in Lean 4 face a granularity dilemma: step-level tactic prediction with tree search provides dense local signals but fragments coherent proof processes, while whole-proof generation preserves global structure but requires complex end-to-end generation. The paper aims to find an optimal supervision granularity that balances these trade-offs.
AI.method: The paper proposes segment-level supervision, a training data construction strategy that extracts locally coherent proof segments from proof trajectories for training policy models. This same strategy is reused at inference time to trigger short rollouts for existing step-level models. Additionally, a goal-aware rollout mechanism is introduced to focus the rollout on relevant proof goals.
AI.result: Trained on STP, LeanWorkbook, and NuminaMath-LEAN, the models achieve proof success rates of 64.84%, 60.90%, and 66.31% on miniF2F respectively, consistently outperforming both step-level and whole-proof baselines. Goal-aware rollout improves BFS-Prover-V2-7B from 68.77% to 70.74% and InternLM2.5-StepProver from 59.59% to 60.33% while reducing inference costs.
AI.conclusion: Appropriate supervision granularity (segment-level) better aligns model learning with proof structure and search, achieving superior performance over both finer-grained step-level and coarser-grained whole-proof approaches. The segment-level strategy is effective for both training and inference-time improvement.

title: Rethinking Positional Encoding for Neural Vehicle Routing
summary: Transformer-based models have become the dominant paradigm for neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) of vehicle routing problems (VRPs), yet the role of positional encoding (PE) in these architectures remains largely unexplored. Unlike natural language, where tokens are uniformly spaced on a line, routing solutions exhibit several properties that render standard NLP positional encodings inadequate. In this work, we formalize three such structural properties that a routing-aware PE should respect, namely anisometric node distances, cyclic and direction-aware topology, and hierarchical depot-anchored global multi-route structure, combining them with a unifying design principle of geometric grounding. Guided by these criteria, we analyze and compare PE methods spanning NLP, graph-transformer, and routing-specific families, and propose a hierarchical anisometric PE that combines a distance-indexed, circularly consistent in-route encoding with a depot-anchored angular cross-route encoding. Extensive experiments across diverse VRP variants demonstrate that geometry-grounded PE consistently outperforms index-based alternatives, with gains that transfer across problem variants, model architectures, and distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies three structural properties that positional encodings (PE) should satisfy for neural combinatorial optimization of vehicle routing problems (anisometric distances, cyclic/direction-aware topology, hierarchical depot-anchored structure), proposes a geometry-grounded hierarchical anisometric PE combining distance-indexed circular in-route encoding with depot-anchored angular cross-route encoding, and shows consistent improvements over index-based alternatives across VRP variants, architectures, and distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Positional encoding in Transformer-based NCO for VRPs is largely unexplored, and standard NLP positional encodings fail to capture routing-specific structural properties such as anisometric node distances, cyclic and direction-aware topology, and hierarchical depot-anchored multi-route structure.
AI.method: The authors formalize three structural properties for routing-aware PE, propose a unifying geometric grounding design principle, analyze existing PE methods across NLP, graph-transformer, and routing-specific families, and introduce a hierarchical anisometric PE that combines distance-indexed circular in-route encoding with depot-anchored angular cross-route encoding.
AI.result: Geometry-grounded PE consistently outperforms index-based alternatives, with gains transferring across problem variants, model architectures, and distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Routing-aware geometric positional encodings are superior to standard index-based PEs for neural combinatorial optimization of VRPs, validating the proposed design principles.

title: Domain Restriction via Multi SAE Layer Transitions
summary: The general-purpose nature of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents a significant challenge for domain-specific applications, often leading to out-of-domain (OOD) interactions that undermine the provider's intent. Existing methods for detecting such scenarios treat the LLM as an uninterpretable black box and overlook the internal processing of inputs. In this work we show that layer transitions provide a promising avenue for extracting domain-specific signature. Specifically, we present several lightweight ways of learning on internal dynamics encoded using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) that exhibit great capability in distinguishing OOD texts. Building on top of SAEs representation transitions enables us to better interpret the LLM internal evolution of input processing and shed light on its decisions. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the method and benchmark it with the gemma-2 2B and 9B models. Our results emphasize the efficacy of the internal process in capturing fine-grained input-related details.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using internal layer transitions of LLMs, encoded via sparse autoencoders (SAEs), to detect out-of-domain (OOD) inputs. The method outperforms black-box approaches by leveraging interpretable internal dynamics, and is evaluated on Gemma-2 2B and 9B models.
AI.motivation: LLMs are general-purpose but often face out-of-domain (OOD) inputs in domain-specific applications, which undermines provider intent. Existing detection methods treat LLMs as black boxes and ignore internal processing, motivating the need for interpretable, internal-state-based OOD detection.
AI.method: The authors propose learning on internal dynamics encoded using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). They extract domain-specific signatures from layer transitions within the LLM, using lightweight learning methods on SAE representations to distinguish OOD texts.
AI.result: The method demonstrates strong capability in distinguishing OOD texts, and the analysis shows that internal process captures fine-grained input-related details. Benchmarking on Gemma-2 2B and 9B models confirms efficacy.
AI.conclusion: Layer transitions encoded with SAEs provide a promising, interpretable approach for OOD detection in LLMs, moving beyond black-box methods and shedding light on internal decision-making.

title: When Simulation Lies: A Sim-to-Real Benchmark and Domain-Randomized RL Recipe for Tool-Use Agents
comment: Dataset, code, and benchmark leaderboard are available at https://github.com/WillChow66/robustbench-tc-release.git and https://huggingface.co/spaces/willchow66/robustbench-tc-leaderboard
summary: Tool-use language agents are evaluated on benchmarks that assume clean inputs, unambiguous tool registries, and reliable APIs. Real deployments violate all these assumptions: user typos propagate into hallucinated tool names, a misconfigured request timeout can stall an agent indefinitely, and duplicate tool names across servers can freeze an SDK. We study these failures as a sim-to-real gap in the tool-use partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where deployment noise enters through the observation, action space, reward-relevant metadata, or transition dynamics. We introduce RobustBench-TC, a benchmark with 22 perturbation types organized by these four POMDP components, each grounded in a verified GitHub issue or documented tool-calling failure. Across 21 models from 1.5B to 32B parameters (including the closed-source o4-mini), the robustness profile is sharply uneven: observation perturbations reduce accuracy by less than 5%, while reward-relevant and transition perturbations reduce accuracy by roughly 40% and 30%, respectively; scale alone does not close these gaps. We then propose ToolRL-DR, a domain-randomization reinforcement learning (RL) recipe that trains a tool-use agent on perturbation-augmented trajectories spanning the three statically encodable POMDP components. On a 3B backbone, ToolRL-DR-Full retains roughly three-quarters of clean accuracy and reaches an aggregate perturbed accuracy comparable to open-source 14B function-calling baselines while substantially narrowing the gap to o4-mini. It closes approximately 27% of the Transition gap despite never seeing transition perturbations in training, suggesting that RL on adversarial static tool-use inputs induces a more persistent retry policy that transfers to unseen runtime failures. The dataset, code and benchmark leaderboard are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a sim-to-real gap in tool-use language agents due to deployment perturbations (typos, timeouts, duplicate names), introduces RobustBench-TC with 22 perturbation types across four POMDP components, shows that observation perturbations cause <5% accuracy drop while reward/transition perturbations cause ~30-40% drop, and proposes ToolRL-DR—a domain-randomization RL method that on a 3B backbone retains ~75% clean accuracy and matches 14B baselines, closing ~27% of the transition gap via transfer from static perturbations.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume clean inputs, unambiguous tool registries, and reliable APIs, but real deployments suffer from user typos, misconfigured timeouts, and duplicate tool names. The authors aim to study and bridge this sim-to-real gap in tool-use language agents.
AI.method: The authors formalize deployment failures via four POMDP components (observation, action space, reward-relevant metadata, transition dynamics), build RobustBench-TC with 22 perturbation types from real GitHub issues, and propose ToolRL-DR—a domain-randomization RL recipe training on perturbation-augmented trajectories spanning three statically encodable POMDP components.
AI.result: Observation perturbations reduce accuracy <5%; reward-relevant and transition perturbations reduce accuracy ~40% and ~30% respectively; scale alone doesn't close gaps.
