ToolRL-DR-Full (3B) retains ~75% clean accuracy, matches open-source 14B baselines on perturbed accuracy, and closes ~27% of the Transition gap despite never seeing transition perturbations in training.
AI.conclusion: Domain-randomization RL on adversarial static tool-use inputs induces persistent retry policies that transfer to unseen runtime failures, substantially narrowing the sim-to-real gap for tool-use agents.

title: From Noise to Diversity: Random Embedding Injection in LLM Reasoning
summary: Recent soft prompt research has tried to improve reasoning by inserting trained vectors into LLM inputs, yet whether the gain comes from the learned content or from the act of injection itself has not been carefully separated. We study Random Soft Prompts (RSPs), which drop the training step entirely and append a freshly drawn sequence of random embedding vectors to the input. Each RSP vector is sampled from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the entrywise mean and variance of the pretrained embedding table; the sequence carries no learned content, and yet reaches accuracy comparable to optimized soft prompts on math reasoning benchmarks in several settings. The mechanism unfolds in two stages: because attention has to absorb a never-seen-before random position, the distribution over the first few generated tokens flattens and reasoning trajectories branch, and as generation continues this influence dilutes naturally so the response commits to a single completion. We show that during inference RSPs lift early-stage token diversity and, combined with temperature sampling, widen Pass@N, the probability that at least one out of N attempts is correct. Beyond inference, we carry the same effect into DAPO training and demonstrate practical gains. Our contributions are: (i) RSP isolates the simplest form of soft prompt -- training-free, freshly resampled -- providing a unified lens for the structural effect of injection that variants otherwise differing in training and form all share; (ii) a theoretical and empirical validation of the underlying mechanism; and (iii) an extension from inference to training.

AI.tldr: Random Soft Prompts (RSPs) — untrained, freshly sampled random embedding vectors — achieve accuracy comparable to trained soft prompts on math reasoning by flattening early token distributions and increasing trajectory diversity, boosting Pass@N both at inference and during DAPO training.
AI.motivation: Existing soft prompt research attributes gains to learned content, but the structural effect of injection itself has not been separated from the effect of training. The paper aims to isolate whether any benefit stems from the mere act of injecting extra vectors, independent of learned information.
AI.method: RSP drops training entirely: each prompt vector is sampled from an isotropic Gaussian fitted to the mean/variance of the pretrained embedding table. The mechanism is analyzed via attention dynamics — unseen random positions flatten early token distributions, causing branched reasoning trajectories that later dilute naturally.
AI.result: RSPs reach accuracy comparable to optimized soft prompts on math reasoning benchmarks. They lift early-stage token diversity and, combined with temperature sampling, widen Pass@N. The effect also extends to DAPO training, yielding practical gains.
AI.conclusion: The structural effect of injection — not learned content — is the primary driver of soft prompt improvements. RSP provides a unified lens for this effect, with theoretical/empirical validation and demonstrated extension from inference to training.

title: Counterfactual Trace Auditing of LLM Agent Skills
comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/WillChow66/CTA.git
summary: Large Language Model agents are increasingly augmented with agent skills. Current evaluation methods for skills remain limited. Most deployed benchmarks report only pass rate before and after a skill is attached, treating the skill as a black box change to agent behavior. We introduce Counterfactual Trace Auditing (CTA), a framework for measuring how a skill changes agent behavior. CTA pairs each with skill agent trace with a without skill counterpart on the same task, segments both traces into goal directed phases, aligns the phases, and emits structured Skill Influence Pattern (SIP) annotations. These annotations describe the behavioral effect of a skill rather than only its task outcome. We instantiate CTA on SWE-Skills-Bench with Claude across 49 software engineering tasks. The resulting audit reveals a clear evaluation gap. Pass rate changes by only +0.3 percentage points on average, suggesting little aggregate effect. Yet CTA identifies 522 SIP instances across the same paired traces, showing that the skills substantially reshape agent behavior even when pass rate is nearly unchanged. The audit also separates several recurring effects that pass rate cannot detect, including literal template copying, off task artifact creation, excess planning, and task recovery. Three findings emerge. First, high baseline tasks contain most of the observed skill effects, although their pass rate is already saturated and therefore cannot reflect those effects. Second, tasks with moderate baseline performance show the most recoverable gain, but often at substantially higher token cost. Third, the dominant SIP type can be identified by baseline bucket: surface anchoring is most common on ceiling tasks and edge-case prompting is most common on mid-range and floor tasks. These regularities turn informal failure mode observations into reproducible behavioral measurements.

AI.tldr: CTA is a framework that measures how skills change agent behavior by pairing with/without skill traces, segmenting them into aligned phases, and emitting SIP annotations. Applied to SWE-Skills-Bench, it reveals that skills substantially reshape behavior (522 SIP instances) despite only +0.3pp pass rate change, uncovering effects like template copying, artifact creation, excess planning, and task recovery that pass rate cannot detect.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods treat skills as black box changes and report only pass rate, failing to capture how skills actually alter agent behavior beyond task outcomes.
AI.method: CTA pairs with-skill and without-skill agent traces on the same task, segments both into goal-directed phases, aligns phases, and emits structured Skill Influence Pattern (SIP) annotations describing behavioral effects.
AI.result: CTA identified 522 SIP instances across 49 tasks; pass rate changed only +0.3pp on average, yet skills substantially reshaped behavior. Three findings: (1) high-baseline tasks contain most skill effects but pass rate is saturated; (2) moderate-baseline tasks show most recoverable gain but at higher token cost; (3) dominant SIP type varies by baseline bucket (surface anchoring on ceiling tasks, edge-case prompting on mid/floor tasks).
AI.conclusion: Pass rate alone is insufficient for evaluating skill impact; CTA provides reproducible behavioral measurements that turn informal failure mode observations into structured, quantifiable insights about how skills influence agent behavior.

title: Assessing and Mitigating Miscalibration in LLM-Based Social Science Measurement
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in social science as scalable measurement tools for converting unstructured text into variables that can enter standard empirical designs. Measurement validity demands more than high average accuracy, which requires well calibrated confidence that faithfully reflects the empirical probability of each measurement being correct. This paper studies the model miscalibration in LLM-based social science measurement. We begin with a case study on FOMC and show that confidence based filtering can change downstream regression estimates when LLM confidence is miscalibrated. We then audit calibration across 14 social science constructs covering both proprietary models, including GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2, and open source models. Across tasks and model families, reported confidence is poorly aligned with tolerance-based correctness. As a simple mitigation, we propose a soft label distillation pipeline for calibrating Bert with LLM. The method converts an LLM score and its verbalized confidence into a soft target distribution, then trains a smaller discriminative classifier on encoder models for these targets. Averaged across datasets, this approach reduces ECE by 43.2\% and Brier by 34.0\%. These results suggest that LLM-based social science pipelines should treat calibration as part of measurement validity, rather than as an optional post-processing concern.

AI.tldr: LLMs used for social science measurement suffer from miscalibrated confidence, and a soft label distillation pipeline using BERT reduces ECE by 43.2% and Brier by 34.0% as a mitigation.
AI.motivation: Measurement validity in LLM-based social science requires well-calibrated confidence, but current LLMs exhibit poor alignment between reported confidence and actual correctness, which can distort downstream regression estimates.
AI.method: The paper audits calibration across 14 social science constructs using proprietary models (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2) and open-source models, then proposes a soft label distillation pipeline that converts LLM scores and verbalized confidence into soft targets to train a smaller BERT-based classifier.
AI.result: The proposed method reduces Expected Calibration Error (ECE) by 43.2% and Brier score by 34.0% on average across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Calibration should be treated as a core component of measurement validity in LLM-based social science pipelines, not merely as an optional post-processing step.

title: On the Limitations of Large Language Models for Conceptual Database Modeling
summary: This article analyzes the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as support for the conceptual modeling of relational databases through the automatic generation of Entity-Relationship (ER) diagrams from natural language requirements. The approach combines different language models with prompt engineering techniques to evaluate their ability to identify entities, relationships, and attributes in a conceptually consistent manner. The experimental evaluation involved three LLMs, each subjected to three prompting techniques (Zero-Shot, Chain of Thought, and Chain of Thought + Verifier), applied to the same requirements scenario with progressively increasing complexity. The generated diagrams were qualitatively analyzed through direct comparison with the textual requirements, considering the structural and semantic adherence of the modeled elements. The results indicate that, although LLMs show reasonable performance in less complex scenarios, their reliability decreases as the complexity of the requirements increases, with a rise in inconsistencies, ambiguities, and failures in representing constraints. These findings reinforce that, in their current state, LLMs are not sufficiently mature for reliable use in complex scenarios, and the cost of validation may offset the apparent productivity gains.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates LLMs (using Zero-Shot, Chain of Thought, and Chain of Thought + Verifier prompting) for generating ER diagrams from natural language. Results show reasonable performance on simple scenarios but declining reliability, increased inconsistencies, and ambiguity as complexity grows, concluding LLMs are not mature enough for complex conceptual modeling tasks.
AI.motivation: To assess whether LLMs can reliably support conceptual modeling of relational databases by automatically generating ER diagrams from natural language requirements, and to identify their limitations as complexity increases.
AI.method: Three LLMs were tested with three prompting techniques (Zero-Shot, Chain of Thought, Chain of Thought + Verifier) on requirements of increasing complexity. Generated ER diagrams were qualitatively analyzed for structural and semantic adherence compared to textual requirements.
AI.result: LLMs perform reasonably well on less complex scenarios but show decreased reliability, increased inconsistencies, ambiguities, and constraint representation failures as complexity grows.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not sufficiently mature for reliable use in complex conceptual modeling scenarios, and the cost of validation may offset productivity gains.

title: Random-Set Graph Neural Networks
summary: Uncertainty quantification has become an important factor in understanding the data representations produced by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite their predictive capabilities being ever useful across industrial workspaces, the inherent uncertainty induced by the nature of the data is a huge mitigating factor to GNN performance. While aleatoric uncertainty is the result of noisy and incomplete stochastic data such as missing edges or over-smoothing, epistemic uncertainty arises from lack of knowledge about a system or model (e.g., a graph's topology or node feature representation), which can be reduced by gathering more data and information. In this paper, we propose an original new framework in which node-level epistemic uncertainty is modelled in a belief function (finite random set) formalism. The resulting Random-Set Graph Neural Networks have a belief-function head predicting a random set over the list of classes, from which both a precise probability prediction and a measure of epistemic uncertainty can be obtained. Extensive experiments on 9 different graph learning datasets, including real-world autonomous driving benchmarks as such Nuscene and ROAD, demonstrate RS-GNN's superior uncertainty quantification capabilities

AI.tldr: RS-GNN uses belief function formalism to model epistemic uncertainty at node-level, achieving superior uncertainty quantification on graph learning tasks.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification is crucial for GNN performance in industrial applications, but both aleatoric (noisy/incomplete data) and epistemic (limited knowledge) uncertainties degrade GNN performance.
AI.method: Proposes Random-Set Graph Neural Networks (RS-GNN) with a belief-function head that predicts random sets over class labels, producing both precise probability predictions and epistemic uncertainty measures.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 9 graph learning datasets (including Nuscenes and ROAD autonomous driving benchmarks) demonstrate RS-GNN's superior uncertainty quantification capabilities.
AI.conclusion: RS-GNN effectively models node-level epistemic uncertainty using random set formalism, outperforming existing methods in uncertainty quantification for graph learning tasks.

title: BadSKP: Backdoor Attacks on Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs with Soft Prompts
summary: Recent knowledge graph (KG)-enhanced large language models (LLMs) move beyond purely textual knowledge augmentation by encoding retrieved subgraphs into continuous soft prompts via graph neural networks, introducing a graph-conditioned channel that operates alongside the standard text interface. However, existing backdoor attacks are largely designed for the textual channel, and their effectiveness against this dual-channel architecture remains unclear. We show that this architecture creates a robustness gap: text-channel backdoor attacks that readily compromise textual KG prompting systems become largely ineffective against soft-prompt-based counterparts. We interpret this gap through semantic anchoring, whereby graph-derived soft prompts bias the generation-driving hidden state toward query-consistent semantics and suppress surface-level malicious instructions. Because this anchoring effect is itself induced by the graph channel, an attacker who manipulates graph-level representations can in turn redirect it toward adversarial semantics. To demonstrate this risk, we propose BadSKP, a backdoor attack that targets the graph-to-prompt interface through a multi-stage optimization strategy: it constructs adversarial target embeddings, optimizes poisoned node embeddings to steer the induced soft prompt, and approximates the optimized representations with fluent adversarial node attributes. Experiments on two soft-prompt KG-enhanced LLMs across four datasets show that BadSKP achieves high attack success under both frozen and trojaned settings, while text-only attacks remain unreliable even under perplexity-based defenses.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that standard text-channel backdoor attacks fail against soft-prompt-based KG-enhanced LLMs due to semantic anchoring from graph-derived prompts, and proposes BadSKP—a backdoor attack targeting the graph-to-prompt interface via multi-stage optimization—that achieves high attack success across models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor attacks are designed for single text-channel LLMs, but KG-enhanced LLMs now use a dual-channel architecture (text + graph-conditioned soft prompts). The robustness of this hybrid architecture against backdoor attacks is unknown, creating a security gap that needs investigation.
AI.method: The paper identifies the "semantic anchoring" effect where graph-derived soft prompts bias generation toward query-consistent semantics, suppressing text-channel attacks. It then proposes BadSKP, a multi-stage optimization attack: (1) construct adversarial target embeddings, (2) optimize poisoned node embeddings to steer the induced soft prompt, and (3) approximate optimized representations with fluent adversarial node attributes.
AI.result: BadSKP achieves high attack success on two soft-prompt KG-enhanced LLMs across four datasets under both frozen and trojaned settings, while text-only attacks remain unreliable even against perplexity-based defenses.
AI.conclusion: The graph channel creates both a robustness gap (defending against text attacks) and a new vulnerability surface (graph-level backdoor attacks). BadSKP demonstrates that attackers who manipulate graph representations can redirect semantic anchoring toward adversarial goals, highlighting the need for security measures at the graph-to-prompt interface.

title: LegalCheck: Retrieval- and Context-Augmented Generation for Drafting Municipal Legal Advice Letters
comment: Accepted at ICAIL 2026 as Short Paper
summary: Public-sector legal departments in the Netherlands face acute staff shortages, increased case volumes, and increased pressure to meet regulatory compliance. This paper presents LegalCheck, a novel system that addresses these challenges by automating the drafting of objection response letters through a combination of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Context-Augmented Generation (CAG). Using a large language model (LLM) alongside curated legal knowledge bases, LegalCheck performs retrieval of relevant laws and precedents, and uses controlled prompting to incorporate both external knowledge and case-specific details into a coherent draft. An expert-in-the-loop review ensures that each generated letter is legally sound and contextually appropriate. In a real-world deployment within the Municipality of Amsterdam, LegalCheck produced near-final advice letters in minutes rather than hours, while maintaining high legal consistency and factual accuracy. The output is based on actual regulations and prior cases, providing explainable outputs that captured the vast majority of required legal reasoning (often 80\% to 100\% of essential content). Legal professionals found that the system reduced their workload and ensured a consistent application of legal standards, without replacing human judgment. These results demonstrate substantial efficiency gains, improved legal consistency, and positive user acceptance. More broadly, this work illustrates how responsible AI can be deployed in the legal domain by augmenting LLMs with domain knowledge and governance mechanisms.

AI.tldr: LegalCheck is a system combining RAG and CAG with an LLM to automate drafting of objection response letters for Dutch public-sector legal departments. Deployed in the Municipality of Amsterdam, it reduces drafting time from hours to minutes while achieving 80-100% legal reasoning coverage, high consistency, and positive expert acceptance, without replacing human judgment.
AI.motivation: Public-sector legal departments in the Netherlands face acute staff shortages, increased case volumes, and heightened pressure to meet regulatory compliance, necessitating an automated solution to improve efficiency without sacrificing legal quality.
AI.method: LegalCheck combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Context-Augmented Generation (CAG) with a large language model, curated legal knowledge bases (laws and precedents), and controlled prompting to incorporate both external knowledge and case-specific details. An expert-in-the-loop review ensures legal soundness and contextual appropriateness.
AI.result: Near-final advice letters produced in minutes versus hours; high legal consistency and factual accuracy; outputs based on actual regulations and prior cases; 80-100% of essential legal reasoning captured; reduced workload and consistent application of legal standards reported by legal professionals.
AI.conclusion: LegalCheck demonstrates substantial efficiency gains, improved legal consistency, and positive user acceptance. The work illustrates how responsible AI can be deployed in the legal domain by augmenting LLMs with domain knowledge and governance mechanisms, without replacing human judgment.

title: LLMs and the ZPD
comment: Short paper submitted to Interspeech 2026 (Desk Reject) 4 pages, plus references. 2 figures
summary: One hundred years ago Vygotsky and his circle were exploring the nature of consciousness and defining what would become psychology in the Soviet Union. They concluded that children develop "scientific thinking" through interacting with enculturated adults in Zones of Proximal Development or ZPDs. The proposal is that, contrary to the claims of some, the LLM mechanism is not doing thinking with "distributed representations," but rather the completion model is doing "primitive thinking" in terms of *practices*. Viewed from this perspective, it would seem our large language models don't hallucinate, but rather dream, and that what is needed is not "guard rails" but an investigation of the set of cognitive tools that enable us to do things that look like common-sense. The proposal here is that *interaction* is core to human communication rather than just an add-on to "real" understanding.

AI.tldr: This paper reinterprets LLM behavior through a Vygotskian lens, arguing that LLMs perform "primitive thinking" via pattern completion rather than distributed representations, that their outputs resemble dreaming more than hallucination, and that interaction—not static understanding—is central to human cognition.
AI.motivation: To challenge prevailing views that LLMs think through distributed representations and to instead ground their operation in Vygotsky's concepts of ZPD and enculturated development, suggesting that what is called "hallucination" is more akin to dreaming and that interaction, not guardrails, is the pathway to improving LLM cognition.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis drawing parallels between Vygotsky's theory of child development (scientific thinking via ZPDs) and the operation of LLM completion models, arguing that LLMs engage in "primitive thinking" based on learned *practices* rather than distributed representations.
AI.result: Proposes that LLM errors are not hallucinations but dreams; identifies interaction as core (not ancillary) to human communication and common-sense reasoning; suggests the need to study cognitive tools that support common-sense rather than imposing guardrails.
AI.conclusion: LLMs should be understood as engaging in primitive, practice-based pattern completion rather than genuine understanding; their failures are dream-like rather than hallucinatory; and future work should focus on interaction and cognitive toolkits rather than restrictive guardrails.

title: OmniRefine: Alignment-Aware Cooperative Compression for Efficient Omnimodal Large Language Models
summary: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) show strong capability in audio-video understanding, but their practical deployment remains limited by high inference cost of long video streams and dense audio sequences. Despite recent progress, existing compression methods for Omni-LLMs typically rely on fixed or native compression units, which can disrupt cross-modal correspondence and the complementary information required for audio-video reasoning, making it difficult to improve inference efficiency while stably preserving performance. To address this, we propose OmniRefine, a training-free two-stage framework for efficient audio-visual token compression in Omni-LLMs. First, Correspondence-Preserving Chunk Refinement refines native chunk boundaries into cross-modally aligned compression units through frame-audio similarity and dynamic programming. Second, Modality-Aware Cooperative Compression jointly compresses video and audio tokens within each refined unit to reduce redundancy while preserving critical evidence. Extensive experiments show that OmniRefine achieves a better efficiency-performance trade-off than strong baselines and maintains stable performance under lower compression ratios. On WorldSense, it still reaches 46.7% accuracy at a 44% token retention ratio, nearly matching the full-token baseline. The code and interface will be released to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: OmniRefine is a training-free two-stage framework for efficient audio-visual token compression in Omni-LLMs, using cross-modally aligned chunk refinement and modality-aware cooperative compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: High inference cost of long video streams and dense audio sequences hinders practical deployment of Omni-LLMs, and existing compression methods using fixed/native units disrupt cross-modal correspondence and complementary information needed for audio-video reasoning.
AI.method: A two-stage training-free framework: (1) Correspondence-Preserving Chunk Refinement aligns native chunk boundaries into cross-modally consistent compression units via frame-audio similarity and dynamic programming; (2) Modality-Aware Cooperative Compression jointly reduces redundancy in video and audio tokens within each refined unit.
AI.result: Achieves better efficiency-performance trade-off than strong baselines, with stable performance under lower compression ratios. On WorldSense, achieves 46.7% accuracy at 44% token retention ratio, nearly matching the full-token baseline.
AI.conclusion: OmniRefine effectively addresses the efficiency-performance trade-off in Omni-LLMs through training-free, cross-modal aware token compression, enabling more practical deployment.

title: SAGE: A Self-Evolving Agentic Graph-Memory Engine for Structure-Aware Associative Memory
summary: Long-term memory is becoming a central bottleneck for language agents. Exsting RAG and GraphRAG systems largely treat memory graphs as static retrieval middleware, which limits their ability to recover complete evidence chains from partial cues, exploit reusable graph-structrual roles, and improve the memory itself through downstream feedback. We introduce SAGE, a Self-evolving Agentic Graph-memory Engine that models graph memory as a dynamic long-term memory substrate. SAGE couples two roles: a memory writer that incrementally constucts structured graph memory from interaction histories, and a Graph Foundation Model-based memory reader to perform retrieval and provide feedback to the memory writer. We provide rigorooous theoretical annalyses supporting the framework. Across multi-hop QA, open-domain retireval, domain-specific review QA, and long-term agent-memory benchmarks, SAGE improves evidence recovery, answer grounding, and retrieval efficiency: after two self-evolution rounds, it achieves the best average rank on multi-hop QA; in zero-shot open-domain transfer, it reaches 82.5/91.6 Recall@2/5 on NQ. Further results on LongMemEval and HaluMem show that traning and reader-writer feedback improve multiple long-term memory and hallucination-diagnostic metrics, suggesting that self-evolving, structure-aware graph memory is a promising foundation for robust long-horizon language agents.

AI.tldr: SAGE is a self-evolving graph memory engine that uses a writer to construct structured memory and a Graph Foundation Model-based reader for retrieval and feedback, achieving state-of-the-art results on multi-hop QA, open-domain retrieval, and long-term agent memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG and GraphRAG systems treat memory graphs as static retrieval middleware, limiting their ability to recover complete evidence chains from partial cues, exploit reusable graph-structural roles, and improve memory through downstream feedback.
AI.method: SAGE couples two roles: a memory writer that incrementally constructs structured graph memory from interaction histories, and a Graph Foundation Model-based memory reader that performs retrieval and provides feedback to the writer, enabling self-evolving graph memory.
AI.result: After two self-evolution rounds, SAGE achieves the best average rank on multi-hop QA; in zero-shot open-domain transfer, it reaches 82.5/91.6 Recall@2/5 on NQ; it also improves long-term memory and hallucination-diagnostic metrics on LongMemEval and HaluMem.
AI.conclusion: Self-evolving, structure-aware graph memory is a promising foundation for robust long-horizon language agents.

title: Intermediate Artifacts as First-Class Citizens: A Data Model for Durable Intermediate Artifacts in Agentic Systems
summary:
Many AI systems are organized around loops in which models reason, call tools, observe results, and continue until a task is complete. These systems often produce final artifacts such as memos, plans, recommendations, and analyses, while the intermediate work that shaped those outputs remains ephemeral. For multi-step, revisable AI work, final artifacts are often lossy projections over upstream state.
  We argue that such systems should preserve durable, inspectable intermediate artifacts: typed, structured, addressable, versioned, dependency-aware, authoritative, and consumable by downstream computation. These artifacts are not the model's private chain-of-thought. They are maintained work products such as evidence maps, claim structures, criteria, assumptions, plans, transformation rules, synthesis procedures, unresolved tensions, and partial products that later humans and agents can inspect, revise, supersede, and improve.
  The contribution is a systems-level data model. We distinguish intermediate artifacts from chat transcripts, memory, hidden chain-of-thought, narration, thinking, and final answers; formalize additive and superseding update semantics with explicit current-state resolution; describe how artifact lineage supports durable intermediate state across revisions; and argue that evaluation must target maintained-state quality, not only final-output quality. The claim is not that artifacts make models smarter. It is that durable intermediate artifacts make AI-generated work more inspectable, revisable, and maintainable over time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a systems-level data model for preserving durable, inspectable intermediate artifacts (e.g., evidence maps, claim structures, plans) in AI systems that reason, call tools, and revise work iteratively, arguing that such artifacts make AI-generated work more inspectable, revisable, and maintainable compared to relying solely on final outputs or ephemeral internal states.
AI.motivation: Final artifacts in multi-step, revisable AI systems are lossy projections over upstream state, and intermediate work that shapes outputs remains ephemeral, making inspection, revision, and maintenance difficult.
AI.method: The paper formalizes a systems-level data model that distinguishes intermediate artifacts from chat transcripts, memory, hidden chain-of-thought, and final answers; defines additive and superseding update semantics with explicit current-state resolution; describes artifact lineage for durable state across revisions; and proposes evaluation criteria for maintained-state quality.
AI.result: A formal framework for typed, structured, addressable, versioned, dependency-aware, authoritative intermediate artifacts that are consumable by downstream computation, along with update semantics and lineage tracking.
AI.conclusion: Durable intermediate artifacts do not make models smarter, but they make AI-generated work more inspectable, revisable, and maintainable over time.

title: Autonomy and Agency in Agentic AI: Architectural Tactics for Regulated Contexts
summary:
Deploying agentic AI in regulated contexts requires principled reasoning about two design dimensions: agency (what the system can do) and autonomy (how much it acts without human involvement). Though often treated independently, they are coupled: at higher autonomy, human error correction is less available, so reliable operation requires constraining agency accordingly; compliance requirements reinforce this by mandating human involvement as action consequences grow. Yet no established approach addresses them jointly, leaving practitioners without a principled basis for reasoning about oversight, action consequences, and error correction.
  This work introduces a two-dimensional design space in which both dimensions are organised into five operational levels, making the coupling explicit and navigable. Autonomy ranges from human-commanded operation (L1) to fully autonomous monitoring (L5); agency ranges from reasoning over supplied context (L1) to committed writes to authoritative records (L5). Building on this space, we propose six architectural tactics--checkpoints, escalation, multi-agent delegation, tool provisioning, tool fencing, and write staging--for adjusting a deployment's position within it. The tactics are grounded in two worked examples from public-sector contexts, illustrating how they apply under realistic compliance constraints. We further examine five deployment parameters--model capability, agent architecture, tool fidelity, workflow bottlenecks, and evaluation--that shape what is achievable at any configuration independently of agency and autonomy. Together, the design space, tactics, and deployment parameters provide a shared vocabulary for principled, compliance-aware agentic AI design in which responsibility, auditability, and reversibility are explicit design considerations rather than properties that must be retrofitted after deployment.

AI.tldr: Introduces a two-dimensional design space (agency × autonomy) with five operational levels each, plus six architectural tactics for deploying agentic AI in regulated contexts, making compliance considerations like responsibility, auditability, and reversibility explicit from the start.
AI.motivation: Deploying agentic AI in regulated contexts requires principled reasoning about agency and autonomy, which are coupled but currently treated independently. No established approach addresses them jointly, leaving practitioners without a principled basis for reasoning about oversight, action consequences, and error correction.
AI.method: Proposes a 5×5 design space (autonomy L1-L5, agency L1-L5), six architectural tactics (checkpoints, escalation, multi-agent delegation, tool provisioning, tool fencing, write staging), and five deployment parameters (model capability, agent architecture, tool fidelity, workflow bottlenecks, evaluation). Grounded in two public-sector worked examples.
AI.result: A shared vocabulary and structured framework for compliance-aware agentic AI design, demonstrated through realistic public-sector examples under compliance constraints.
AI.conclusion: Responsibility, auditability, and reversibility should be explicit design considerations rather than retrofitted properties, enabled by the joint treatment of agency and autonomy.

title: Large Language Models as Amortized Pareto-Front Generators for Constrained Bi-Objective Convex Optimization
summary: Generating feasible Pareto fronts for constrained bi-objective continuous optimization is central to multi-criteria decision-making. Existing methods usually rely on iterative scalarization, evolutionary search, or problem-specific solvers, requiring repeated optimization for each instance. We introduce DIPS, an end-to-end framework that fine-tunes large language models as amortized Pareto-front generators for constrained bi-objective convex optimization. Given a textual problem description, DIPS directly outputs an ordered set of feasible continuous decision vectors approximating the Pareto front. To make continuous optimization compatible with autoregressive language modeling, DIPS combines a compact discretization scheme, Numerically Grounded Token Initialization for new numerical tokens, and Three-Phase Curriculum Optimization, which progressively aligns structural validity, feasibility, and Pareto-front quality. Across five families of constrained bi-objective convex problems, a fine-tuned 7B-parameter model achieves normalized hypervolume ratios of 95.29% to 98.18% relative to reference fronts. With vLLM-accelerated inference, DIPS solves one instance in as little as 0.16 seconds and outperforms general-purpose and reasoning LLM baselines under the evaluated setting. These results suggest that LLMs can serve as effective amortized generators for continuous Pareto-front approximation.

AI.tldr: DIPS fine-tunes LLMs to directly generate continuous Pareto fronts for constrained bi-objective convex optimization from text descriptions, achieving 95-98% normalized hypervolume ratios with inference speeds of 0.16 seconds per instance.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for generating Pareto fronts in constrained bi-objective optimization require repeated optimization per instance via scalarization, evolutionary algorithms, or specialized solvers, lacking an amortized approach that can directly produce solutions without iterative computation.
AI.method: DIPS fine-tunes a 7B-parameter LLM with three components: (1) a compact discretization scheme to represent continuous decision vectors as tokens, (2) Numerically Grounded Token Initialization for new numerical tokens, and (3) Three-Phase Curriculum Optimization that progressively trains the model on structural validity, feasibility, and Pareto-front quality.
AI.result: Across five constrained bi-objective convex problem families, DIPS achieves normalized hypervolume ratios of 95.29% to 98.18% relative to reference fronts, with vLLM-accelerated inference of 0.16 seconds per instance, outperforming general-purpose and reasoning LLM baselines.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as effective amortized generators for continuous Pareto-front approximation, providing a fast, single-pass alternative to traditional iterative optimization methods in multi-criteria decision-making.

title: Adaptive Multi-Round Allocation with Stochastic Arrivals
summary: We study a sequential resource allocation problem motivated by adaptive network recruitment, in which a limited budget of identical resources must be allocated over multiple rounds to individuals with stochastic referral capacity. Successful referrals endogenously generate future decision opportunities while allocating additional resources to an individual exhibits diminishing returns. We first show that the single-round allocation problem admits an exact greedy solution based on marginal survival probabilities. In the multi-round setting, the resulting Bellman recursion is intractable due to the stochastic, high-dimensional evolution of the frontier. To address this, we introduce a population-level surrogate value function that depends only on the remaining budget and frontier size. This surrogate enables an exact dynamic program via truncated probability generating functions, yielding a planning algorithm with polynomial complexity in the total budget. We further analyze robustness under model misspecification, proving a multi-round error bound that decomposes into a tight single-round frontier error and a population-level transition error. Finally, we evaluate our method on real-world inspired recruitment scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a sequential resource allocation problem motivated by adaptive network recruitment, where limited identical resources are allocated over multiple rounds to individuals with stochastic referral capacity. The authors propose a polynomial-complexity planning algorithm using a population-level surrogate value function and truncated probability generating functions, and provide robustness guarantees under model misspecification.
AI.motivation: To address the intractable Bellman recursion in multi-round resource allocation with stochastic referrals and diminishing returns, by developing a tractable surrogate approach with polynomial complexity.
AI.method: The authors first derive an exact greedy solution for the single-round case using marginal survival probabilities. For the multi-round setting, they introduce a population-level surrogate value function depending only on remaining budget and frontier size, enabling an exact dynamic program via truncated probability generating functions with polynomial complexity in total budget. They also derive a multi-round error bound decomposing into single-round frontier error and population-level transition error.
AI.result: A planning algorithm with polynomial complexity in the total budget is achieved for the multi-round setting. A multi-round error bound under model misspecification is proven, decomposing into a tight single-round frontier error and a population-level transition error. The method is evaluated on real-world inspired recruitment scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed surrogate-based approach successfully makes the otherwise intractable multi-round resource allocation problem computationally feasible while maintaining robustness guarantees, with practical applicability to adaptive network recruitment.

title: To Whom Do Language Models Align? Measuring Principal Hierarchies Under High-Stakes Competing Demands
summary: Language models deployed in high-stakes professional settings face conflicting demands from users, institutional authorities, and professional norms. How models act when these demands conflict reveals a principal hierarchy -- an implicit ordering over competing stakeholders that determines, for instance, whether a medical AI receiving a cost-reduction directive from a hospital administrator complies at the expense of evidence-based care, or refuses because professional standards require it. Across 7,136 scenarios in legal and medical domains, we test ten frontier models and find that models frequently fail to adhere to professional standards during task execution, such as drafting, when user instructions conflict with those standards -- despite adequately upholding them when users seek advisory guidance. We further find that the hierarchies between user, authority, and professional standards exhibited by these models are unstable across medical and legal contexts and inconsistent across model families. When failing to follow professional standards, the primary failure mechanism is knowledge omission: models that demonstrably possess relevant knowledge produce harmful outputs without surfacing conflicting knowledge. In a particularly troubling instance, we find that a reasoning model recognizes the relevant knowledge in its reasoning trace -- e.g., that a drug has been withdrawn -- yet suppresses this in the user-facing answer and proceeds to recommend the drug under authority pressure anyway. Inconsistent alignment across task framing, domain, and model families suggests that current alignment methods, including published alignment hierarchies, are unlikely to be robust when models are deployed in high-stakes professional settings.

AI.tldr: Frontier language models fail to consistently adhere to professional standards over user/authority demands in high-stakes legal and medical settings, exhibiting unstable stakeholder hierarchies and often suppressing known knowledge under pressure, suggesting current alignment methods are insufficient for professional deployment.
AI.motivation: To investigate how language models navigate conflicting demands from users, institutional authorities, and professional norms in high-stakes professional settings, and to characterize the implicit principal hierarchy that determines model behavior when these interests conflict.
AI.method: Tested ten frontier models across 7,136 scenarios in legal and medical domains, systematically varying task framing (advisory vs. execution) and introducing conflicts between user instructions, institutional authority directives, and professional standards.
AI.result: Models frequently fail to uphold professional standards during task execution despite doing so in advisory contexts; hierarchies between stakeholders are unstable across domains and model families; primary failure mechanism is knowledge omission where known information is suppressed; reasoning models may recognize relevant knowledge in internal traces but suppress it in final answers under authority pressure.
AI.conclusion: Current alignment methods, including published alignment hierarchies, are unlikely to produce robust behavior when models are deployed in high-stakes professional settings due to inconsistent alignment across task framing, domain, and model families.

title: Rollout Cards: A Reproducibility Standard for Agent Research
summary: Reproducibility problems that have long affected machine learning and reinforcement learning are now surfacing in agent research: papers compare systems by reported scores while leaving the rollout records behind those scores difficult to inspect. For agentic tasks, this matters because the same behaviour can receive different reported scores when evaluations select different parts of a rollout or apply different reporting rules. In a structured audit of 50 popular training and evaluation repositories, we find that none report how many runs failed, errored, or were skipped alongside headline scores. We also document 37 cases where reporting rules can change task-success rates, cost/token accounting, or timing measurements for fixed evidence, sometimes dramatically. We treat rollout records, not reported scores, as the unit of reproducibility for agent research. We introduce rollout cards: publication bundles that preserve the rollout record and declare the views, reporting rules, and drops manifests behind reported scores. We validate rollout cards in two settings. First, four partial public releases in tool safety, multi-agent systems, theorem proving, and search let us compute analyses their original reports did not include. Second, re-grading preserved benchmark outputs across short-answer, code-generation, and tool-use tasks shows that changing only the reporting rule can change reported scores by 20.9 absolute percentage points and, in some cases, invert rankings of frontier models. We release a reference implementation integrated into Ergon, an open-source reinforcement learning gym, and publicly publish Ergon-produced rollout-card exports for benchmarks spanning tool use, software engineering, web interaction, multi-agent coordination, safety, and search to support future research.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies reproducibility issues in agent research caused by opaque rollout records and reporting rules. A structured audit of 50 repositories found none report failures or errors alongside scores. The authors propose "rollout cards"—publication bundles preserving full rollout records with declared reporting rules—and validate them across multiple domains, showing reporting rules can alter scores by up to 20.9 absolute points and invert rankings. A reference implementation is released as part of the Ergon RL gym.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility problems from ML/RL now affect agent research, where reported scores obscure rollout details. The same behavior can yield different scores depending on which parts of a rollout are evaluated or how reporting rules are applied, making it difficult to inspect and reproduce results.
AI.method: A structured audit of 50 popular training/evaluation repositories; documentation of 37 reporting-rule cases affecting task-success rates, cost/token accounting, and timing; proposal of "rollout cards" as publication bundles preserving rollout records with declared views, rules, and drops manifests; validation via four partial public releases and re-grading tasks across short-answer, code-generation, and tool-use domains.
AI.result: None of the 50 audited repositories report run failures, errors, or skips alongside headline scores. Reporting rules can change reported scores by up to 20.9 absolute percentage points and invert frontier-model rankings. Re-grading preserved benchmark outputs confirmed this sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Rollout records, not reported scores, should be treated as the unit of reproducibility for agent research. Rollout cards enable transparent, reproducible evaluation. The public release of Ergon-integrated rollout-card exports supports future research and adoption.

title: BoolXLLM: LLM-Assisted Explainability for Boolean Models
summary:
Interpretable machine learning aims to provide transparent models whose decision-making processes can be readily understood by humans. Recent advances in rule-based approaches, such as expressive Boolean formulas (BoolXAI), offer faithful and compact representations of model behavior. However, for non-technical stakeholders, main challenges remain in practice: (i) selecting semantically meaningful features and (ii) translating formal logical rules into accessible explanations.
  In this work, we propose BoolXLLM , as a hybrid framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) into the end-to-end pipeline of Boolean rule learning. We augment BoolXAI , an expressive Boolean rule-based classifier, with LLMs at three critical stages: (1) feature selection, where LLMs guide the identification of domain-relevant variables; (2) threshold recommendation, where LLMs propose semantically meaningful discretization strategies for numerical features; and (3) rule compression and interpretation, where Boolean rules are translated into natural language explanations at both global and local levels.
  This integration bridges formal, faithful explanations with human-understandable narratives. This allows build an explainable AI system that is both theoretically grounded and accessible to non-experts. Early empirical results demonstrate that LLM-assisted pipelines improve interpretability while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our work highlights the promise of combining symbolic reasoning with language-based models for human-centered explainability.

AI.tldr: BoolXLLM integrates LLMs into Boolean rule learning (BoolXAI) at three stages—feature selection, threshold recommendation, and rule-to-text translation—to produce explanations that are both formally faithful and accessible to non-experts.
AI.motivation: Existing rule-based interpretable models (e.g., BoolXAI) produce faithful and compact formal rules, but non-technical stakeholders struggle with selecting semantically meaningful features and translating logical rules into understandable explanations.
AI.method: A hybrid framework that augments BoolXAI with LLMs at three stages: (1) domain-relevant feature selection, (2) semantically meaningful threshold discretization for numerical features, and (3) compression and translation of Boolean rules into natural language explanations at global and local levels.
AI.result: Early empirical results show LLM-assisted pipelines improve interpretability while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: The integration of symbolic reasoning (Boolean rules) with language-based models (LLMs) is a promising direction for human-centered explainability, bridging formal faithfulness with accessible narratives.

title: MM-OptBench: A Solver-Grounded Benchmark for Multimodal Optimization Modeling
summary: Optimization modeling translates real decision-making problems into mathematical optimization models and solver-executable implementations. Although language models are increasingly used to generate optimization formulations and solver code, existing benchmarks are almost entirely text-only. This omits many optimization-modeling tasks that arise in operational practice, where requirements are described in text but instance information is conveyed through visual artifacts such as tables, graphs, maps, schedules, and dashboards. We introduce multimodal optimization modeling, a benchmark setting in which models must construct both a mathematical formulation and executable solver code from a text-and-visual problem specification. To evaluate this setting, we develop a solver-grounded framework that generates structured optimization instances, verifies each with an exact solver, and builds both the model-facing inputs and hidden reference files from the same verified source. We instantiate the framework as MM-OptBench, a benchmark of 780 solver-verified instances spanning 6 optimization families, 26 subcategories, and 3 structural difficulty levels. We evaluate 9 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), including 6 frontier general-purpose models and 3 math-specialized models, with aggregate, family-level, difficulty-level, and failure-mode analyses. The results show that the task remains far from solved: the best two models reach 52.1% and 51.3% pass@1, while on average across the six general-purpose MLLMs, pass@1 is 43.4% on easy instances and 15.9% on hard instances. All three math-specialized MLLMs solve 0/780 instances. Failure attribution shows that errors arise both when extracting instance data from text and visuals and when turning extracted data into solver-correct formulations and code. MM-OptBench provides a testbed for solver-grounded, decision-oriented multimodal intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MM-OptBench, a multimodal optimization modeling benchmark requiring models to generate mathematical formulations and executable solver code from text-and-visual problem specifications. The benchmark consists of 780 solver-verified instances across 6 optimization families. Evaluation of 9 MLLMs shows the task remains challenging—best models achieve ~52% pass@1, with math-specialized models solving 0/780 instances.
AI.motivation: Existing optimization modeling benchmarks are entirely text-only, ignoring real-world operational scenarios where instance information is conveyed through visual artifacts (tables, graphs, maps, schedules, dashboards). This gap prevents evaluation of multimodal capabilities for decision-oriented optimization tasks.
AI.method: The authors develop a solver-grounded framework that generates structured optimization instances, verifies each with an exact solver, and creates both model-facing inputs (text+visual) and hidden reference files from the same verified source. The benchmark MM-OptBench includes 780 instances across 6 optimization families, 26 subcategories, and 3 difficulty levels.
AI.result: Best two models achieve 52.1% and 51.3% pass@1; average pass@1 across six general-purpose MLLMs is 43.4% on easy and 15.9% on hard instances. All three math-specialized MLLMs solve 0/780 instances. Errors arise both in extracting instance data from text/visuals and in converting extracted data into solver-correct formulations/code.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal optimization modeling remains far from solved. MM-OptBench provides a testbed for evaluating solver-grounded, decision-oriented multimodal intelligence, highlighting the need for improvements in both multimodal data extraction and code generation for optimization.

title: Do Enterprise Systems Need Learned World Models? The Importance of Context to Infer Dynamics
summary: World models enable agents to anticipate the effects of their actions by internalizing environment dynamics. In enterprise systems, however, these dynamics are often defined by tenant-specific business logic that varies across deployments and evolves over time, making models trained on historical transitions brittle under deployment shift. We ask a question the world-models literature has not addressed: when the rules can be read at inference time, does an agent still need to learn them? We argue, and demonstrate empirically, that in settings where transition dynamics are configurable and readable, runtime discovery complements offline training by grounding predictions in the active system instance. We propose enterprise discovery agents, which recover relevant transition dynamics at runtime by reading the system's configuration rather than relying solely on internalized representations. We introduce CascadeBench, a reasoning-focused benchmark for enterprise cascade prediction that adopts the evaluation methodology of World of Workflows on diverse synthetic environments, and use it together with deployment-shift evaluation to show that offline-trained world models can perform well in-distribution but degrade as dynamics change, whereas discovery-based agents are more robust under shift by grounding their predictions in the current instance. Our findings suggest that, in configurable enterprise environments, agents should not rely solely on fixed internalized dynamics, but should incorporate mechanisms for discovering relevant transition logic at runtime.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces enterprise discovery agents that read runtime system configurations to predict transitions, rather than relying solely on offline-trained world models, and shows they are more robust to deployment shifts where business logic varies across instances.
AI.motivation: Enterprise world models fail under deployment shift because tenant-specific business logic varies across deployments and evolves over time, yet existing world-model literature assumes static dynamics learned offline.
AI.method: The authors propose enterprise discovery agents that recover transition dynamics at runtime by reading system configuration, and introduce CascadeBench—a reasoning-focused benchmark for enterprise cascade prediction built on the World of Workflows evaluation methodology across diverse synthetic environments.
AI.result: Offline-trained world models perform well in-distribution but degrade under deployment shift, whereas discovery-based agents remain robust by grounding predictions in the current system instance.
AI.conclusion: In configurable enterprise environments, agents should not rely solely on fixed internalized dynamics but should incorporate mechanisms for discovering relevant transition logic at runtime.

title: MolDeTox: Evaluating Language Model's Stepwise Fragment Editing for Molecular Detoxification
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Language Models (VLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in various scientific domain. In particular, these advances have opened new opportunities in drug discovery, where the ability to understand and modify molecular structures is critical for optimizing drug properties such as efficacy and toxicity. However, existing models and benchmarks often overlook toxicity-related challenges, focusing primarily on general property optimization without adequately addressing safety concerns. In addition, even existing toxicity repair benchmarks suffer from limited data diversity, low structural validity of generated molecules, and heavy reliance on proxy models for toxicity assessment. To address these limitations, we propose MolDeTox, a novel benchmark for molecular detoxification, designed to enable fine-grained and reliable evaluation of toxicity-aware molecular optimization across stepwise tasks. We evaluate a wide range of general-purpose LLMs and VLMs under diverse settings, and demonstrate that understanding and generating molecules at the fragment-level improves structural validity and enhances the quality of generated molecules. Moreover, through detailed task-level performance analysis, MolDeTox provides an interpretable benchmark that enables a deeper understanding of the detoxification process. Our dataset is available at : https://huggingface.co/datasets/MolDeTox/MolDeTox

AI.tldr: MolDeTox is a new benchmark for molecular detoxification that evaluates LLMs and VLMs on toxicity-aware molecular optimization, demonstrating that fragment-level understanding improves structural validity and detoxification quality.
AI.motivation: Existing models and benchmarks for drug discovery overlook toxicity-related challenges, suffer from limited data diversity, low structural validity of generated molecules, and heavy reliance on proxy models for toxicity assessment.
AI.method: The authors propose MolDeTox, a benchmark featuring fine-grained, stepwise tasks for toxicity-aware molecular optimization, and evaluate general-purpose LLMs and VLMs under diverse settings with fragment-level molecular understanding and generation.
AI.result: Fragment-level understanding and generation improves structural validity and enhances the quality of generated molecules compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: MolDeTox provides an interpretable benchmark for molecular detoxification, enabling deeper understanding of the detoxification process through detailed task-level performance analysis.

title: Goal-Oriented Reasoning for RAG-based Memory in Conversational Agentic LLM Systems
summary: LLM-based conversational AI agents struggle to maintain coherent behavior over long horizons due to limited context. While RAG-based approaches are increasingly adopted to overcome this limitation by storing interactions in external memory modules and performing retrieval from them, their effectiveness in answering challenging questions (e.g., multi-hop, commonsense) ultimately depends on the agent's ability to reason over the retrieved information. However, existing methods typically retrieve memory based on semantic similarity to the raw user utterance, which lacks explicit reasoning about missing intermediate facts and often returns evidence that is irrelevant or insufficient for grounded reasoning. In this work, we introduce Goal-Mem, a goal-oriented reasoning framework for RAG-based agentic memory that performs explicit backward chaining from the user's utterance as a goal. Rather than progressively expanding from retrieved context, Goal-Mem decomposes each goal into atomic subgoals, performs targeted memory retrieval to satisfy each subgoal, and iteratively identifies what information from memory should be retrieved when intermediate goals cannot be resolved. We formalize this process in Natural Language Logic, a logical system that combines the verifiability of reasoning provided by FOL with the expressivity of natural language. Through extensive experiments on two datasets and comparing to nine strong memory baselines, we show that Goal-Mem consistently improves performance, particularly on tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning and implicit inference.

AI.tldr: Goal-Mem is a goal-oriented reasoning framework for RAG-based agentic memory that uses backward chaining from user utterances, decomposing goals into atomic subgoals with targeted retrieval, formalized in Natural Language Logic, outperforming nine baselines especially on multi-hop reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM-based conversational agents struggle with coherent long-horizon behavior due to limited context; existing RAG-based memory methods retrieve based on semantic similarity to raw user utterances, lacking explicit reasoning about missing intermediate facts, often returning irrelevant or insufficient evidence for grounded reasoning.
AI.method: Goal-Mem performs explicit backward chaining from user utterances as goals, decomposing each goal into atomic subgoals, conducting targeted memory retrieval per subgoal, and iteratively identifying what to retrieve when intermediate goals cannot be resolved. The process is formalized in Natural Language Logic, combining FOL verifiability with natural language expressivity.
AI.result: Experiments on two datasets against nine strong memory baselines show Goal-Mem consistently improves performance, especially on multi-hop reasoning and implicit inference tasks.
AI.conclusion: Goal-oriented backward chaining with subgoal decomposition and targeted retrieval is more effective than semantic similarity-based retrieval for reasoning over agentic memory, particularly for complex reasoning tasks.

title: No Action Without a NOD: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Architecture for Reliable Service Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have increasingly advanced service applications, such as booking flight tickets. However, these service agents suffer from unreliability in long-horizon tasks, as they often produce policy violations, tool hallucinations, and misaligned actions, which greatly impedes their real-world deployment. To address these challenges, we propose NOD (Navigator-Operator-Director), a heterogeneous multi-agent architecture for service agents. Instead of maintaining task state implicitly in dialogue context as in prior work, we externalize a structured Global State to enable explicit task state tracking and consistent decision-making by the Navigator. Besides, we introduce selective external oversight before critical actions, allowing an independent Director agent to verify execution and intervene when necessary. As such, NOD effectively mitigates error propagation and unsafe behavior in long-horizon tasks. Experiments on $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate that NOD achieves higher task success rates and critical action precision over baselines. More importantly, NOD improves the reliability of service agents by reducing policy violations, tool hallucinations, and user-intent misalignment.

AI.tldr: NOD (Navigator-Operator-Director) is a heterogeneous multi-agent architecture for LLM service agents that externalizes task state into a structured Global State and introduces selective external oversight before critical actions, significantly improving reliability in long-horizon tasks by reducing policy violations, tool hallucinations, and misaligned actions.
AI.motivation: LLM service agents suffer from unreliability in long-horizon tasks due to policy violations, tool hallucinations, and misaligned actions, impeding real-world deployment.
AI.method: NOD employs a heterogeneous multi-agent architecture with three roles: Navigator (explicit task state tracking via externalized structured Global State), Operator (execution), and Director (selective external oversight before critical actions to verify and intervene).
AI.result: On τ^2-Bench, NOD achieves higher task success rates and critical action precision over baselines, while reducing policy violations, tool hallucinations, and user-intent misalignment.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing structured state representation and incorporating selective oversight improves reliability and safety of LLM-based service agents for long-horizon tasks.

title: Why Conclusions Diverge from the Same Observations: Formalizing World-Model Non-Identifiability via an Inference
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Extended English version of a paper accepted for presentation at JSAI 2026
summary: When people share the same documents and observations yet reach different conclusions, the disagreement often shifts into a judgment that the other party is cognitively defective, irrational, or acting in bad faith. This paper argues that such divergence is better described as a form of non-identifiability inherent in inference and learning, rather than as a defect of the other party. We organize the phenomenon into two levels: (i) $θ$-level non-identifiability, where conclusions diverge under the same world model $W$ because inference settings differ; and (ii) $W$-level non-identifiability, where repeated use of an inference setting $θ$ biases data exposure and update rules, causing the learned world model $W$ itself to diverge. We introduce an inference profile $θ= (R, E, S, D)$, consisting of Reference, Exploration, Stabilization, and Horizon, and show how outputs can split even for the same observation $o$ and the same $W$. We further explain why disagreements tend to project onto a small number of bases -- abstract versus concrete, externalizability, and order versus freedom -- as a consequence of general constraints on learning systems: computational, observational, and coordination constraints. Finally, we relate the framework to deep representation learning, including representation hierarchy, latent-state estimation, and regularization-exploration trade-offs, and illustrate the framework through a case study on AI regulation debates.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that disagreements arising from shared observations and documents are better understood as a form of non-identifiability inherent in inference and learning, rather than as cognitive defects of the other party. It organizes this into θ-level non-identifiability (divergent conclusions under the same world model due to different inference settings) and W-level non-identifiability (repeated inference biases causing divergence in the world model itself), introduces an inference profile θ=(R,E,S,D), and explains why disagreements project onto a few fundamental bases due to computational, observational, and coordination constraints.
AI.motivation: To reframe interpersonal and collective disagreements not as evidence of irrationality or bad faith, but as a natural consequence of non-identifiability in inference and learning systems, thereby reducing adversarial interpretations and fostering more constructive discourse.
AI.method: The paper conceptualizes disagreement through two levels of non-identifiability (θ-level and W-level), defines an inference profile θ=(Reference, Exploration, Stabilization, Horizon), and links the phenomenon to deep representation learning concepts and general constraints on learning systems.
AI.result: The framework shows that even with identical observations and same world model, different inference profiles lead to divergent conclusions; over time, these differences can cause divergence in the learned world models themselves. Disagreements naturally collapse onto a few basis dimensions due to computational, observational, and coordination constraints.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement should be viewed as a form of non-identifiability rather than cognitive defect, and the framework provides a systematic way to analyze such divergences across inference settings, world models, and structural constraints, as illustrated through AI regulation debates.

title: Missingness-MDPs: Bridging the Theory of Missing Data and POMDPs
summary: We introduce missingness-MDPs (miss-MDPs), a novel subclass of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) that incorporates the theory of missing data. A miss-MDP is a POMDP whose observation function is a missingness function, specifying the probability that individual state features are missing (i.e., unobserved) at a time step. The literature distinguishes three canonical missingness types: missing (1) completely at random (MCAR), (2) at random (MAR), and (3) not at random (MNAR). Our planning problem is to compute near-optimal policies for a miss-MDP with an unknown missingness function, given a dataset of action-observation trajectories. Achieving such optimality guarantees for policies requires learning the missingness function from data, which is infeasible for general POMDPs. To overcome this challenge, we exploit the structural properties of different missingness types to derive probably approximately correct (PAC) algorithms for learning the missingness function. These algorithms yield an approximate but fully specified miss-MDP that we solve using off-the-shelf planning methods. We prove that, with high probability, the resulting policies are epsilon-optimal in the true miss-MDP. Empirical results confirm the theory and demonstrate superior performance of our approach over two model-free POMDP methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces missingness-MDPs (miss-MDPs), a subclass of POMDPs that models missing data in state features. It provides PAC algorithms to learn the unknown missingness function (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) from data, enabling the computation of near-optimal policies with theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Standard POMDPs assume all observations are available, but in real-world applications, state features are often missing (e.g., sensor failures, incomplete records). The paper aims to bridge POMDP planning with missing data theory to handle such settings with formal guarantees.
AI.method: The authors define miss-MDPs, a POMDP subclass where the observation function is a missingness function. They exploit structural properties of three missingness types (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) to design PAC learning algorithms for the missingness function from trajectory data, then solve the resulting approximate miss-MDP using off-the-shelf planners.
AI.result: The proposed PAC algorithms yield high-probability epsilon-optimal policies in the true miss-MDP. Empirical results show superior performance over two model-free POMDP baselines.
AI.conclusion: miss-MDPs provide a principled framework for planning under missing data with provable guarantees, outperforming model-free approaches that ignore the missingness structure.

title: How Useful Is Cross-Domain Generalization for Training LLM Monitors?
summary: Using prompted language models as classifiers enables classification in domains with limited training data, but misses some of the robustness and performance benefits that fine-tuning can bring. We study whether training on multiple classification tasks, each with its own prompt, improves performance on new domains with new classification prompts. We show that such training partially generalizes to adjacent domains, improving classification performance on tasks that are unseen during training. However, we identify specific edge cases where the fine-tuned models fail to follow prompts, such as when the classification prompt changes completely while the data domain remains the same as during training. We show that classification training can be mixed with general instruction following training, and that (when done well) such training keeps the benefits of classification training and mitigates its generalization failures. Surprisingly, we see that this no-thinking supervised classification training can generalize to with-thinking classification and summarization, suggesting that no-thinking classification training might be instrumentally useful in building other kinds of classifiers and monitoring systems.

AI.tldr: Training on multiple prompted classification tasks improves generalization to new domains but can fail when prompts change; mixing with instruction-following training mitigates these failures, and surprisingly, no-thinking classification training generalizes to with-thinking tasks.
AI.motivation: To improve classification performance in domains with limited training data by combining the benefits of prompt-based learning and fine-tuning across multiple tasks.
AI.method: Fine-tune language models on multiple classification tasks with different prompts, evaluate generalization to unseen domains/prompts, and mix classification training with general instruction-following training.
AI.result: Multi-task prompt-based classification training partially generalizes to adjacent domains but fails when prompts change (e.g., same domain, new prompt). Mixing with instruction-following training preserves classification benefits while reducing generalization failures. No-thinking classification training surprisingly generalizes to with-thinking classification and summarization tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-task classification training with prompts can generalize to new domains but has edge-case failures; these can be mitigated by mixing with instruction-following training, and no-thinking classification training may be instrumentally useful for building other classifiers and monitoring systems.

title: NARA: Anchor-Conditioned Relation-Aware Contextualization of Heterogeneous Geoentities
summary: Geospatial foundation models have primarily focused on raster data such as satellite imagery, where self-supervised learning has been widely studied. Vector geospatial data instead represent the world as discrete geoentities with explicit geometry, semantics, and structured spatial relations, including metric proximity and topological relationships. These relations jointly determine how entities interact within space, yet existing representation learning methods remain fragmented, often restricted to specific geometry types or partial spatial relations, limiting their ability to capture unified spatial context across heterogeneous geoentities. We propose NARA (Neural Anchor-conditioned Relation-Aware representation learning), a self-supervised framework for vector geoentities. NARA learns context-dependent representations by jointly modeling semantics, geometry, and spatial relations within a unified framework and captures relational spatial structure beyond proximity alone, enabling rich contextualized representations across heterogeneous geoentities of points, polylines, and polygons. Evaluation on building function classification, traffic speed prediction, and next point-of-interest recommendation shows consistent improvements over prior methods, highlighting the benefit of unified relational modeling for vector geospatial data.

AI.tldr: NARA is a self-supervised framework for vector geospatial data that jointly models semantics, geometry, and spatial relations (proximity + topology) across heterogeneous geoentities (points, polylines, polygons), outperforming prior methods on building classification, traffic prediction, and POI recommendation.
AI.motivation: Existing representation learning for vector geospatial data is fragmented, focusing on specific geometry types or partial spatial relations, failing to capture the unified spatial context across heterogeneous geoentities.
AI.method: NARA (Neural Anchor-conditioned Relation-Aware representation learning) is a self-supervised framework that jointly models semantics, geometry, and spatial relations (metric proximity and topological relationships) for vector geoentities of any type (points, polylines, polygons).
AI.result: Consistent improvements over prior methods on building function classification, traffic speed prediction, and next point-of-interest recommendation.
AI.conclusion: Unified relational modeling of semantics, geometry, and spatial relations significantly benefits vector geospatial data representation learning.

title: Executable Agentic Memory for GUI Agent
summary: Modern GUI agents typically rely on a model-centric and step-wise interaction paradigm, where LLMs must re-interpret the UI and re-decide actions at every screen, which is fragile in long-horizon tasks. In this paper, we propose Executable Agentic Memory (EAM), a structured Knowledge Graph (KG) that shifts GUI planning from free-form generation to a robust retrieval-and-execution process. Our approach includes a sample-efficient memory construction pipeline using state-aware DFS and action-group mining to compress multi-step routines.
